Things that falsely raise DAS28: fibromyalgia and central sensitisation (high TJC and patient global), OA, depression, high ESR from age, anaemia or paraprotein. Things that falsely lower it: IL-6 or JAK blockade suppressing CRP and ESR (DAS28 overestimates remission on tocilizumab, so prefer CDAI). Score Remission Low Moderate High DAS28 <2.6 ≤3.2 ≤5.1 >5.1 ≤3.3 ≤11 ≤26 >26 SDAI ≤2.8 ≤10 ≤22 >22 CDAI Boolean remission: TJC, SJC, CRP (mg/dL) and patient global (0–10) each ≤1; patient global ≤2 is now accepted. SDAI = TJC28 + SJC28 + PtGA + PhGA + CRP (mg/dL); CDAI omits CRP, so it can be calculated at the bedside. DAS28 ignores the feet. Once the target is sustained, review every 3–6 months. Radiographs of hands and feet yearly in the first years. Function is measured with HAQ-DI (0–3).

question: A woman with seropositive RA has taken methotrexate 10 mg weekly for 3 months (DAS28-CRP 4.8), or takes 20 mg weekly with persistent nausea and an inadequate response. What should happen before methotrexate is abandoned? Also tested as: A patient taking methotrexate 20 mg weekly has persistent nausea and an inadequate response despite good adherence. Renal and liver function are normal. What is the most reasonable step before abandoning methotrexate?

options.A: Add an IL-17 or IL-23 inhibitor
options.B: At least 1 month before conception, continuing folic acid
options.C: Withhold methotrexate, discuss with the rheumatology team and repeat the tests promptly
options.D: Optimise it: increase to 20–25 mg weekly, switch to subcutaneous administration (better bioavailability and tolerability), optimise folic acid and reassess within 1–3 months
options.E: Consider tapering adalimumab by dose reduction or interval extension while continuing methotrexate

explanation: Methotrexate should be titrated rapidly to an optimal dose (usually 20–25 mg weekly, or 0.3 mg/kg) before it can be judged to have failed. Subcutaneous administration improves bioavailability and often reduces gastrointestinal intolerance. Apparent failure that is not true failure: non-adherence (ask about "methotrexate day" omissions and intolerance), inadequate dose or duration (<3 months at target dose), non-inflammatory pain, wrong diagnosis (PsA, CPPD, PMR, CTD). Intolerance strategies: split oral dose 12 hours apart, evening dosing, antiemetic, higher folate, SC route. If still not at target after 3–6 months on optimised methotrexate, escalate to a b/tsDMARD (next entry). Combination csDMARD therapy (triple therapy) is an alternative strategy where access to biologics is limited (and in NICE pathways), but it adds toxicity.

question: A patient with seropositive RA remains active (DAS28-CRP about 4.6) despite 6 months of optimised methotrexate off glucocorticoids. What is the next step, and how does the choice change in a 68-year-old current smoker with a previous MI? Also tested as: A 68-year-old man with RA has active disease despite optimised methotrexate. He is a current smoker and had a myocardial infarction 3 years ago. Which is the most appropriate next treatment?

options.A: Add a biologic DMARD, or consider a JAK inhibitor after risk assessment; in older patients, smokers or those with CV, malignancy or VTE risk, choose a biologic (such as a TNF inhibitor or abatacept)
options.B: Consider tapering adalimumab by dose reduction or interval extension while continuing methotrexate
options.C: Individualised treatment with respiratory input, based on the lung pattern, its progression and the joint disease
options.D: Optimise it: increase to 20–25 mg weekly, switch to subcutaneous administration (better bioavailability and tolerability), optimise folic acid and reassess within 1–3 months
options.E: Methotrexate with short-term glucocorticoid bridging, started as soon as RA is diagnosed, ideally within

explanation: If the target is not reached with an optimised methotrexate strategy after 3–6 months, a bDMARD should be added; a JAK inhibitor may be considered after weighing cardiovascular, malignancy and thromboembolic risk. JAK inhibitors should be used only if no suitable alternative exists in patients aged 65 or over, current or long-term past smokers, or those with cardiovascular, malignancy or VTE risk factors. Access may also depend on local commissioning criteria. Choosing the next drug by comorbidity: - Heart failure (NYHA III–IV) or demyelination: avoid TNFi. - Prior diverticulitis or perforation: avoid IL-6R inhibitors; caution with JAKi. - Recent malignancy or lymphoma: rituximab is preferred. - Recurrent serious infection: abatacept or rituximab (check IgG). - Pregnancy plans: certolizumab or another TNFi. - Cannot take methotrexate: IL-6R inhibitor or JAKi as monotherapy. - ILD: abatacept or rituximab. - Seronegative disease: rituximab works less well. - Obesity: IV or weight-based dosing (tocilizumab IV, infliximab), or a non-TNF drug. The current EULAR position is that methotrexate failure is itself a poor prognostic factor, so there is no longer a separate step of trying a second csDMARD in patients without poor prognostic factors. NICE access criteria in England still specify DAS28 thresholds (>5.1 for severe disease, and 3.2–5.1 for moderate disease for some drugs). Biosimilars are the first choice where available. Combine with methotrexate where possible.

question: A 58-year-old woman has been in sustained DAS28 remission for 18 months on methotrexate 15 mg weekly and adalimumab 40 mg fortnightly. Glucocorticoids were stopped 2 years ago. She asks about reducing medication. What is the most appropriate advice?

options.A: Switch to another TNF inhibitor or to a drug with a different mechanism
options.B: Optimise it: increase to 20–25 mg weekly, switch to subcutaneous administration (better bioavailability and tolerability), optimise folic acid and reassess within 1–3 months
options.C: Adapt exercise to symptoms, maintaining movement and rehabilitation while avoiding overload of acutely inflamed joints
options.D: Paternal low-dose methotrexate exposure is considered compatible with conception
options.E: Consider tapering adalimumab by dose reduction or interval extension while continuing methotrexate

explanation: In sustained remission without glucocorticoids, b/tsDMARDs may be tapered, especially when combined with a csDMARD. Stopping all DMARDs commonly leads to flare. Tapering should be gradual with a plan to return to the previous dose if flare occurs. Flare risks during tapering: RF/ACPA positivity, Doppler activity on ultrasound, short remission duration, stopping rather than spacing, and stopping the csDMARD first. Sequence: GC off → b/tsDMARD interval extension or dose reduction (after ≥6 months of sustained remission) → csDMARD dose reduction last. Complete DMARD withdrawal is rarely successful (flare in about 50%), but most patients regain control after restarting. Ultrasoundguided tapering does not clearly beat clinical tapering.

question: A patient with RA on adalimumab and methotrexate initially responded well but lost response after 18 months. Low trough levels and anti-drug antibodies are found. What is an appropriate next step?

options.A: Consider tapering adalimumab by dose reduction or interval extension while continuing methotrexate
options.B: Individualised treatment with respiratory input, based on the lung pattern, its progression and the joint disease
options.C: Switch to another TNF inhibitor or to a drug with a different mechanism
options.D: TNF inhibitors
options.E: Prior infection history, glucocorticoid exposure, vaccination status, comorbidities and the infection profile of each option

explanation: After failure of a first bDMARD, any other bDMARD (from the same or another class) or a JAK inhibitor (after risk assessment) can be used. Immunogenicity-driven secondary failure is a good reason to try another TNF inhibitor. Combining biologics is not recommended. Primary non-response (no improvement by 3–6 months) suggests switching mechanism. Secondary loss of response with anti-drug antibodies can respond to a second TNFi (or adding methotrexate). Rituximab works best in seropositive disease. After two mechanisms fail, consider D2T assessment. Never combine two biologics (infection risk without added efficacy).

question: A patient with RA has a history of multiple sclerosis and needs a biologic. Which drug class should generally be avoided?

options.A: A TNF inhibitor
options.B: Individualised treatment with respiratory input, based on the lung pattern, its progression and the joint disease
options.C: TNF inhibitors
options.D: Switch to another TNF inhibitor or to a drug with a different mechanism
options.E: Prior infection history, glucocorticoid exposure, vaccination status, comorbidities and the infection profile of each option

explanation: TNF inhibitors have been associated with new or worsening demyelinating disease and are avoided in established demyelination. Other TNFi neurological effects: optic neuritis, transverse myelitis, Guillain-Barré or CIDP-like neuropathy, PML (rare, more with rituximab). New neurology on a TNFi also needs exclusion of TB meningitis and Listeria. Safer choices with MS or demyelination: rituximab (also an MS therapy), abatacept, IL-6R inhibitors, JAKi (after risk assessment). If demyelination occurs on a TNFi, stop it permanently.

question: A 71-year-old man with RA has NYHA class III heart failure and active disease despite methotrexate. Which treatment is usually avoided?

options.A: Individualised treatment with respiratory input, based on the lung pattern, its progression and the joint disease
options.B: Monoclonal TNF inhibitors (infliximab, adalimumab) treat both; avoid etanercept (ineffective in IBD) and
options.C: A TNF inhibitor
options.D: Prior infection history, glucocorticoid exposure, vaccination status, comorbidities and the infection profile of each option
options.E: TNF inhibitors

explanation: TNF inhibitors can worsen moderate-to-severe (NYHA III-IV) heart failure. A non-TNF biologic is preferred. NYHA I–II: use TNFi cautiously, with echo and monitoring. NYHA III–IV: avoid (worse outcomes in heart-failure trials of infliximab and etanercept). Alternatives: abatacept, rituximab, tocilizumab or sarilumab. Note the lipid rise with IL-6R inhibition. JAKi are generally avoided with established CVD.

question: A 66-year-old male ex-smoker with high-titre anti-CCP RA has bibasal crackles. HRCT shows basal reticulation, traction bronchiectasis and honeycombing. Which pattern is most likely?

options.A: Methotrexate with short-term glucocorticoid bridging, started as soon as RA is diagnosed, ideally within
options.B: ACPA specificity exceeds 95% and positivity is associated with erosive disease; high-titre ACPA
options.C: Usual interstitial pneumonia
options.D: Seronegative RA remains possible; diagnosis rests on clinical synovitis and exclusion of alternatives
options.E: They are classification criteria and do not replace clinical diagnosis; she scores 5 points and does not yet meet the criteria

explanation: UIP is the commonest HRCT pattern in RA-ILD, unlike most other connective tissue disease-related ILDs where NSIP predominates. Risk factors include male sex, older age, smoking, high-titre RF/ACPA and the MUC5B promoter variant. Differential of RA-ILD: methotrexate pneumonitis (acute, rare), other drug lung toxicity (leflunomide, TNFi exacerbation, rituximab), infection (TB, PJP, NTM), heart failure, bronchiectasis and obliterative bronchiolitis (airways disease), Caplan's nodules, lung cancer (higher in RA), smoking-related ILD (RB-ILD, DIP), and coexisting IPF (MUC5B). Clinically significant in about 10% (subclinical in up to 30%). UIP is the commonest pattern, then NSIP. UIP, extensive disease, low FVC or DLCO, older age, male sex and high-titre RF/ACPA predict progression and death. Screen at-risk patients with HRCT (PFTs alone miss cases), plus PFTs including DLCO and a 6-minute walk test. Monitor PFTs every 3–6 months for 1–2 years, then every 6–12 months; repeat HRCT at 1–2 years.

question: A patient with RA-associated interstitial lung disease has active arthritis and needs treatment escalation. Which approach is most appropriate?

options.A: Use a national risk tool that includes RA (such as QRISK3), reassess regularly, and control disease activity and traditional risk factors
options.B: Individualised treatment with respiratory input, based on the lung pattern, its progression and the joint disease
options.C: A TNF inhibitor
options.D: Prior infection history, glucocorticoid exposure, vaccination status, comorbidities and the infection profile of each option
options.E: TNF inhibitors

explanation: RA-ILD needs multidisciplinary assessment. Options depend on ILD pattern, severity and progression; agents such as rituximab, abatacept or mycophenolate are used on a case-by-case basis, and antifibrotics may be considered for progressive fibrosis. Options: - Immunosuppression for ILD: mycophenolate, rituximab or azathioprine. - Joints: abatacept is often chosen (it may stabilise ILD); JAKi have observational data. - Antifibrotics: nintedanib for progressive pulmonary fibrosis (INBUILD); pirfenidone in UIP (TRAIL1). - Methotrexate can usually continue in stable ILD. Use TNFi cautiously because of reports of ILD exacerbation. - Supportive: stop smoking, vaccinate, pulmonary rehabilitation, oxygen, early transplant referral. - Steroids: short-term only; avoid long-term high doses. Manage in an ILD MDT.

question: A woman with long-standing seropositive RA has recurrent infections, splenomegaly and neutrophils of 0.6 x 10I/L, not drug-related. Which test best distinguishes Felty's syndrome from T-cell large granular lymphocyte leukaemia?

options.A: Peripheral blood flow cytometry with T-cell receptor gene rearrangement studies
options.B: TNF inhibitors
options.C: Switch to another TNF inhibitor or to a drug with a different mechanism
options.D: Use a national risk tool that includes RA (such as QRISK3), reassess regularly, and control disease activity and traditional risk factors
options.E: Prior infection history, glucocorticoid exposure, vaccination status, comorbidities and the infection profile of each option

explanation: Felty's syndrome and T-LGL leukaemia overlap clinically and both associate with HLA-DR4. An expanded clonal CD3+CD8+CD57+ population supports T-LGL leukaemia. Neutropenia in RA: drugs (methotrexate, sulfasalazine, leflunomide, tocilizumab, rituximab late-onset neutropenia, JAKi); Felty's syndrome; T-LGL leukaemia; SLE overlap ("rhupus"); B12 or folate deficiency; viral infection; hypersplenism (cirrhosis); myelodysplasia. Felty's triad: seropositive (often nodular, long-standing) RA, splenomegaly and neutropenia (<2.0), plus leg ulcers, recurrent infections, lymphadenopathy, vasculitis and nodular regenerative hyperplasia of the liver (with portal hypertension). It is strongly linked to HLA-DR4. Large granular lymphocytes may be seen on the blood film in both Felty's and T-LGL leukaemia. Felty's: control RA (methotrexate first-line; rituximab for refractory disease). Use G-CSF for severe infection (it can flare arthritis or vasculitis). Splenectomy is a last resort. T- LGL leukaemia: methotrexate, ciclosporin or cyclophosphamide, with haematology input.

question: A 72-year-old woman with 25 years of erosive RA is listed for hip replacement under general anaesthesia. She reports occasional occipital headache. What is the most important pre-operative investigation?

options.A: Usual interstitial pneumonia
options.B: Lateral cervical spine imaging in flexion and extension (or MRI)
options.C: Prior infection history, glucocorticoid exposure, vaccination status, comorbidities and the infection profile of each option
options.D: A TNF inhibitor
options.E: Consider tapering adalimumab by dose reduction or interval extension while continuing methotrexate

explanation: Atlantoaxial subluxation is common in long-standing erosive RA and may be asymptomatic. An anterior atlanto-dental interval over 3 mm is abnormal. Detecting instability before intubation prevents cord injury. Occipital headache in RA: atlanto-axial disease vs cervical spondylosis, GCA (in older people), C2 neuralgia, medication-overuse headache. Cervical RA patterns: anterior atlanto-axial subluxation (commonest; anterior ADI >3 mm abnormal; posterior ADI <14 mm or anterior ADI >9–10 mm indicates high myelopathy risk); basilar invagination (cranial settling, with brainstem compression and risk of sudden death); subaxial "staircase" subluxation. Symptoms: occipital pain, Lhermitte's sign, hand clumsiness, gait disturbance, bladder dysfunction. Flexion–extension radiographs (performed carefully), MRI for cord compression, CT for bone. Anaesthetic plan: inline stabilisation, fibreoptic intubation, soft collar. Surgery (C1–C2 fusion, occipito-cervical fixation) for myelopathy or severe instability.

question: A patient with RA presents with a painful red eye with reduced vision. Ophthalmology confirms necrotising scleritis. What does this most strongly indicate?

options.A: Active synovial inflammation with increased vascularity
options.B: Acute, unilateral, recurrent (often alternating) anterior uveitis with a painful red eye, photophobia and blurred vision; same-day ophthalmology for topical corticosteroid and a cycloplegic; for recurrent attacks a
options.C: TNF inhibitors
options.D: Prior infection history, glucocorticoid exposure, vaccination status, comorbidities and the infection profile of each option
options.E: Systemic vasculitic disease activity requiring urgent systemic immunosuppression

explanation: Necrotising scleritis in RA reflects systemic vasculitis and carries significant morbidity and mortality without treatment. High-dose glucocorticoids plus a DMARD or biologic are used with urgent ophthalmology involvement. Red eye in RA: - Episcleritis: mild discomfort, normal vision, blanches with phenylephrine, self-limiting. - Scleritis: severe boring pain, tender, violaceous, sightthreatening. - Necrotising scleritis or scleromalacia perforans: painless thinning. - Peripheral ulcerative keratitis (corneal melt): an emergency. - Keratoconjunctivitis sicca: secondary Sjögren's. - Drug effects: GC cataract or glaucoma, hydroxychloroquine retinopathy. - Infectious keratitis or uveitis in immunosuppressed patients: HSV, VZV, CMV. Other features of rheumatoid vasculitis (long-standing seropositive nodular disease, smokers): nail-fold infarcts, purpura, leg ulcers, digital gangrene, mononeuritis multiplex, scleritis and PUK, mesenteric or renal involvement. Low complement and high-titre RF are typical. Incidence has fallen from about 5% to ≤1%. High-dose GC (including IV methylprednisolone) plus rituximab or cyclophosphamide for necrotising scleritis, PUK or systemic vasculitis. TNFi (adalimumab or infliximab) is also used for scleritis. Topical lubricants and ophthalmology-led local care.

question: Which approach best fits cardiovascular risk management in a 55-year-old UK patient with RA?

options.A: Use a national risk tool that includes RA (such as QRISK3), reassess regularly, and control disease activity and traditional risk factors
options.B: Systemic vasculitic disease activity requiring urgent systemic immunosuppression
options.C: Individualised treatment with respiratory input, based on the lung pattern, its progression and the joint disease
options.D: TNF inhibitors
options.E: Prior infection history, glucocorticoid exposure, vaccination status, comorbidities and the infection profile of each option

explanation: RA confers excess cardiovascular risk. Assessment should be repeated at least every 5 years and after major treatment changes, with good disease control and judicious use of NSAIDs and glucocorticoids. RA roughly doubles CV risk (IHD 1.5–2×; heart failure about 2×; VTE 1.5–2×). The "lipid paradox": active inflammation lowers cholesterol. ACPA is linked to CV death. QRISK3 includes RA, SLE, steroid use and severe mental illness. If the risk tool does not include RA, multiply the calculated risk by 1.5. Lipids should be measured when disease is stable. Statins have the same efficacy as in the general population (TRACE-RA showed a trend to benefit). Disease control (methotrexate, TNFi) is associated with fewer events. Minimise NSAIDs and GC. Check lipids 4–8 weeks after starting IL-6R or JAKi (the LDL rise with IL-6 blockade has not translated into excess events).

question: When should annual hydroxychloroquine retinopathy screening begin, and how does this change with risk factors (for example 5.5 mg/kg/day and eGFR 52)? Also tested as: A patient has taken hydroxychloroquine at 4.5 mg/kg/day for 2 years, with normal renal function and no tamoxifen use. Baseline retinal assessment was normal. When should annual retinal screening start?

options.A: Optimise it: increase to 20–25 mg weekly, switch to subcutaneous administration (better bioavailability and tolerability), optimise folic acid and reassess within 1–3 months
options.B: Monoclonal TNF inhibitors (infliximab, adalimumab) treat both; avoid etanercept (ineffective in IBD) and
options.C: After 5 years of treatment in patients without risk factors; after 1 year if risk factors are present (dose above 5 mg/kg/day, eGFR below 60 or concomitant tamoxifen)
options.D: Methotrexate with short-term glucocorticoid bridging, started as soon as RA is diagnosed, ideally within
options.E: Consider tapering adalimumab by dose reduction or interval extension while continuing methotrexate

explanation: For patients without additional risk factors, annual screening starts after 5 years of therapy. If risk factors are present (dose above 5 mg/kg/day, eGFR below 60 or tamoxifen), annual monitoring starts after 1 year, and the dose should also be reduced to 5 mg/kg/day or less. Screening uses spectral-domain OCT with widefield fundus autofluorescence; routine baseline testing for new starters is no longer recommended in current UK guidance, although the EULAR course still advises baseline imaging within the first year. Other retinal or visual problems in rheumatology patients: GC cataract and central serous chorioretinopathy, uveitis, retinal vasculitis (Behçet's, SLE), APS retinal vein occlusion, CMV retinitis (immunosuppression). Patients of Asian heritage often show extramacular (pericentral) toxicity, so widefield imaging is needed. Toxicity is irreversible and can progress after stopping. Early loss is parafoveal (bull's-eye maculopathy is a late sign). Dose by actual body weight, ≤5 mg/kg/day (e.g. 60 kg gives 300 mg/day, which can be given as alternating 200/400 mg). If definite toxicity is found, stop the drug and discuss alternatives with the ophthalmologist.

question: What is the usual perioperative approach to methotrexate and to a subcutaneous TNF inhibitor in a patient with RA having an elective joint replacement? Also tested as: A patient with RA on a subcutaneous TNF inhibitor is due to have elective joint replacement. What is the usual perioperative approach?

options.A: ASDAS below 1.3 is inactive disease; a fall of 1.1 or more is a clinically important improvement, so a fall of
options.B: Individualised treatment with respiratory input, based on the lung pattern, its progression and the joint disease
options.C: Continue methotrexate in most patients (unless renal function is unstable or there is infection); withhold the biologic so that surgery falls at the end of its dosing interval, restarting once the wound is healing and there is no infection
options.D: Monoclonal TNF inhibitors (infliximab, adalimumab) treat both; avoid etanercept (ineffective in IBD) and
options.E: Consider gradual tapering of the TNF inhibitor rather than stopping it

explanation: Continuing methotrexate does not increase wound complications and reduces flare risk. Biologic timing depends on the drug's dosing interval. Glucocorticoids should not be stopped abruptly perioperatively. Individual surgical and anaesthetic advice still applies. Surgery timing (ACR/AAHKS-based, as in the EULAR course): | Drug | Interval | Operate in | |---|---|---| | Etanercept | weekly | week 2 | | Adalimumab, sarilumab | 2weekly | week 3 | | Golimumab SC | monthly | week 5 | | Infliximab | 4, 6 or 8-weekly | week 5, 7 or 9 | | Tocilizumab | SC weekly / IV 4-weekly | week 2 / week 5 | | Abatacept | SC weekly / IV monthly | week 2 / week 5 | | Rituximab | 6monthly | month 7 | | Ustekinumab | 12-weekly | week 13 | | JAK inhibitors | daily | stop 3 days before; operate on day 4 | Continue csDMARDs (methotrexate, leflunomide, sulfasalazine, hydroxychloroquine). Continue the usual GC dose; routine supraphysiological "stress dosing" is not needed for most patients on their usual dose, but anaesthetists may give hydrocortisone cover for major surgery in long-term users (see the GC entry). Restart about 14 days after surgery once healing is satisfactory. Assess the cervical spine before intubation. Do not delay emergency surgery; hold the biologic until healed. Continue all drugs for minor procedures (dental, skin, cataract).

question: A patient with active inflammatory arthritis asks whether he should exercise during a flare. What is the best advice?

options.A: Prior infection history, glucocorticoid exposure, vaccination status, comorbidities and the infection profile of each option
options.B: Individualised treatment with respiratory input, based on the lung pattern, its progression and the joint disease
options.C: Neither treats axial disease; sulfasalazine may be considered for peripheral arthritis, and local glucocorticoid injection may help peripheral arthritis or enthesitis
options.D: Monoclonal TNF inhibitors (infliximab, adalimumab) treat both; avoid etanercept (ineffective in IBD) and
options.E: Adapt exercise to symptoms, maintaining movement and rehabilitation while avoiding overload of acutely inflamed joints

explanation: Tailored exercise improves function, cardiovascular health and fatigue in inflammatory arthritis. Core non-drug care: education and a written flare plan; aerobic plus strengthening exercise (safe even in active disease, with isometric work for hot joints); hand exercises (SARAH programme); splints; podiatry and orthoses; occupational therapy and joint protection; work support; CBT for pain, fatigue and mood; smoking cessation; healthy weight; Mediterranean-style diet. Fatigue is one of the most troublesome symptoms and often persists in remission. Treat anaemia, depression and sleep problems, and use graded exercise and CBT-based self-management.

question: A patient with RA (or axial SpA) reports worsening pain with high patient-reported scores, but there are no swollen joints, CRP is normal and imaging shows no active inflammation. What should be considered before escalating immunosuppression? Also tested as: A patient with axial SpA has a very high BASDAI score, but CRP is normal, MRI shows no active inflammation and he has widespread tenderness consistent with fibromyalgia. He has failed one TNF inhibitor. What is the best next step?

options.A: Consider gradual tapering of the TNF inhibitor rather than stopping it
options.B: ASDAS below 1.3 is inactive disease; a fall of 1.1 or more is a clinically important improvement, so a fall of
options.C: Monoclonal TNF inhibitors (infliximab, adalimumab) treat both; avoid etanercept (ineffective in IBD) and
options.D: Non-inflammatory pain (fibromyalgia, central sensitisation, structural damage, secondary OA mechanical pain), mood and sleep disturbance, and other comorbidity; reassess the diagnosis and objective inflammation before switching
options.E: Neither treats axial disease; sulfasalazine may be considered for peripheral arthritis, and local glucocorticoid injection may help peripheral arthritis or enthesitis

explanation: Treatment should match demonstrable inflammatory activity. Disease activity scores (DAS28, BASDAI) can be inflated by non-inflammatory pain, fibromyalgia, mechanical pain and mood. Before switching, confirm the diagnosis, adherence, objective inflammatory activity (swollen joints, CRP, ultrasound or MRI) and the reason for failure. Pain mechanisms in RA: nociceptive (synovitis, damage, secondary OA); neuropathic (carpal tunnel syndrome, cervical myelopathy, vasculitic neuropathy); nociplastic (fibromyalgia in about 20%). Other drivers: depression and anxiety (1 in 3–4), obesity, hypothyroidism, vitamin D deficiency, statin myalgia, GC withdrawal, osteonecrosis or insufficiency fracture. Separate pain plan: exercise, CBT and pain management programmes, sleep hygiene, judicious analgesia (avoid long-term opioids and gabapentinoids), duloxetine or amitriptyline for selected patients, and treatment of entrapment neuropathy. Use CDAI or ultrasound to judge inflammation. In axSpA, ASDAS (which includes CRP) is less affected by pain than BASDAI.

question: A patient with RA has recurrent serious infections and active disease. What should be reviewed before choosing the next treatment?

options.A: Prior infection history, glucocorticoid exposure, vaccination status, comorbidities and the infection profile of each option
options.B: Individualised treatment with respiratory input, based on the lung pattern, its progression and the joint disease
options.C: A TNF inhibitor
options.D: Monoclonal TNF inhibitors (infliximab, adalimumab) treat both; avoid etanercept (ineffective in IBD) and
options.E: Peripheral blood flow cytometry with T-cell receptor gene rearrangement studies

explanation: Glucocorticoid dose is a major modifiable infection risk. Abatacept and IL-6 or TNF inhibitors differ in serious infection profiles. Serious infection risk is highest in the first 6–12 months of therapy; TNFi raises it roughly 1.5–2×. GC dose is the strongest modifiable factor. Abatacept probably has the lowest serious-infection risk; rituximab adds the risk of hypogammaglobulinaemia; JAKi add zoster risk. Taper GC to ≤5 mg or stop. Vaccinate (influenza, pneumococcal, COVID-19, recombinant zoster). Treat bronchiectasis (sputum clearance, consider prophylactic azithromycin, though note the QT interaction with hydroxychloroquine). Check IgG. Prefer abatacept or rituximab (if IgG is normal). Treat skin and foot portals of entry.

question: A 29-year-old man has 7 months of inflammatory back pain, MRI sacroiliitis, negative HLA-B27 and a good response to naproxen. Does he meet the ASAS axial SpA classification criteria, and through which arm?

options.A: About 8% of the white UK population carries HLA-B27 and most never develop spondyloarthritis
options.B: Neither treats axial disease; sulfasalazine may be considered for peripheral arthritis, and local glucocorticoid injection may help peripheral arthritis or enthesitis
options.C: Management principles are the same; biologics require objective evidence of inflammation (raised CRP or MRI inflammation)
options.D: Bilateral grade 2 or more, or unilateral grade 3-4
options.E: He meets the imaging arm: sacroiliitis plus at least one SpA feature

explanation: The criteria apply to back pain of 3 months or more starting before age 45. The imaging arm requires sacroiliitis (active MRI inflammation or definite radiographic change) plus at least one SpA feature; inflammatory back pain and good NSAID response each count. The clinical arm requires HLA-B27 plus at least two features. Mimics of axSpA: mechanical or degenerative back pain; fibromyalgia (a common misdiagnosis in women); osteitis condensans ilii; DISH; sacral insufficiency fracture; septic sacroiliitis (unilateral; S. aureus, TB, Brucella); post-partum or athletic BME; SAPHO; hyperparathyroidism (subchondral resorption at the SIJ); fluorosis; X-linked hypophosphataemia (enthesopathy); ochronosis; Paget's; metastases; hypermobility. ASAS features: IBP, arthritis, heel enthesitis, uveitis, dactylitis, psoriasis, Crohn's or colitis, good NSAID response, family history, HLA-B27, raised CRP. Peripheral SpA criteria require arthritis, enthesitis or dactylitis plus ≥1 of (uveitis, psoriasis, IBD, preceding infection, B27, sacroiliitis) or ≥2 of (arthritis, enthesitis, dactylitis, IBP history, family history). Referral strategy: chronic back pain (≥3 months) starting before 45 plus at least one of IBP, B27, imaging sacroiliitis, peripheral SpA features, uveitis, psoriasis, IBD, family history, NSAID response or raised CRP. Screen patients presenting to ophthalmology, dermatology and gastroenterology. The original ASAS criteria performed below target in the inception cohort (sensitivity 82%, specificity 77%), and misuse as diagnostic criteria led to over-labelling. Classification is not diagnosis.

question: Which MRI finding defines active sacroiliitis in axial SpA, and how should a small area of sacroiliac bone marrow oedema be interpreted in a postpartum woman with mechanical back pain and a normal CRP? Also tested as: A 31-year-old postpartum woman with mechanical low back pain has a small area of sacroiliac bone marrow oedema on MRI, no other SpA features and a normal CRP. How should the MRI finding be interpreted?

options.A: About 8% of the white UK population carries HLA-B27 and most never develop spondyloarthritis
options.B: An IL-17 inhibitor
options.C: Management principles are the same; biologics require objective evidence of inflammation (raised CRP or MRI inflammation)
options.D: He meets the imaging arm: sacroiliitis plus at least one SpA feature
options.E: Periarticular (subchondral) bone marrow oedema (osteitis) on STIR or fat-suppressed T2 sequences in a typical location defines active sacroiliitis; but BME is non-specific and occurs in healthy people, athletes and postpartum women, so clinical context is essential

explanation: Bone marrow oedema clearly present and typically located is required. Structural lesions such as erosions and fat metaplasia support the diagnosis but do not alone define active sacroiliitis. Sacroiliac bone marrow oedema is not specific: its distribution, extent, accompanying structural lesions and the clinical picture determine significance, and overdiagnosis is a recognised problem. Non-SpA causes of SIJ BME: post-partum (up to about 60% shortly after delivery), runners and military recruits, mechanical back pain (up to about 20% of healthy people), osteitis condensans ilii (iliac-sided triangular sclerosis in multiparous women; sacrum normal, no erosions), insufficiency fracture (H-shaped sacral pattern), septic sacroiliitis (unilateral, effusion, soft-tissue oedema), degenerative change in older people, gout or CPPD of the SIJ (rare). Mechanical BME typically sits in the anterior iliac side of the lower joint, is small and has no erosions. Erosions and fat metaplasia (backfill, ankylosis) add specificity. Synovitis, capsulitis or enthesitis alone do not qualify. Sequences: STIR or T2 fat-suppressed for activity, T1 for structural lesions. Contrast is rarely needed. Do not request SIJ MRI as a screening test when pre-test probability is low. In post-partum women, consider repeating MRI after 6–12 months if the clinical picture is unclear.

question: Which modified New York grading of sacroiliitis is required for radiographic axial SpA (ankylosing spondylitis)?

options.A: Bilateral grade 2 or more, or unilateral grade 3-4
options.B: Management principles are the same; biologics require objective evidence of inflammation (raised CRP or MRI inflammation)
options.C: He meets the imaging arm: sacroiliitis plus at least one SpA feature
options.D: Consider gradual tapering of the TNF inhibitor rather than stopping it
options.E: Aortitis with aortic root dilatation and fibrosis extending into the conduction system

explanation: Modified New York criteria require radiographic sacroiliitis (bilateral grade 2 or more, or unilateral grade 3-4) plus at least one clinical criterion: inflammatory back pain for over 3 months, limited lumbar motion, or reduced chest expansion. Radiographic SIJ sclerosis without SpA: OCI, DISH (bridging of the upper ligamentous part only), degenerative change, hyperparathyroidism, Paget's, renal osteodystrophy. Grade Appearance 0 normal 1 suspicious 2 minimal: small erosions or sclerosis, no change in width 3 unequivocal: erosions, sclerosis, widening, narrowing, partial ankylosis 4 complete ankylosis Inter-reader agreement on plain films is poor. Low-dose CT resolves equivocal X-rays (erosions, sclerosis, ankylosis) but shows no inflammation.

question: A 26-year-old man with mechanical low back pain has a positive HLA-B27 result ordered by his GP. What does this result mean?

options.A: Aortitis with aortic root dilatation and fibrosis extending into the conduction system
options.B: About 8% of the white UK population carries HLA-B27 and most never develop spondyloarthritis
options.C: Bridging syndesmophytes with vertebral fusion in advanced axial SpA
options.D: He meets the imaging arm: sacroiliitis plus at least one SpA feature
options.E: RF can occur in chronic infection, other autoimmune disease and older adults, and is not diagnostic without a compatible clinical picture

explanation: HLA-B27 is found in roughly 85-95% of white patients with AS but also about 8% of the general population, so its predictive value in unselected back pain is low. It is useful only with clinical and imaging findings. HLA-B27 in context: present in about 85–95% of white AS patients but only about 50% in African and Middle Eastern populations. Prevalence in Europe is 6–9% (higher in Scandinavians, about 14–16%; very high in Haida and other indigenous groups). Only 1–5% of carriers develop axSpA (10–30% if a first-degree relative is affected). Request it only with a clinical suspicion of SpA (≥1 SpA feature). A positive result in non-specific mechanical back pain adds little; a negative result lowers but does not exclude probability.

question: Which ASDAS-CRP values define disease activity states, and how should a fall from 3.6 to 2.4 twelve weeks after starting a TNF inhibitor be interpreted? Also tested as: Twelve weeks after starting a TNF inhibitor for axial SpA, ASDAS-CRP has fallen from 3.6 to 2.4. What is the most appropriate interpretation?

options.A: Monoclonal TNF inhibitors (infliximab, adalimumab) treat both; avoid etanercept (ineffective in IBD) and
options.B: Consider gradual tapering of the TNF inhibitor rather than stopping it
options.C: ASDAS below 1.3 is inactive disease; a fall of 1.1 or more is a clinically important improvement, so a fall of
options.D: Management principles are the same; biologics require objective evidence of inflammation (raised CRP or MRI inflammation)
options.E: Treat latent TB (for example 3 months of isoniazid with rifampicin), starting the TNF inhibitor after at least 1 month if urgent, or on completion

explanation: 1.2 supports continuing treatment ASDAS: below 1.3 inactive; 1.3 to below 2.1 low; 2.1 to 3.5 high; above 3.5 very high disease activity. A fall of 1.1 or more is clinically important improvement and 2.0 or more is major improvement. Continuation is supported by an ASDAS improvement of at least 1.1 units after 12–16 weeks. ASDAS-CRP combines back pain, morning stiffness duration, patient global, peripheral pain or swelling, and CRP. BASDAI (6 patient questions; ≥4 means active) is the traditional NICE threshold, with a response defined as a ≥2point (or 50%) fall. ASDAS is preferred because it includes CRP and has validated cut-offs. Treat-to-target: ASDAS <2.1, ideally <1.3. Review every 3–6 months while active. Repeat imaging is not routine; spinal X-ray progression is assessed no more often than every 2 years.

question: What is first-line treatment for active axial SpA, when is a biologic indicated (for example persistent ASDAS 3.3 after naproxen then etoricoxib at full dose for 6 weeks), and which non-drug measures remain important after starting it? Also tested as: A 34-year-old woman with axial SpA has persistent inflammatory back pain despite naproxen and then etoricoxib at full dose over 6 weeks. ASDAS-CRP is 3.3. She has no peripheral arthritis, uveitis, psoriasis or IBD. What is the most appropriate next step? | A patient with axial SpA asks what non-drug management remains important after starting a biologic. What is the best answer?

options.A: A full-dose NSAID with exercise and education first; after at least two NSAIDs over 4 weeks with ASDAS still 2.1 or more, start a TNF or IL-17 inhibitor (or a JAK inhibitor after risk assessment); exercise, physiotherapy,
options.B: Management principles are the same; biologics require objective evidence of inflammation (raised CRP or MRI inflammation)
options.C: Neither treats axial disease; sulfasalazine may be considered for peripheral arthritis, and local glucocorticoid injection may help peripheral arthritis or enthesitis
options.D: Consider gradual tapering of the TNF inhibitor rather than stopping it
options.E: ASDAS below 1.3 is inactive disease; a fall of 1.1 or more is a clinically important improvement, so a fall of

explanation: education and smoking cessation remain core throughout NSAIDs are first-line, used continuously if needed for symptom control, after considering gastrointestinal, renal and cardiovascular risk. b/tsDMARDs are indicated when ASDAS is 2.1 or more despite at least two NSAIDs over a total of 4 weeks; a TNF inhibitor or IL-17 inhibitor is the usual first choice. Exercise and physiotherapy remain core treatment regardless of drug therapy, and smoking worsens disease activity and structural progression. 60–80% respond to NSAIDs within 48–72 hours, and a good response supports the diagnosis. All b/tsDMARDs achieve ASAS40 in about 40–50% (vs 15–25% with placebo). Response is best in younger patients with short disease duration, raised CRP and MRI inflammation. Longterm TNFi (>4 years) is associated with slower syndesmophyte formation. NSAID safety: coxib or NSAID plus PPI for GI risk; naproxen has the most neutral CV profile; monitor eGFR and BP; avoid after 20 weeks of pregnancy. Choosing the first b/tsDMARD: recurrent uveitis or IBD → mAb TNFi (or upadacitinib); significant psoriasis → IL- 17i (or TNFi); pregnancy plans → certolizumab; age ≥65, smoking, CV or VTE risk → avoid JAKi; otherwise a biosimilar TNFi on cost. Licensing: bimekizumab and upadacitinib are licensed for both r- and nr-axSpA; tofacitinib for r-axSpA. Non-drug: supervised exercise (land or water, group) beats home exercise; passive modalities have little evidence; stop smoking; manage weight. Surgery: THR for structural hip disease regardless of age; corrective osteotomy at specialist centres. After first b/tsDMARD failure: check the diagnosis, adherence and non-inflammatory pain (fibromyalgia, mechanical pain, fracture, hip OA). After primary TNFi non-response, change mechanism (IL-17i or JAKi); after loss of response or intolerance, a second TNFi is reasonable. Response rates fall with each switch.

question: What is the role of conventional synthetic DMARDs and of long-term oral glucocorticoids in axial SpA? Also tested as: A patient with axial SpA asks whether oral prednisolone could control his inflammatory back pain long term. What is the best advice?

options.A: Adapt exercise to symptoms, maintaining movement and rehabilitation while avoiding overload of acutely inflamed joints
options.B: Neither treats axial disease; sulfasalazine may be considered for peripheral arthritis, and local glucocorticoid injection may help peripheral arthritis or enthesitis
options.C: Consider gradual tapering of the TNF inhibitor rather than stopping it
options.D: He meets the imaging arm: sacroiliitis plus at least one SpA feature
options.E: Management principles are the same; biologics require objective evidence of inflammation (raised CRP or MRI inflammation)

explanation: csDMARDs do not meaningfully treat axial inflammation; sulfasalazine is the best-evidenced csDMARD for peripheral SpA arthritis. Systemic glucocorticoids have little evidence of benefit in axial disease and cause cumulative harm. Do not delay biologics to try csDMARDs in purely axial disease. Image-guided SIJ steroid injection can help selected patients. A short oral GC course may bridge a peripheral flare. Use paracetamol or tramadol only for residual pain; avoid long-term strong opioids.

question: What is the typical presentation of SpA-associated uveitis, how is an acute attack managed, and which biologic is preferred when a patient with axial SpA has three attacks a year? Also tested as: Which ocular presentation is most typical of spondyloarthritis-associated uveitis? | A patient with ankylosing spondylitis presents with a painful red eye, photophobia and blurred vision. What is the most appropriate management?

options.A: Systemic vasculitic disease activity requiring urgent systemic immunosuppression
options.B: Management principles are the same; biologics require objective evidence of inflammation (raised CRP or MRI inflammation)
options.C: Neither treats axial disease; sulfasalazine may be considered for peripheral arthritis, and local glucocorticoid injection may help peripheral arthritis or enthesitis
options.D: Bilateral grade 2 or more, or unilateral grade 3-4
options.E: Acute, unilateral, recurrent (often alternating) anterior uveitis with a painful red eye, photophobia and blurred vision; same-day ophthalmology for topical corticosteroid and a cycloplegic; for recurrent attacks a

explanation: monoclonal anti-TNF antibody such as adalimumab HLA-B27-associated uveitis presents with a painful red eye, photophobia and blurred vision. It needs same-day slitlamp assessment, topical corticosteroids and a cycloplegic, with review of systemic therapy if recurrent. Monoclonal anti-TNF antibodies reduce uveitis recurrence. Etanercept is less effective at preventing uveitis (and may trigger it), and IL-17 inhibitors have a weaker evidence base. Uveitis patterns by disease: | Pattern | Disease | |---|---| | Acute, unilateral, alternating anterior, painful | HLA-B27 (axSpA, ReA, IBD), Behçet's (anterior with hypopyon) | | Chronic, bilateral, silent anterior | ANA+ oligoarticular JIA, IBD (sometimes), PsA (more often bilateral and chronic than B27-AAU) | | Granulomatous (mutton-fat KPs), panuveitis | sarcoidosis, Blau, TB, syphilis, VKH | | Posterior with retinal vasculitis or occlusive vasculitis | Behçet's, SLE, APS, susceptibility to CMV or toxoplasma | | Tubulointerstitial nephritis and uveitis | TINU (adolescents) | Other red eyes: conjunctivitis (ReA), episcleritis or scleritis (RA, AAV, RP, IBD), keratitis (HSV, PUK), acute angleclosure glaucoma. Complications of recurrent AAU: posterior synechiae (irregular pupil), cataract, glaucoma (including steroidinduced), cystoid macular oedema. A hypopyon in a white eye suggests Behçet's. Severe attacks may need periocular or systemic GC. For prevention: adalimumab (licensed for non-infectious uveitis) or infliximab, certolizumab or golimumab; sulfasalazine modestly reduces attacks if a biologic is not indicated. Teach patients to seek same-day care for a painful red eye.

question: A patient with axial SpA, RA or psoriatic arthritis also has active Crohn's disease and needs a biologic. Which agents treat both, and which should be avoided? Also tested as: A patient with RA and coexisting Crohn's disease needs a TNF inhibitor. Which TNF inhibitor should be avoided? | A patient with PsA, extensive psoriasis and active polyarthritis has active Crohn's disease. Which biologic class should be avoided?

options.A: ASDAS below 1.3 is inactive disease; a fall of 1.1 or more is a clinically important improvement, so a fall of
options.B: Consider gradual tapering of the TNF inhibitor rather than stopping it
options.C: An IL-17 inhibitor
options.D: Prior infection history, glucocorticoid exposure, vaccination status, comorbidities and the infection profile of each option
options.E: Monoclonal TNF inhibitors (infliximab, adalimumab) treat both; avoid etanercept (ineffective in IBD) and

explanation: IL-17 inhibitors (can provoke or worsen IBD) Monoclonal TNF inhibitors treat both the joint disease and inflammatory bowel disease, whereas the soluble receptor etanercept is ineffective in IBD and IL-17 inhibitors can exacerbate it. In PsA, IL-12/23 or IL-23 inhibitors and some JAK inhibitors also treat both peripheral joints and IBD, but IL-23 pathway drugs do not treat axial disease. Gut-and-joint drug map: | Drug | Gut | Axial | Peripheral | |- --|---|---|---| | Infliximab, adalimumab | Crohn's + UC | I | I | | Certolizumab | Crohn's (some regions) | I | I | | Golimumab | UC | I | I | | Upadacitinib | Crohn's + UC | I | I | | Ustekinumab, risankizumab, guselkumab | Crohn's + UC | I | I (PsA) | | Vedolizumab | gut-selective | I (may unmask arthritis) | I | | Etanercept | I | I | I | | IL-17i | worsens | I | I | Use NSAIDs cautiously (short courses or coxibs) in IBD. Sulfasalazine and mesalazine treat mild colitis and peripheral arthritis. Thiopurines and methotrexate help IBD maintenance but not axial disease. Co-manage with gastroenterology.

question: A 41-year-old woman with axial SpA has extensive plaque psoriasis (about 15% body surface area) and active spinal disease despite NSAIDs. Which agent is generally preferred?

options.A: Consider gradual tapering of the TNF inhibitor rather than stopping it
options.B: Monoclonal TNF inhibitors (infliximab, adalimumab) treat both; avoid etanercept (ineffective in IBD) and
options.C: Add an IL-17 or IL-23 inhibitor
options.D: An IL-17 inhibitor
options.E: Management principles are the same; biologics require objective evidence of inflammation (raised CRP or MRI inflammation)

explanation: For axial SpA with extensive or high-impact psoriasis, the 2025 BSR guideline prefers an IL-17 inhibitor or a monoclonal TNF inhibitor, ideally with dermatology input. IL-23 inhibitors treat psoriasis but did not show efficacy in axial SpA trials, and etanercept is less effective for skin. The 2025 BSR axSpA guideline prefers an IL-17i or a monoclonal TNFi when psoriasis is extensive or highimpact. IL-17A/F (bimekizumab) gives very high skin clearance (PASI 90 to 100) but more oral candidiasis. Etanercept is less effective for skin, and IL-23 inhibitors do not treat axial disease. Co-manage with dermatology. Consider nail and scalp disease, and genital and flexural sites, as high-impact. Paradoxical psoriasis on a TNFi points towards switching to an IL-17 or IL-23 pathway drug.

question: A 45-year-old woman with axial SpA has been in sustained remission on a TNF inhibitor for 2 years and asks to reduce treatment. Which is most appropriate?

options.A: An IL-17 inhibitor
options.B: ASDAS below 1.3 is inactive disease; a fall of 1.1 or more is a clinically important improvement, so a fall of
options.C: Management principles are the same; biologics require objective evidence of inflammation (raised CRP or MRI inflammation)
options.D: Monoclonal TNF inhibitors (infliximab, adalimumab) treat both; avoid etanercept (ineffective in IBD) and
options.E: Consider gradual tapering of the TNF inhibitor rather than stopping it

explanation: In sustained remission, tapering a biologic can be considered as a shared decision. The 2025 BSR axial SpA guideline does not recommend withdrawing targeted therapy in sustained remission, because discontinuation is associated with a high flare rate. In sustained remission (ASDAS <1.3 for ≥6 months), reduce the dose or extend the interval as a shared decision. Complete withdrawal leads to flare in most patients within months, although most regain response on restarting.

question: A man with long-standing ankylosing spondylitis falls from standing height and has new neck pain, with no fracture on plain radiographs. What is the next step, and how should his bone health be managed? Also tested as: A patient with ankylosing spondylitis has progressive spinal stiffness and osteoporosis on DXA. In addition to disease-modifying treatment, what advice is most important?

options.A: Diffuse idiopathic skeletal hyperostosis (DISH)
options.B: Urgent CT (and/or MRI) of the whole spine, because fractures follow minor trauma and are missed on plain films; long term, assess and treat fracture risk alongside extension exercise, smoking cessation and falls reduction
options.C: Aortitis with aortic root dilatation and fibrosis extending into the conduction system
options.D: Bilateral grade 2 or more, or unilateral grade 3-4
options.E: Bone resorption at the distal end with proliferative new bone at the base of the adjacent phalanx

explanation: The ankylosed spine is rigid and osteoporotic. Fractures follow minor trauma, are often missed on plain films, are frequently unstable and may be non-contiguous, so cross-sectional imaging of the whole spine is required. Axial SpA increases vertebral fracture risk, which should be assessed and treated in addition to controlling inflammation. New spinal pain in AS: unstable three-column fracture (cervicothoracic or thoracolumbar junction), Andersson lesion (spondylodiscitis or pseudarthrosis), infective discitis, cauda equina syndrome from dural ectasia with arachnoid diverticula (in long-standing disease), atlantoaxial subluxation, epidural haematoma. Immobilise in the patient's usual posture and never force the neck straight. Spine DXA is falsely normal or high because of syndesmophytes, so use hip DXA (or lateral spine or QCT). CT of the whole spine, plus MRI if there are neurological signs. Urgent spinal surgical opinion. Long term: bisphosphonate where indicated, vitamin D, falls prevention and control of inflammation. DISH carries the same fracture risk.

question: A 62-year-old man with long-standing ankylosing spondylitis has an early diastolic murmur at the left sternal edge and a PR interval of 240 ms. Which pathology best explains both findings?

options.A: Bone resorption at the distal end with proliferative new bone at the base of the adjacent phalanx
options.B: He meets the imaging arm: sacroiliitis plus at least one SpA feature
options.C: About 8% of the white UK population carries HLA-B27 and most never develop spondyloarthritis
options.D: Aortitis with aortic root dilatation and fibrosis extending into the conduction system
options.E: Bilateral grade 2 or more, or unilateral grade 3-4

explanation: AS-associated aortitis causes aortic regurgitation, and subaortic fibrosis can extend to the AV node, causing conduction defects from first-degree to complete heart block. Aortic regurgitation with conduction disease: AS or HLA- B27 aortitis, ReA, Takayasu, GCA, syphilitic aortitis, Marfan or Loeys-Dietz (root dilatation without conduction disease), relapsing polychondritis, Cogan's syndrome, IgG4-related aortitis, Behçet's. Carditis in HLA-B27 disease features aortic root thickening, AR, subaortic fibrous "bump", and AV conduction block (first-degree to complete). Conduction disease can occur without other SpA features ("B27 lone heart block"). CV risk is increased overall (inflammation, NSAIDs, smoking). ECG, echo and cardiology review. Pacing for high-grade block. Valve or root surgery as indicated. Control inflammation and CV risk factors.

question: What does a "bamboo spine" on radiography represent?

options.A: 3 points; he meets the criteria
options.B: He meets the imaging arm: sacroiliitis plus at least one SpA feature
options.C: Management principles are the same; biologics require objective evidence of inflammation (raised CRP or MRI inflammation)
options.D: Bridging syndesmophytes with vertebral fusion in advanced axial SpA
options.E: About 8% of the white UK population carries HLA-B27 and most never develop spondyloarthritis

explanation: Bamboo spine reflects syndesmophytes bridging disc spaces in late radiographic axial SpA. Spinal new bone: syndesmophytes (thin, vertical, marginal; axSpA); non-marginal "chunky" syndesmophytes and paravertebral ossification, asymmetric (PsA, ReA); flowing anterior ossification (DISH); osteophytes (horizontal then vertical, degenerative); fluorosis; ochronosis (disc calcification); hypoparathyroidism (ligament calcification); X-linked hypophosphataemia (enthesopathy).

question: How does the management of non-radiographic axial SpA compare with that of radiographic axial SpA?

options.A: He meets the imaging arm: sacroiliitis plus at least one SpA feature
options.B: Consider gradual tapering of the TNF inhibitor rather than stopping it
options.C: Bilateral grade 2 or more, or unilateral grade 3-4
options.D: Management principles are the same; biologics require objective evidence of inflammation (raised CRP or MRI inflammation)
options.E: Neither treats axial disease; sulfasalazine may be considered for peripheral arthritis, and local glucocorticoid injection may help peripheral arthritis or enthesitis

explanation: Both forms are managed similarly. Biologic eligibility in non-radiographic disease requires objective inflammation. nr-axSpA and r-axSpA have a similar symptom burden and similar treatment response. Women are more often nonradiographic. NICE eligibility for biologics in nr-axSpA requires a raised CRP or MRI inflammation.

question: A 71-year-old man with type 2 diabetes has thoracic spinal stiffness. Radiographs show flowing anterior ossification along four contiguous thoracic vertebrae with preserved disc heights and normal sacroiliac joints. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.A: SAPHO syndrome
options.B: About 8% of the white UK population carries HLA-B27 and most never develop spondyloarthritis
options.C: An IL-17 inhibitor
options.D: 3 points; he meets the criteria
options.E: Diffuse idiopathic skeletal hyperostosis (DISH)

explanation: DISH shows flowing anterolateral ossification over at least four contiguous vertebrae with preserved disc height and no sacroiliac erosion or fusion. It is associated with diabetes, obesity and metabolic syndrome. DISH: older (>50), obese, diabetic men; mechanical stiffness with little pain; right-sided thoracic flowing ossification over ≥4 contiguous levels; preserved discs; normal SIJ (bridging may occur at the upper ligamentous portion); peripheral enthesophytes; dysphagia or airway problems from cervical osteophytes; normal CRP; B27 not increased. Analgesia, physiotherapy, management of metabolic risk, and surgery for dysphagia or myelopathy. Treat it like AS regarding fracture risk after trauma (whole-spine CT). Heterotopic ossification after hip replacement is more common.

question: A 24-year-old man develops a hot swollen knee and heel pain 3 weeks after urethritis. Urine NAAT is positive for Chlamydia trachomatis. Synovial fluid culture is negative and crystals are absent. What is the most appropriate management?

options.A: Treat the chlamydial infection (for example doxycycline for 7 days), arrange partner notification, and treat the arthritis with NSAIDs or joint injection
options.B: Septic arthritis: send Gram stain and culture and start empirical antibiotics pending results; do not inject steroid or label it gout until infection has been assessed
options.C: About 8% of the white UK population carries HLA-B27 and most never develop spondyloarthritis
options.D: Calcium pyrophosphate crystals
options.E: 3 points; he meets the criteria

explanation: Reactive arthritis requires treatment of the triggering genitourinary infection and contact tracing, but prolonged antibiotics do not alter the arthritis. NSAIDs and intra-articular glucocorticoid are first-line; sulfasalazine is used for chronic disease. Monoarthritis after urethritis: reactive arthritis vs disseminated gonococcal infection (tenosynovitis, pustules, migratory pattern), septic arthritis, gout, HIVassociated arthritis, early PsA or IBD arthritis. Enteric ReA triggers: Salmonella, Shigella, Campylobacter, Yersinia, C. difficile. Post-streptococcal ReA follows S. pyogenes. Onset 1–4 weeks after infection. Asymmetric lower-limb oligoarthritis, enthesitis, dactylitis, conjunctivitis or AAU, circinate balanitis, keratoderma blennorrhagicum, oral ulcers, sterile urethritis. B27 is positive in 60–80%. Most cases resolve in 6–12 months; 15–30% become chronic or recurrent. NSAIDs and IA steroid; a short oral GC course for severe polyarthritis. Treat active chlamydia (and partners) and test for other STIs including HIV. Antibiotics do not help postenteric ReA. Sulfasalazine or methotrexate for chronic disease; TNFi for refractory disease.

question: A 33-year-old woman with ulcerative colitis develops an asymmetrical oligoarthritis of a knee and ankle during a colitis flare. What is the expected course of this arthritis?

options.A: Avoid debridement (pathergy); give systemic immunosuppression
options.B: Consider gradual tapering of the TNF inhibitor rather than stopping it
options.C: Apremilast
options.D: 3 points; he meets the criteria
options.E: This pattern usually parallels bowel activity and is self-limiting

explanation: Type 1 enteropathic arthritis affects fewer than five large joints and parallels IBD activity. Type 2 is a small-joint polyarthritis independent of gut activity. NSAIDs can worsen IBD and are used cautiously. Type Joints Course Links Type 1 <5 parallels IBD erythema (pauciarticular) activity, selfnodosum, large limiting (<10 joints uveitis weeks) Type 2 ≥5 independent of uveitis (polyarticular) IBD, persistent small joints HLA-B27 Axial SIJ and independent of (50–70%) spine IBD Control the bowel disease (type 1 improves with it). Use NSAIDs cautiously (short courses or coxibs). Sulfasalazine for peripheral arthritis; IA steroid; mAb TNFi or upadacitinib for both. Vedolizumab can unmask arthritis. Look for other IBD-associated features: erythema nodosum, pyoderma gangrenosum, AAU, episcleritis, PSC.

question: A 42-year-old woman has palmoplantar pustulosis and painful swelling over the sternoclavicular joints. Imaging shows osteitis and hyperostosis of the anterior chest wall. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.A: SAPHO syndrome
options.B: Methotrexate; oral glucocorticoids are not routine and, if needed, are used only at low dose for short periods
options.C: 3 points; he meets the criteria
options.D: TNF inhibitors
options.E: Diffuse idiopathic skeletal hyperostosis (DISH)

explanation: SAPHO (synovitis, acne, pustulosis, hyperostosis, osteitis) characteristically affects the anterior chest wall. Treatment includes NSAIDs, bisphosphonates and, in refractory cases, TNF inhibitors. Anterior chest wall pain and swelling: SAPHO; CRMO or CNO (paediatric equivalent); SpA (sternoclavicular, manubriosternal); septic sternoclavicular arthritis (IV drug use, diabetes); Tietze syndrome or costochondritis; condensing osteitis of the clavicle; Friedrich's disease (avascular necrosis of the medial clavicle); malignancy (lymphoma, metastasis); fibrous dysplasia. Bone scan shows the "bull's head" sign at the sternocostoclavicular region. Skin disease (palmoplantar pustulosis, severe acne, hidradenitis) may precede or follow osteitis by years. Cultures may grow Cutibacterium acnes (debated significance). NSAIDs first. Bisphosphonates (IV pamidronate or zoledronate) for osteitis. TNFi for refractory disease. Also methotrexate or sulfasalazine, IL-17 or IL-23 inhibitors (skin), and JAKi (case series). Short courses of doxycycline or azithromycin have mixed results. Paradoxical PPP can occur on TNFi.

question: A 45-year-old man has inflammatory arthritis of a knee and two DIP joints. He has no current or past psoriasis, but his mother has psoriasis. He has nail pitting and RF is negative. How does he score on the CASPAR criteria?

options.A: Methotrexate; oral glucocorticoids are not routine and, if needed, are used only at low dose for short periods
options.B: Psoriatic arthritis with dactylitis: diffuse swelling of a whole digit from flexor tenosynovitis, joint synovitis and soft-tissue inflammation
options.C: Consider gradual tapering of the TNF inhibitor rather than stopping it
options.D: As clinically relevant, because impact and sensitive sites matter as well as body surface area
options.E: 3 points; he meets the criteria

explanation: CASPAR requires inflammatory articular disease plus 3 or more points: current psoriasis 2 (or personal history 1, or family history 1 if no personal history), typical nail dystrophy 1, negative RF 1, dactylitis 1 and juxta-articular new bone formation 1. Here: family history 1 + nails 1 + RF negative 1 = 3. DIP-predominant arthritis: PsA vs nodal or erosive OA (bony nodes, older women, mechanical), gout (tophi, crystals), multicentric reticulohistiocytosis (coral-bead papules), reactive arthritis, and RA (DIPs usually spared). Nail disease mimics: onychomycosis (send clippings), trauma, lichen planus. CASPAR: inflammatory articular disease (joint, spine or entheseal) plus ≥3 points from: - current psoriasis 2, or personal history 1, or family history 1 (if no personal history) - typical nail dystrophy (pitting, onycholysis, hyperkeratosis) 1 - negative RF 1 - dactylitis (current or recorded) 1 - juxta-articular new bone on hand or foot Xray 1 Specificity about 99%, sensitivity about 91%. Look for occult psoriasis: scalp, ears, umbilicus, natal cleft, perianal skin and nails. Consider a dermatology opinion. Screen for comorbidities at diagnosis.

question: A patient with psoriasis has a diffusely swollen second toe, nail pitting and DIP synovitis. What is the diagnosis, and what is dactylitis? Also tested as: What best describes dactylitis in psoriatic arthritis?

options.A: 66 swollen and 68 tender joint counts, CRP, patient global assessment and patient pain
options.B: 3 points; he meets the criteria
options.C: Methotrexate; oral glucocorticoids are not routine and, if needed, are used only at low dose for short periods
options.D: Psoriatic arthritis with dactylitis: diffuse swelling of a whole digit from flexor tenosynovitis, joint synovitis and soft-tissue inflammation
options.E: Bone resorption at the distal end with proliferative new bone at the base of the adjacent phalanx

explanation: Dactylitis, nail dystrophy and DIP involvement are characteristic of PsA. Dactylitis is a hallmark of PsA and other SpA, and persistent dactylitis is a target for treatment escalation. Causes of a sausage digit: PsA, ReA, other SpA; gout or tophaceous disease; sarcoid dactylitis (lytic phalangeal lesions, lupus pernio); TB dactylitis (spina ventosa, children); sickle cell dactylitis (hand-foot syndrome, infants); syphilis; septic tenosynovitis (Kanavel signs: fusiform swelling, flexed posture, pain on passive extension, sheath tenderness); trauma; thyroid acropachy; secondary hypertrophic osteoarthropathy. "Hot" (tender, acute) dactylitis predicts erosion more than "cold" (non-tender) dactylitis. Feet are more often affected than hands. Ultrasound shows flexor tenosynovitis with soft-tissue oedema. NSAIDs and local steroid injection to the tendon sheath. csDMARDs have limited efficacy. Persistent dactylitis warrants a bDMARD (TNFi, IL-17i or IL-23i).

question: Hand radiographs in a patient with long-standing psoriatic arthritis show a pencil-in-cup deformity. What causes this appearance?

options.A: Aortitis with aortic root dilatation and fibrosis extending into the conduction system
options.B: Methotrexate; oral glucocorticoids are not routine and, if needed, are used only at low dose for short periods
options.C: 66 swollen and 68 tender joint counts, CRP, patient global assessment and patient pain
options.D: Proactive assessment of cardiovascular and metabolic risk, obesity, mood and smoking
options.E: Bone resorption at the distal end with proliferative new bone at the base of the adjacent phalanx

explanation: Osteolysis with adjacent new bone formation is typical of PsA. Other features include periostitis, ivory phalanx, ankylosis and relative preservation of bone density. Arthritis mutilans (telescoping "opera-glass" digits) in PsA vs RA, multicentric reticulohistiocytosis, neuropathic arthropathy, hyperparathyroidism or renal osteodystrophy, leprosy, and erosive OA (gull-wing deformity, which is central and not pencil-in-cup). Other PsA radiographic features: fluffy periostitis, enthesophytes, acro-osteolysis, DIP ankylosis, "ivory phalanx" (sclerosis of the distal phalanx), absence of periarticular osteopenia, ray pattern, asymmetric SIJ disease, chunky paramarginal syndesmophytes.

question: What are the seven criteria for minimal disease activity (MDA) in psoriatic arthritis, and how many must be met?

options.A: Methotrexate; oral glucocorticoids are not routine and, if needed, are used only at low dose for short periods
options.B: Bone resorption at the distal end with proliferative new bone at the base of the adjacent phalanx
options.C: Tender joints 1 or less, swollen joints 1 or less, PASI 1 or less (or BSA 3% or less), patient pain VAS 15 or less, patient global VAS 20 or less, HAQ 0.5 or less, and tender entheseal points 1 or less; 5 of 7 are required
options.D: 66 swollen and 68 tender joint counts, CRP, patient global assessment and patient pain
options.E: Proactive assessment of cardiovascular and metabolic risk, obesity, mood and smoking

explanation: MDA criteria: tender joints 1 or less, swollen joints 1 or less, PASI 1 or less (or BSA 3% or less), patient pain VAS 15 or less, patient global VAS 20 or less, HAQ 0.5 or less and tender entheseal points 1 or less. RF status forms part of classification, not disease activity. MDA (≥5 of 7): TJC ≤1, SJC ≤1, PASI ≤1 or BSA ≤3%, pain VAS ≤15, PtGA VAS ≤20, HAQ ≤0.5, tender entheses ≤1. VLDA requires all 7 and is the closest to complete remission. MDA captures skin and enthesitis, whereas DAPSA does not. Treat-to-target: assess every 3 months while active; adjust if there is no improvement by 3 months or the target is not met by 6 months (TICOPA showed better outcomes with tight control).

question: Which components make up the DAPSA score in psoriatic arthritis?

options.A: Bone resorption at the distal end with proliferative new bone at the base of the adjacent phalanx
options.B: Psoriatic arthritis with dactylitis: diffuse swelling of a whole digit from flexor tenosynovitis, joint synovitis and soft-tissue inflammation
options.C: Proactive assessment of cardiovascular and metabolic risk, obesity, mood and smoking
options.D: Methotrexate; oral glucocorticoids are not routine and, if needed, are used only at low dose for short periods
options.E: 66 swollen and 68 tender joint counts, CRP, patient global assessment and patient pain

explanation: DAPSA sums 66 swollen and 68 tender joints, CRP (mg/dL), patient global and pain scores. Remission is 4 or less, low activity above 4 to 14, moderate above 14 to 28 and high above 28. DAPSA remission ≤4, low ≤14, moderate ≤28, high >28; cDAPSA omits CRP (useful on IL-6 or JAK blockade or with a normal CRP). DAPSA ignores skin, enthesitis and axial disease, so pair it with domain measures.

question: A woman with newly diagnosed PsA has 7 swollen joints and moderate plaque psoriasis. What is the most appropriate first DMARD, and what is the role of oral glucocorticoids? Also tested as: What is the role of oral glucocorticoids in psoriatic arthritis?

options.A: 66 swollen and 68 tender joint counts, CRP, patient global assessment and patient pain
options.B: Apremilast
options.C: Neither treats axial disease; sulfasalazine may be considered for peripheral arthritis, and local glucocorticoid injection may help peripheral arthritis or enthesitis
options.D: Methotrexate; oral glucocorticoids are not routine and, if needed, are used only at low dose for short periods
options.E: Add an IL-17 or IL-23 inhibitor

explanation: A csDMARD should be started promptly for polyarthritis, with methotrexate preferred when skin involvement is relevant. Hydroxychloroquine is ineffective in PsA. Systemic glucocorticoids have limited benefit, can provoke pustular or erythrodermic psoriasis on withdrawal and cause cumulative harm; intra-articular injection is useful for oligoarticular flares. Other csDMARDs: leflunomide (good evidence, TOPAS) and sulfasalazine (peripheral arthritis only, little skin effect). Ciclosporin is rarely used (nephrotoxicity, hypertension). Hydroxychloroquine is ineffective and may flare psoriasis. Poor-prognosis features that justify early escalation: polyarticular disease, raised CRP, dactylitis, erosions, high HAQ, nail disease. Methotrexate 15–25 mg weekly with folate. Consider FIB-4 or elastography if NAFLD or alcohol excess is suspected (common in PsA). If methotrexate is unsuitable (liver disease, pregnancy plans), use leflunomide or sulfasalazine, or proceed directly to a biologic. Enthesitis and axial disease bypass csDMARDs.

question: A patient with PsA has active polyarthritis despite methotrexate 20 mg weekly for 4 months and extensive plaque psoriasis (PASI 14). What is the most appropriate next step?

options.A: At least 1 month before conception, continuing folic acid
options.B: An IL-17 inhibitor
options.C: Add an IL-17 or IL-23 inhibitor
options.D: Optimise it: increase to 20–25 mg weekly, switch to subcutaneous administration (better bioavailability and tolerability), optimise folic acid and reassess within 1–3 months
options.E: Methotrexate; oral glucocorticoids are not routine and, if needed, are used only at low dose for short periods

explanation: After csDMARD failure in peripheral PsA a bDMARD is started. With relevant skin disease, IL-17A, IL-17A/F, IL-23 or IL- 12/23 inhibitors may be preferred because of their greater skin efficacy than TNF inhibitors. Biologic choice by domain: | Situation | Preferred | |---|---| | Significant psoriasis | IL-17A (secukinumab, ixekizumab), IL-17A/F (bimekizumab) or IL-23 (guselkumab, risankizumab) | | Axial | TNFi or IL-17i (JAKi) | | Uveitis | mAb TNFi | | IBD | mAb TNFi, IL-23i or ustekinumab, upadacitinib; avoid IL-17i | | Nails | IL-17, IL-23 or TNFi | | Enthesitis or dactylitis | any bDMARD (TNF, IL-17, IL-23) | | Pregnancy plans | certolizumab | Step 3 (bDMARD failure): switch bDMARD, or JAKi (tofacitinib, upadacitinib) after CV, VTE and cancer risk assessment. Abatacept is an option but has little skin effect. Weight loss improves response.

question: A 66-year-old woman with PsA has mild oligoarthritis despite methotrexate and declines injections. A biologic or JAK inhibitor is not considered appropriate. Which oral drug is most suitable?

options.A: Methotrexate; oral glucocorticoids are not routine and, if needed, are used only at low dose for short periods
options.B: Add an IL-17 or IL-23 inhibitor
options.C: Apremilast
options.D: This pattern usually parallels bowel activity and is self-limiting
options.E: An IL-1 inhibitor such as canakinumab or anakinra

explanation: In mild disease with inadequate response to at least one csDMARD where a biologic or JAK inhibitor is not appropriate, a PDE4 inhibitor may be considered. Intra-articular glucocorticoid also helps oligoarticular flares. Apremilast: modest efficacy, no laboratory monitoring, oral; GI upset and weight loss; mood monitoring. Suited to mild oligoarticular disease without poor prognostic factors, or skin-predominant disease, when a b/tsDMARD is unsuitable. Deucravacitinib (TYK2) is licensed for psoriasis, with PsA trials ongoing. Image-guided or landmark IA steroid for single joints. Consider subcutaneous options if the patient will accept them later, and offer self-injection support.

question: A patient with PsA has persistent Achilles enthesitis confirmed on ultrasound despite two NSAIDs and a local programme of physiotherapy. Peripheral joints are quiet. What is the most appropriate next step?

options.A: Apremilast
options.B: Add an IL-17 or IL-23 inhibitor
options.C: Methotrexate; oral glucocorticoids are not routine and, if needed, are used only at low dose for short periods
options.D: Start a biologic DMARD such as a TNF or IL-17 inhibitor csDMARDs have little effect on enthesitis. Persistent, clinically significant enthesitis after NSAIDs warrants a bDMARD. Glucocorticoid injection into or around the
options.E: An IL-1 inhibitor such as canakinumab or anakinra

explanation: Achilles tendon is avoided because of rupture risk. Heel pain: SpA enthesitis (Achilles insertion, plantar fascia) vs mechanical Achilles tendinopathy (mid-portion, athletic), plantar fasciopathy, retrocalcaneal bursitis, Haglund deformity, calcaneal stress fracture, fluoroquinolone tendinopathy, gout or xanthoma (familial hypercholesterolaemia, with nodular thickened tendons), DISH or enthesophytes, X-linked hypophosphataemia. Ultrasound signs of enthesitis: hypoechogenicity, thickening, Doppler signal at the insertion, erosions and enthesophytes. Fibromyalgia tender points can mimic enthesitis on examination. csDMARDs do not help enthesitis. Use NSAIDs, physiotherapy, heel raises and orthoses, then a bDMARD (TNFi, IL-17i, IL-23i or JAKi). Never inject steroid into the Achilles tendon. Plantar fascia injection, if used, should be given from the medial side, not through the heel pad.

question: A patient with mild-looking psoriasis has distressing genital and scalp lesions and active arthritis. How should the skin disease be weighed when choosing treatment?

options.A: Methotrexate; oral glucocorticoids are not routine and, if needed, are used only at low dose for short periods
options.B: Prior infection history, glucocorticoid exposure, vaccination status, comorbidities and the infection profile of each option
options.C: As clinically relevant, because impact and sensitive sites matter as well as body surface area
options.D: 3 points; he meets the criteria
options.E: Add an IL-17 or IL-23 inhibitor

explanation: Psoriasis is clinically relevant when it is extensive or has substantial impact, including scalp, nail, genital and flexural disease. This influences drug choice and joint care with dermatology. Define clinically relevant psoriasis as BSA >10%, PASI >10, DLQI >10, or involvement of special sites (scalp, nails, genital, palmoplantar, flexural, face). Choose agents with high skin efficacy (IL-17 or IL-23). Topicals and phototherapy for mild skin disease. Deucravacitinib, methotrexate, ciclosporin or acitretin are dermatological options; acitretin is teratogenic for 3 years after stopping.

question: Paradoxical psoriasiform eruptions, including palmoplantar pustulosis, are a recognised class effect of which drugs?

options.A: Switch to losartan or a calcium-channel blocker
options.B: 1 mg, followed 1 hour later by 0.5 mg on day 1, then low dose until the flare settles
options.C: HLA-B*58:01 genotyping
options.D: TNF inhibitors
options.E: SAPHO syndrome

explanation: Paradoxical psoriasis is a recognised class effect of TNF inhibitors. Management includes topical therapy, switching TNF inhibitor or changing to an IL-17 or IL-23 pathway agent. Paradoxical reactions to TNFi: psoriasis (palmoplantar pustulosis, scalp, plaques), hidradenitis, IBD (etanercept), uveitis (etanercept), sarcoid-like granulomas, drug-induced lupus (anti-dsDNA, anti-histone), vasculitis, demyelination, alopecia areata. Main differential: true psoriasis flare, or eczema and fungal infection of the feet. Paradoxical psoriasis is driven by unopposed plasmacytoid dendritic cell type I IFN. It occurs with any TNFi and in any indication (including in patients without prior psoriasis, e.g. Crohn's or RA). It is more common in women and smokers. Mild: topical steroids or vitamin D analogues, continuing the TNFi. Moderate to severe: switch to an IL-17 or IL-23 pathway drug (or ustekinumab, which treats both if IBD is present). Switching TNFi helps in some patients but recurrence is common.

question: Alongside inflammatory disease control, which comorbidity strategy is particularly important in psoriatic arthritis?
