Other drug causes of tendinopathy: statins (rare), aromatase inhibitors (tenosynovitis, trigger finger), local steroid injection, anabolic steroids, isotretinoin. Patient factors: age >60, renal failure, transplant recipients, RA, diabetes, gout. Avoid fluoroquinolones unless there is no alternative, particularly with concomitant GC (MHRA advice). If tendon pain develops: stop the drug, rest the tendon and get ultrasound. A ruptured Achilles needs orthopaedic review (Simmonds' test).

question: A 64-year-old woman with knee osteoarthritis develops sudden pain and swelling of the right calf after gardening. A crescent of bruising appears below the medial malleolus. What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.A: Radiofrequency denervation after a positive medial branch block
options.B: Posterior tibial nerve under the flexor retinaculum
options.C: Refer to a hand surgeon to discuss needle fasciotomy or limited fasciectomy
options.D: Compression ultrasound of the leg
options.E: Plantar fascia and calf stretching, supportive footwear and load modification

explanation: A ruptured popliteal (Baker's) cyst mimics DVT, and the two can coexist. Ultrasound distinguishes them. The 'crescent sign' of bruising around the malleolus suggests cyst rupture, but DVT must still be excluded before treatment. Acute calf pain: DVT, ruptured Baker's cyst ("pseudothrombophlebitis"), gastrocnemius (medial head) tear ("tennis leg"), plantaris rupture, compartment syndrome, cellulitis, superficial thrombophlebitis, haematoma on anticoagulation, popliteal artery aneurysm thrombosis (pulses), myositis. Compression ultrasound. Treat the underlying knee synovitis (aspiration and IA steroid). Analgesia and elevation for cyst rupture. Anticoagulate if DVT is confirmed (both can coexist).

question: A 24-year-old footballer has 6 months of deep groin pain on sitting and during kicking. Pain is reproduced by passive hip flexion, adduction and internal rotation. Radiographs show a non-spherical femoral head-neck junction. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.A: Transient osteoporosis of the hip
options.B: MRI of both hips
options.C: Spondylolysis (pars interarticularis stress fracture)
options.D: Lumbar spinal stenosis (neurogenic claudication)
options.E: Femoroacetabular impingement (cam type)

explanation: A positive FADIR test with a cam deformity indicates femoroacetabular impingement, which can cause labral and chondral damage. Management starts with activity modification and physiotherapy; arthroscopic surgery is considered for persistent symptoms. SUFE presents in younger adolescents. Young adult hip or groin pain: FAI (cam or pincer) with labral tear vs adductor-related groin pain, inguinal-related pain (sportsman's hernia), osteitis pubis, femoral neck stress fracture (urgent MRI; tension-side fractures need surgery), AVN, SUFE (adolescents), DDH, iliopsoas tendinopathy or bursitis ("snapping hip"), axSpA, sacroiliitis, referred lumbar pain. FADIR (flexion, adduction, internal rotation) is sensitive but not specific. X-ray shows a cam deformity (non-spherical head–neck junction, raised alpha angle) or pincer deformity (crossover sign, acetabular over-coverage). MR arthrogram assesses the labrum and cartilage. Activity modification and physiotherapy (core and hip strengthening). Intra-articular injection can be diagnostic. Hip arthroscopy (FASHIoN and UK FAIT trials showed modest benefit over physiotherapy) for persistent symptoms without significant OA.

question: A patient with low back pain develops bilateral sciatica and new perineal or saddle sensory loss, with or without urinary retention. What is the most appropriate action, and which other back pain features are red flags? Also tested as: A 38-year-old woman has bilateral sciatica and, since this morning, reduced sensation around the anus and perineum. She is still passing urine normally. What is the most appropriate action? | Which feature in a patient with back pain is a red flag requiring urgent assessment rather than routine management?

options.A: Emergency lumbar MRI immediately, at any time of day, with same-day spinal surgical referral; other red flags are fever or immunosuppression (infection), weight loss or a cancer history (malignancy), significant trauma or osteoporosis (fracture), and progressive neurological deficit
options.B: Plantar fascia and calf stretching, supportive footwear and load modification
options.C: Stop both; use an NSAID if needed, keep active, consider epidural steroid if severe
options.D: Aspirate for Gram stain, culture and crystals; start antistaphylococcal antibiotic
options.E: Radiofrequency denervation after a positive medial branch block

explanation: Suspected cauda equina syndrome is a surgical emergency, and delay worsens bladder, bowel and sexual outcomes. Outcomes are best when decompression occurs before retention (incomplete CES, CES-I); established retention (CES-R) carries a worse prognosis. Emergency MRI is indicated regardless of time of day, and a normal bladder scan does not exclude the diagnosis. CES mimics and causes: central disc herniation (the commonest cause, at L4/5 or L5/S1), spinal stenosis with acute decompensation, epidural abscess or haematoma (anticoagulation, post-procedure), metastatic cord or cauda equina compression, AS with dural ectasia (arachnoid diverticula), conus medullaris lesion, GBS, transverse myelitis (SLE, Sjögren's, NMOSD), functional neurological disorder. Non-spinal back pain: AAA, renal colic or pyelonephritis, pancreatitis, gynaecological disease or endometriosis, hip OA, herpes zoster. CES features: bilateral leg symptoms, saddle or perineal anaesthesia, new bladder dysfunction (reduced sensation, poor stream, retention), bowel incontinence, sexual dysfunction, reduced anal tone. A history of cancer is the most specific red flag; others have low specificity individually. The national pathway (GIRFT) aims for MRI within about 4 hours. Do a post-void bladder scan, but do not wait for retention. Red-flag bloods: FBC, CRP or ESR, protein electrophoresis and free light chains, calcium, ALP, PSA. Spondylodiscitis: blood cultures and biopsy before antibiotics if stable, and treat for at least 6 weeks. Metastatic spinal cord compression: dexamethasone and urgent oncology.

question: A 74-year-old man has bilateral buttock and thigh aching after walking 200 m. It is relieved by sitting or leaning forward on a shopping trolley but not by standing still. Foot pulses are normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.A: Spondylolysis (pars interarticularis stress fracture)
options.B: Lumbar spinal stenosis (neurogenic claudication)
options.C: Femoroacetabular impingement (cam type)
options.D: Lateral femoral cutaneous nerve entrapment
options.E: Posterior tibial nerve under the flexor retinaculum

explanation: Neurogenic claudication is relieved by lumbar flexion (sitting, stooping) rather than by simply stopping, and pulses are preserved. Vascular claudication eases on standing still. MRI confirms canal stenosis; decompression is considered for disabling or progressive symptoms. Hip OA (groin pain, reduced internal rotation), trochanteric pain syndrome, peripheral neuropathy, venous claudication, spinal AVM, ATTR amyloid (lumbar stenosis is an early "red flag" feature). Feature Neurogenic Vascular Relief sitting or flexion standing still (minutes) (seconds to minutes) Posture worse with irrelevant extension or standing Cycling, uphill tolerated provokes walking symptoms Pulses and normal reduced ABPI Sensory common uncommon symptoms Flexion-based physiotherapy, walking or cycling programme, weight loss, analgesia. Epidural steroids give little benefit in stenosis. Decompression (laminectomy) beats continued conservative care for severe, refractory symptoms. Adding fusion is usually unnecessary without instability (Swedish Spinal Stenosis Study).

question: A 29-year-old man has 3 weeks of L5 sciatica with no neurological deficit or red flags. His GP started pregabalin and diazepam. What is the most appropriate advice?

options.A: Radiofrequency denervation after a positive medial branch block
options.B: Stop both; use an NSAID if needed, keep active, consider epidural steroid if severe
options.C: Aspirate for Gram stain, culture and crystals; start antistaphylococcal antibiotic
options.D: Explain the pain mechanism, support graded activity and rehabilitation, and address psychosocial factors while remaining alert to red flags
options.E: Exercise and psychological therapy, considering an antidepressant, and tapering analgesics

explanation: Gabapentinoids, other antiepileptics, oral corticosteroids and benzodiazepines are not recommended for sciatica because of lack of benefit and harms. Older texts suggested diazepam for spasm; this is no longer advised. Most disc-related sciatica improves within 3 months. Sciatica has a lifetime incidence of 13–40% and peaks at 45–64. Most cases improve over 6–12 weeks; large sequestered fragments often regress. 10–20% still have symptoms at 1 year. SLR at 30–70° has about 90% sensitivity; crossed SLR has about 90% specificity for disc herniation. The femoral stretch test assesses L2–L4. Stay active and do physiotherapy. Short-course NSAIDs. Image-guided epidural steroid for acute severe sciatica (short-term relief only; does not reduce surgery). Pregabalin was no better than placebo (PRECISE). Use amitriptyline or duloxetine only selectively, with stopping rules. Microdiscectomy for CES, progressive motor deficit, or disabling pain beyond 6–12 weeks with matching MRI: it gives faster relief, but 1–2-year outcomes are similar.

question: A man has back pain radiating to the dorsum of the foot, weak great toe extension and ankle dorsiflexion, dorsal foot sensory loss and normal reflexes. Which nerve root is affected?

options.A: L5
options.B: Posterior tibial nerve under the flexor retinaculum
options.C: Interdigital (Morton's) neuroma
options.D: Lumbar spinal stenosis (neurogenic claudication)
options.E: Spondylolysis (pars interarticularis stress fracture)

explanation: L5 radiculopathy, usually from an L4/5 disc, causes weakness of EHL, ankle dorsiflexion and hip abduction, with dorsal foot and great toe sensory loss; the major reflexes are usually preserved. A reduced ankle reflex with weak plantarflexion and lateral foot sensory loss indicates S1. Foot drop: L5 radiculopathy (inversion and hip abduction weak, back pain) vs common peroneal neuropathy (inversion spared), sciatic neuropathy (piriformis or deep gluteal syndrome), lumbosacral plexopathy (tumour, haematoma, diabetic amyotrophy), mononeuritis multiplex (vasculitis), MND, HNPP, parasagittal cortical lesion (UMN signs). Root Weakness Sensory Reflex L3 knee extension, hip anterior thigh knee adduction to medial knee L4 knee extension, ankle medial shin knee dorsiflexion and inversion L5 EHL, ankle (medial dorsum of dorsiflexion, hip foot, great hamstring) abduction, inversion toe S1 plantarflexion, lateral foot, ankle eversion, hip sole extension

question: A 15-year-old fast bowler has 2 months of low back pain that is worse on extension and on standing on one leg while extending the spine. Neurology is normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.A: Spondylolysis (pars interarticularis stress fracture)
options.B: Posterior tibial nerve under the flexor retinaculum
options.C: Lumbar spinal stenosis (neurogenic claudication)
options.D: Lateral femoral cutaneous nerve entrapment
options.E: Radiofrequency denervation after a positive medial branch block

explanation: Pars stress fractures, usually at L5, occur in adolescents who repeatedly hyperextend, such as fast bowlers and gymnasts. MRI (or SPECT/CT) detects early stress reaction. Management is activity modification and rehabilitation; bracing is sometimes used. Adolescent extension-related pain: spondylolysis vs facet irritation, Scheuermann's, disc herniation (flexion-related), osteoid osteoma (night pain relieved by NSAIDs), ERA or juvenile SpA, discitis (young children who refuse to walk), tumour (Ewing's, leukaemia, ABC). Pars stress fractures (usually L5) occur in extension sports, with prevalence about 6%. Progression risk is higher in girls, dysplastic slips, high-grade slips and during the growth spurt. Meyerding grades I–V. The "one-legged hyperextension (stork) test" is positive. Rest from sport for 6–12 weeks; core and hamstring physiotherapy; a brace for early (acute) lysis to promote healing; fusion for high-grade (III–IV), progressive or neurologically symptomatic slips.

question: A 16-year-old boy has a rigid thoracic kyphosis that does not correct on extension. Radiographs show wedging of three adjacent vertebrae with Schmorl's nodes. What is the diagnosis?

options.A: Osteomalacia due to vitamin D deficiency
options.B: The 10-year probability of a major osteoporotic fracture and of hip fracture
options.C: Scheuermann's disease
options.D: Spondylolysis (pars interarticularis stress fracture)
options.E: Femoroacetabular impingement (cam type)

explanation: Scheuermann's kyphosis is a structural adolescent kyphosis defined by wedging in at least three adjacent vertebrae. Postural kyphosis corrects on extension. Most cases are managed with extension-focused physiotherapy; bracing or surgery is reserved for severe deformity. Postural kyphosis (corrects on extension), congenital kyphosis, AS (older, sacroiliitis), osteoporotic wedge fractures, infection (TB gibbus), neuromuscular disease. Scheuermann's: wedging ≥5° of ≥3 adjacent vertebrae, endplate irregularity, Schmorl's nodes, rigid thoracic kyphosis >45°. Extension-focused physiotherapy; a brace while still growing; surgery for severe deformity (>70–75°) or intractable pain.

question: A 61-year-old woman has chronic low back pain without sciatica. Non-surgical treatment has failed, and clinical assessment suggests facet joint origin. Her pain is moderate to severe. Which intervention is appropriate to consider?

options.A: Exercise and psychological therapy, considering an antidepressant, and tapering analgesics
options.B: Spondylolysis (pars interarticularis stress fracture)
options.C: Stop both; use an NSAID if needed, keep active, consider epidural steroid if severe
options.D: Femoroacetabular impingement (cam type)
options.E: Radiofrequency denervation after a positive medial branch block

explanation: Radiofrequency denervation can be considered for chronic low back pain thought to arise from the facet joints, but only after a positive diagnostic medial branch block. Facet steroid injections have not shown benefit over placebo, and spinal injections are not recommended for non-specific low back pain. Facet RF denervation (NICE NG59) is used only after a positive diagnostic medial branch block and failed nonsurgical care; benefit in RCTs is mixed (MINT). Other interventions: epidural steroid for acute severe sciatica only; basivertebral nerve ablation for Modic-related chronic LBP (emerging); spinal cord stimulation for persistent spinal pain after surgery with neuropathic leg pain. Do not offer facet steroid injections, discography, fusion or disc replacement for non-specific LBP outside research.

question: A 44-year-old woman has 18 months of chronic primary pain without an identifiable underlying condition. She is taking codeine, pregabalin and naproxen with little benefit. Which management is most appropriate?

options.A: Posterior tibial nerve under the flexor retinaculum
options.B: Radiofrequency denervation after a positive medial branch block
options.C: Stop both; use an NSAID if needed, keep active, consider epidural steroid if severe
options.D: Exercise and psychological therapy, considering an antidepressant, and tapering analgesics
options.E: Plantar fascia and calf stretching, supportive footwear and load modification

explanation: For chronic primary pain, current guidance supports exercise programmes, psychological therapies and acupuncture, and allows consideration of selected antidepressants. Opioids, gabapentinoids, NSAIDs, paracetamol and benzodiazepines should not be started, and existing ones should be reviewed and tapered through shared decisionmaking. NICE NG193 chronic primary pain options: supervised group exercise, CBT or ACT, acupuncture (within a course), and antidepressants (amitriptyline, citalopram, duloxetine, fluoxetine, paroxetine, sertraline). Do not start gabapentinoids, opioids, NSAIDs, paracetamol, benzodiazepines, local anaesthetic or steroid injections, or ketamine. Taper existing opioids and gabapentinoids gradually (about 10% every 2–4 weeks) with shared goals; watch for withdrawal and mood change. Consider a pain management programme. Screen for depression and suicide risk.

question: A 72-year-old woman has a painful acute L1 osteoporotic compression fracture. What does early management involve, and when is vertebral augmentation appropriate?

options.A: The 10-year probability of a major osteoporotic fracture and of hip fracture
options.B: Analgesia and mobilisation; augmentation only for severe persistent pain at a recent fracture
options.C: Hypophosphatasia; avoid bisphosphonates; check pyridoxal-5'-phosphate and ALPL genetics
options.D: Exercise and psychological therapy, considering an antidepressant, and tapering analgesics
options.E: Interdigital (Morton's) neuroma

explanation: Older texts recommended calcitonin for fracture pain, but long-term calcitonin is no longer used because of an increased malignancy risk. Vertebral augmentation is limited to severe persistent pain at a recent fracture confirmed on MRI. Osteoporosis treatment and falls assessment should follow. Acute vertebral fracture: osteoporosis vs metastasis or myeloma (posterior element involvement, convex posterior border and soft-tissue mass on MRI, pedicle destruction, above T5), infection, trauma. Low-energy fracture in a younger patient or a man warrants a secondary osteoporosis screen. Many vertebral fractures are silent (height loss >4 cm, kyphosis). Vertebral fracture assessment on DXA or a lateral spine film detects them. Analgesia (paracetamol, short NSAIDs or opioids with laxatives), early mobilisation, physiotherapy, a short spinal brace in selected patients. NICE TA279: augmentation (vertebroplasty or kyphoplasty) only for severe ongoing pain after a recent fracture confirmed on MRI despite optimal analgesia; sham-controlled trials were mixed. Start osteoporosis treatment (often an anabolic agent if there are multiple vertebral fractures) and a falls assessment.

question: What DXA T-score defines osteoporosis in a postmenopausal woman?

options.A: -2.5 or lower
options.B: Do not stop without follow-on therapy; plan a bisphosphonate (often zoledronate) about 6 months after the last dose
options.C: An oral bisphosphonate (alendronate or risedronate) with calcium and vitamin D repletion; take it once weekly on an empty stomach with plain water, stay upright for at least 30 minutes and delay food for 30 minutes
options.D: Testosterone, myeloma screen, coeliac serology, calcium/PTH and vitamin D
options.E: Analgesia and mobilisation; augmentation only for severe persistent pain at a recent fracture

explanation: A T-score of -2.5 or lower at the lumbar spine, femoral neck or total hip defines osteoporosis; -1.0 to -2.5 is osteopenia. T-scores apply to postmenopausal women and men aged 50 or over. Low BMD is not always osteoporosis: osteomalacia (raised ALP, low phosphate or calcium, Looser zones), myeloma, hyperparathyroidism, renal osteodystrophy, OI, hypophosphatasia, mastocytosis, Gaucher's. Severe or established osteoporosis means T ≤-2.5 plus a fragility fracture. A hip or vertebral fragility fracture establishes osteoporosis clinically regardless of BMD. Fractures of the skull, face, fingers and toes are not fragility sites. Core secondary screen: FBC, ESR or CRP, adjusted calcium, phosphate, ALP, albumin, eGFR, LFTs, 25(OH)D, PTH, TSH, SPEP and FLC, coeliac serology (tTG); testosterone, SHBG, LH and FSH in men. Targeted tests: 24-hour urine calcium, cortisol, tryptase, PSA, HbA1c.

question: What does FRAX estimate?

options.A: The 10-year probability of a major osteoporotic fracture and of hip fracture
options.B: Analgesia and mobilisation; augmentation only for severe persistent pain at a recent fracture
options.C: Testosterone, myeloma screen, coeliac serology, calcium/PTH and vitamin D
options.D: Osteosarcoma arising in pagetic bone
options.E: Scheuermann's disease

explanation: FRAX combines age, sex, BMI, prior fracture, parental hip fracture, smoking, glucocorticoids, RA, secondary osteoporosis and alcohol, with or without femoral neck BMD. Standard FRAX underestimates risk with high-dose glucocorticoids and multiple fractures. FRAX inputs: age, sex, BMI, prior fracture, parental hip fracture, current smoking, GC (≥5 mg for ≥3 months), RA, secondary osteoporosis, alcohol ≥3 units/day, ± femoral neck BMD. It underestimates risk with high-dose GC, recent, multiple or vertebral fractures, falls, diabetes and spine–hip discordance. UK practice (NOGG) uses age-dependent FRAX thresholds with high and very high risk categories. The US uses fixed thresholds (MOF ≥20% or hip ≥3%). QFracture is an alternative UK tool that includes falls and more comorbidities.

question: A woman on prednisolone has, or is about to start, long-term glucocorticoids: for example a 68-year-old on 7.5 mg daily with a wrist fragility fracture and femoral neck T-score -1.8, or a 74-year-old starting 40 mg daily for GCA. How should bone protection be decided? Also tested as: A 74-year-old woman is starting prednisolone 40 mg daily for GCA, expected to continue for more than 3 months. She has no previous fracture. What is the most appropriate bone management?

options.A: Both need bone protection now: prior fragility fracture, age 70 or over, or 7.5 mg/day or more for 3 months or more confer high fracture risk despite an osteopenic T-score, so treatment (such as oral alendronate
options.B: Achilles tendinopathy and tendon rupture
options.C: Analgesia and mobilisation; augmentation only for severe persistent pain at a recent fracture
options.D: Do not stop without follow-on therapy; plan a bisphosphonate (often zoledronate) about 6 months after the last dose
options.E: Lumbar spinal stenosis (neurogenic claudication)

explanation: with calcium and vitamin D) should start with the glucocorticoid without waiting for DXA Glucocorticoids increase fracture risk at higher BMD than in postmenopausal osteoporosis, and fracture risk rises within weeks of starting them. Fracture risk depends on the whole clinical picture. People aged 70 or over, those with a prior fragility fracture, or those on 7.5 mg/day or more for 3 months or more should start bone protection without waiting for DXA. GIOP is the commonest secondary cause. The main mechanism is osteoblast and osteocyte apoptosis (reduced formation), with an early resorption rise, reduced calcium absorption, hypogonadism, and myopathy with falls. Risk rises within 3–6 months even at 2.5–7.5 mg/day. 30–50% of long-term users fracture. Assess within 6 months of starting ≥2.5 mg/day for ≥3 months in adults ≥40 (FRAX + BMD); in under-40s only with a prior fracture or other risks. Adjust FRAX for >7.5 mg/day: MOF ×1.15, hip ×1.2. Moderate risk: oral bisphosphonate first-line; zoledronate if oral is unsuitable. High or very high risk: teriparatide is superior to alendronate for vertebral fractures in GIOP. Denosumab is effective but needs a bisphosphonate follow-on. Ongoing: reassess every 12–18 months; consider stopping bone therapy once GC stops and risk falls. Women of childbearing potential: use bisphosphonates cautiously (long skeletal retention); prefer teriparatide, calcium and vitamin D where possible.

question: What is first-line pharmacological treatment for most postmenopausal women with osteoporosis, and which counselling point is essential for oral alendronate? Also tested as: Which counselling point is essential for oral alendronate?

options.A: Hypophosphatasia; avoid bisphosphonates; check pyridoxal-5'-phosphate and ALPL genetics
options.B: An oral bisphosphonate (alendronate or risedronate) with calcium and vitamin D repletion; take it once weekly on an empty stomach with plain water, stay upright for at least 30 minutes and delay food for 30 minutes
options.C: Transient osteoporosis of the hip
options.D: Radiofrequency denervation after a positive medial branch block
options.E: -2.5 or lower

explanation: Oral bisphosphonates are first-line unless contraindicated or not tolerated, with IV zoledronate as an alternative. Correct administration avoids poor absorption and oesophagitis, and calcium and other medicines should be separated from the dose. Dental review is important. Contraindications to oral bisphosphonates: eGFR <30–35, oesophageal stricture or achalasia, inability to stay upright for 30 minutes, hypocalcaemia, pregnancy. Alternatives: IV zoledronate (needs eGFR ≥35 and hydration) or denosumab (no renal clearance). Fracture reduction: alendronate and risedronate reduce vertebral fractures by about 40–70% and hip fractures by about 40%. Zoledronate (5 mg IV yearly) reduces vertebral fractures by about 70%, reduced mortality after hip fracture, and causes an acute-phase reaction (mainly with the first dose). Denosumab reduces vertebral fractures by about 68% and hip by about 40%. Raloxifene reduces vertebral fractures only, carries VTE risk and reduces breast cancer. HRT is first-line for women <60 or within 10 years of menopause with symptoms. Non-drug measures: progressive resistance and impact exercise, balance training (tai chi, Otago), falls prevention (home hazards, vision, sedative review, hip protectors in care homes), stop smoking, protein 1–1.2 g/kg/day.

question: A 72-year-old with two recent vertebral fractures and a spine T-score of -3.6 needs treatment. What is the best initial approach, and what are the key contraindications of romosozumab and teriparatide? Also tested as: Which is an absolute contraindication to romosozumab? | What are the contraindications to teriparatide?

options.A: Hypophosphatasia; avoid bisphosphonates; check pyridoxal-5'-phosphate and ALPL genetics
options.B: Testosterone, myeloma screen, coeliac serology, calcium/PTH and vitamin D
options.C: Spondylolysis (pars interarticularis stress fracture)
options.D: Analgesia and mobilisation; augmentation only for severe persistent pain at a recent fracture
options.E: An anabolic agent first (teriparatide, or romosozumab if there is no prior MI or stroke), followed by antiresorptive therapy; romosozumab is contraindicated after myocardial infarction or stroke, and teriparatide after skeletal radiotherapy, in

explanation: Paget's disease or unexplained raised ALP, with open epiphyses, bone malignancy or metastases, hypercalcaemia or severe renal impairment Very high fracture risk (recent or multiple vertebral fractures, very low T-score) favours anabolic therapy first, followed by an antiresorptive to consolidate gains. An imbalance in serious cardiovascular events was seen in a pivotal trial of romosozumab, which is given monthly for 12 months only and must be followed by antiresorptive therapy. Because of an osteosarcoma signal in rats, teriparatide is contraindicated in the situations above; treatment is limited to 24 months, and it is effective in glucocorticoid-induced osteoporosis. The EULAR course notes the rat osteosarcoma signal has not been borne out in human surveillance, but the label contraindications still apply. Very high risk includes recent fracture (within 12–24 months, especially vertebral or hip), multiple fractures, fracture on treatment, T ≤-3.0 (≤-3.5 in some guidance), very high FRAX and high-dose GC. VERO: teriparatide beat risedronate for vertebral fractures. ARCH: romosozumab followed by alendronate beat alendronate alone. Abaloparatide (PTHrP analogue, 80 µg) is an alternative. Sequencing: anabolic then antiresorptive is best. Bisphosphonate then anabolic is acceptable but gives a blunted response. Going from denosumab to teriparatide causes transient hip bone loss, so avoid it or overlap the two. Always follow an anabolic immediately with an antiresorptive.

question: A 70-year-old woman has received denosumab 60 mg every 6 months for 5 years. She wants to stop because of planned dental work. What is the most important advice?

options.A: Replete vitamin D (and correct calcium) first, then give the drug and recheck calcium afterwards; in advanced CKD consider CKD-mineral bone disorder before choosing an antiresorptive
options.B: MRI of both hips
options.C: Testosterone, myeloma screen, coeliac serology, calcium/PTH and vitamin D
options.D: Do not stop without follow-on therapy; plan a bisphosphonate (often zoledronate) about 6 months after the last dose
options.E: Exercise and psychological therapy, considering an antidepressant, and tapering analgesics

explanation: Stopping or delaying denosumab causes rapid rebound bone turnover and a risk of multiple vertebral fractures. A bisphosphonate is given as follow-on, with turnover markers guiding further dosing. Rebound after stopping denosumab: turnover overshoots above baseline 3–18 months after the last dose, with a risk of multiple vertebral fractures, especially after longer use and in people with prior vertebral fractures. Denosumab has no drug holiday. Give zoledronate about 6 months after the last denosumab dose, monitoring CTX at 3 and 6 months and repeating zoledronate if CTX rises. Or continue denosumab long term (studied to 10 years). Dental work: routine dentistry is fine. For extractions, there is no need to stop; coordinate timing (dental work about 3–4 months after a dose, next dose after healing) and use good oral hygiene. Biosimilars are now available.

question: A woman on alendronate for 8 years has 2 months of dull thigh pain. Which rare complications are linked to long-term antiresorptives, and what should be done? Also tested as: Osteonecrosis of the jaw and atypical femoral fracture are rare complications most associated with which treatment?

options.A: Transient osteoporosis of the hip
options.B: Hypophosphatasia; avoid bisphosphonates; check pyridoxal-5'-phosphate and ALPL genetics
options.C: Analgesia and mobilisation; augmentation only for severe persistent pain at a recent fracture
options.D: Atypical femoral fracture and osteonecrosis of the jaw; get full-length radiographs of both femora (MRI or isotope imaging if normal and suspicion persists) and stop the bisphosphonate if an AFF or stress reaction is found
options.E: Do not stop without follow-on therapy; plan a bisphosphonate (often zoledronate) about 6 months after the last dose

explanation: Prodromal thigh or groin pain in long-term bisphosphonate users may precede an atypical femoral fracture, which is often bilateral. Osteonecrosis of the jaw and AFF are rare complications of long-term antiresorptive therapy with bisphosphonates or denosumab. Good dental hygiene and dental review before treatment reduce ONJ risk, and drug holidays can be considered in lower-risk long-term bisphosphonate users. Thigh pain on bisphosphonates: AFF or stress reaction vs hip OA, trochanteric pain, L3 radiculopathy, osteomalacia (Looser zone on the medial femoral neck), hypophosphatasia (bisphosphonates worsen it), metastasis, Paget's. AFF: a transverse subtrochanteric or shaft fracture from low energy, with lateral cortical "beaking". Risk rises after 3–5 years and in Asian patients and those on GC. ONJ: exposed necrotic jaw bone for >8 weeks without prior radiation; about 1 in 10,000 to 1 in 100,000 patient-years in osteoporosis, far higher at oncology doses. Risk factors: extraction or implants, poor hygiene, GC, smoking, diabetes, long duration, anti-angiogenic drugs. Other bisphosphonate effects: hypocalcaemia, AF (zoledronate; inconsistent), uveitis or scleritis, oesophagitis. Stop the antiresorptive, give teriparatide, and arrange orthopaedic review (prophylactic intramedullary nailing for incomplete fractures with pain). Image the contralateral femur. Check vitamin D and ALP. Overall, fractures prevented far outnumber AFFs.

question: A woman has taken alendronate for 5 years. When should treatment continue (for example after a prior hip fracture with a hip T-score of -2.6), and when is a drug holiday appropriate (no fractures, no steroids, femoral neck T-score -2.1)? Also tested as: A 69-year-old woman has taken alendronate for 5 years. She has had no fractures, is not on glucocorticoids

options.A: Continue (oral up to 10 years) with a previous hip or vertebral fracture, age 70 or over, a fracture on treatment, or prednisolone 7.5 mg/day or more; otherwise take a drug holiday of about 18 months to 3 years, then reassess
options.B: Testosterone, myeloma screen, coeliac serology, calcium/PTH and vitamin D
options.C: Hypophosphatasia; avoid bisphosphonates; check pyridoxal-5'-phosphate and ALPL genetics
options.D: -2.5 or lower
options.E: Transient osteoporosis of the hip

explanation: After 5 years of oral bisphosphonate (3 years of zoledronic acid), treatment should be reviewed. Continuation is generally advised for people aged 70 or over, those with a previous hip or vertebral fracture, those who fractured on treatment, or those on at least 7.5 mg prednisolone daily. Otherwise, a holiday with reassessment is reasonable. The EULAR course criteria differ slightly: continue at age ≥75 or a hip T-score ≤-2.5 (up to 10 years oral or 6 years IV). FLEX and HORIZON extension trials showed fewer vertebral fractures with continuation in high-risk patients. Reassess BMD and FRAX after about 2 years of holiday, and earlier after a new fracture. Denosumab has no holiday.

question: Before IV zoledronic acid in a housebound 79-year-old with 25(OH)D 18 nmol/L, or before denosumab in an 81-year-old with eGFR 22, what is most important? Also tested as: An 81-year-old woman with CKD stage 4 (eGFR 22) is to start denosumab for osteoporosis. What is most important before the first dose?

options.A: Familial hypocalciuric hypercalcaemia
options.B: Macrophage 1-alpha-hydroxylase; glucocorticoids, fluids, stop vitamin D
options.C: Do not stop without follow-on therapy; plan a bisphosphonate (often zoledronate) about 6 months after the last dose
options.D: Osteosarcoma arising in pagetic bone
options.E: Replete vitamin D (and correct calcium) first, then give the drug and recheck calcium afterwards; in advanced CKD consider CKD-mineral bone disorder before choosing an antiresorptive

explanation: Vitamin D deficiency increases the risk of symptomatic hypocalcaemia after IV bisphosphonates or denosumab, so deficiency should be corrected with a loading regimen first; oral bisphosphonates can start alongside replacement. Denosumab can cause severe symptomatic hypocalcaemia, particularly with eGFR below 30 or on dialysis, so hypocalcaemia and vitamin D deficiency should be corrected first and calcium monitored after dosing. In advanced CKD, CKD-mineral bone disorder (including adynamic bone) should also be considered. Loading dose: cholecalciferol about 300,000 IU over 6–10 weeks (e.g. 50,000 IU weekly for 6 weeks), then 800–2000 IU daily. Recheck calcium at 1 month (this can unmask primary hyperparathyroidism). In CKD 4–5: check PTH and ALP; a bone biopsy helps if turnover is uncertain. Antiresorptives suit high-turnover disease; teriparatide suits adynamic bone. Avoid or reduce bisphosphonates when eGFR is <30–35.

question: A 45-year-old woman with coeliac disease has proximal weakness and diffuse bone pain. Calcium is lownormal, phosphate low, alkaline phosphatase and PTH raised. Radiographs show Looser zones in the pubic rami. What is the diagnosis?

options.A: Macrophage 1-alpha-hydroxylase; glucocorticoids, fluids, stop vitamin D
options.B: X-linked hypophosphataemia; burosumab
options.C: Osteomalacia due to vitamin D deficiency
options.D: Familial hypocalciuric hypercalcaemia
options.E: 68Ga-DOTATATE PET/CT

explanation: Vitamin D deficiency reduces calcium absorption, causing secondary hyperparathyroidism, phosphaturia and defective mineralisation. Looser zones are characteristic. Treatment is vitamin D loading with calcium and management of malabsorption. DIFFERENTIALS & OTHER CAUSES Pattern Ca Causes of osteomalacia: - low/N Vitamin D Calcium-limited: nutritional deficiency deficiency, malabsorption (coeliac, gastric bypass, FGF23-mediated N pancreatic disease), liver (XLH, TIO) disease, CKD, enzymeinducing antiepileptics, vitamin Fanconi N D-dependent rickets (1A, 1B, N/high Hypophosphatasia 2). - Phosphate-limited, FGF23-mediated: XLH, ADHR, Clinical features: bone pain and tenderness (ribs, pelvis, tibiae), proximal myopathy with TIO, fibrous dysplasia, IV ferric a waddling gait (normal CK), and pseudofractures. Looser zones appear at the pubic carboxymaltose. - Phosphaterami, medial femoral neck, ribs and axillary border of the scapula. A bone scan shows limited, renal tubular: Fanconi symmetrical hot spots that mimic metastases. It is often mistaken for fibromyalgia, PMR syndrome (tenofovir, adefovir, or myositis. myeloma light chains, ifosfamide, Wilson's disease); hereditary hypophosphataemic rickets with hypercalciuria; phosphate binders and antacids. - Mineralisation inhibitors: aluminium, fluoride, etidronate. - Low ALP: hypophosphatasia. PO4 ALP PTH 25(OH)D 1,25(OH)2D FGF23 low/N high high low variable N N/mild low high N low or high high inappropriately N N/high low/N low high N N N/high low/N low N N N Vitamin D loading, calcium if intake is low, treat malabsorption (higher doses; activated vitamin D in liver or kidney disease). ALP rises transiently, then normalises over months.

question: A 24-year-old man with short stature, lifelong bowed legs and an affected mother has low phosphate with renal phosphate wasting, normal calcium and raised FGF23. What is the diagnosis and targeted therapy?

options.A: Familial hypocalciuric hypercalcaemia
options.B: Macrophage 1-alpha-hydroxylase; glucocorticoids, fluids, stop vitamin D
options.C: Osteomalacia due to vitamin D deficiency
options.D: X-linked hypophosphataemia; burosumab
options.E: 68Ga-DOTATATE PET/CT

explanation: PHEX mutations cause excess FGF23, renal phosphate wasting and low or inappropriately normal calcitriol. Burosumab neutralises FGF23; conventional therapy is oral phosphate with active vitamin D. XLH is the commonest heritable rickets (X-linked dominant PHEX). Children have bowed legs, short stature and dental abscesses. Adults have pseudofractures, enthesopathy (mimicking SpA or DISH), early OA, hearing loss and spinal stenosis. Burosumab (anti-FGF23) is licensed for children and symptomatic adults and is superior to conventional therapy for healing rickets. Conventional therapy is oral phosphate plus calcitriol; monitor for nephrocalcinosis (renal ultrasound), hyperparathyroidism and urine calcium.

question: A woman in her late 40s or early 50s has recurrent metatarsal stress fractures, early loss of adult teeth (and sometimes chondrocalcinosis) and has been referred for alendronate. ALP is persistently low. What is the diagnosis, which drug should be avoided, and what is the next step? Also tested as: A 46-year-old woman has had recurrent metatarsal stress fractures and lost several adult teeth early. She has been referred for alendronate. Serum alkaline phosphatase is persistently below the reference range. What is the most appropriate next step?

options.A: Familial hypocalciuric hypercalcaemia
options.B: Analgesia and mobilisation; augmentation only for severe persistent pain at a recent fracture
options.C: Osteomalacia due to vitamin D deficiency
options.D: 68Ga-DOTATATE PET/CT
options.E: Hypophosphatasia; avoid bisphosphonates; check pyridoxal-5'-phosphate and ALPL genetics

explanation: A persistently low ALP with stress fractures and premature tooth loss suggests hypophosphatasia (ALPL mutations). A raised pyridoxal-5'-phosphate supports the diagnosis. Bisphosphonates resemble pyrophosphate, an ALP substrate; they and other antiresorptives can worsen the mineralisation defect and have been linked to atypical femoral fractures in this condition. Enzyme replacement (asfotase alfa) is used in severe disease. Other causes of low ALP: zinc or magnesium deficiency, hypothyroidism, Wilson's disease, pernicious anaemia, coeliac disease, milk-alkali syndrome, massive transfusion, cardiac surgery or bypass, recent bisphosphonate or denosumab therapy, glucocorticoids, cachexia, clofibrate. Always confirm low values on repeat testing. Raised urinary phosphoethanolamine. Associations: chondrocalcinosis and CPPD (pyrophosphate accumulation), calcific periarthritis, AFF-like fractures, muscle weakness, pain. Avoid antiresorptives. Teriparatide has been used off-label. Physiotherapy, orthopaedic and dental care.

question: How is Paget's disease monitored and treated: for example a 74-year-old with femoral pain and bowing, ALP 310 U/L and increased uptake throughout the femur, versus a 71-year-old with incidental asymptomatic pelvic disease and mildly raised ALP? Also tested as: What is the main biochemical marker of activity in Paget's disease of bone? | A 71-year-old man has pelvic Paget's disease found incidentally on a CT scan done for another reason. He has no bone pain, and ALP is mildly raised. No surgery is planned. What is the most appropriate management?

options.A: Raised ALP with normal calcium and phosphate is the activity marker; a single zoledronic acid infusion treats pagetic bone pain, but asymptomatic disease is monitored rather than treated to normalise ALP
options.B: ANA positivity alone does not establish SLE or another connective tissue disease
options.C: 68Ga-DOTATATE PET/CT
options.D: Osteosarcoma arising in pagetic bone
options.E: Osteomalacia due to vitamin D deficiency

explanation: ALP reflects increased bone turnover; hypercalcaemia is unusual unless the patient is immobilised. In Paget's disease, a bisphosphonate (zoledronic acid preferred) treats bone pain. Intensive treatment aimed at normalising ALP does not prevent complications better than symptom-directed treatment, so it is not supported in asymptomatic patients. Treatment is still considered before elective surgery on pagetic bone. Teriparatide is contraindicated because of osteosarcoma risk. Sclerotic metastases (prostate, breast), lymphoma, fibrous dysplasia, hyperparathyroidism (brown tumours), mastocytosis, osteopetrosis, hyperostosis frontalis interna, fluorosis. Other causes of raised ALP: liver disease (check GGT), osteomalacia, fracture healing, hyperparathyroidism, metastases, adolescence, pregnancy. 70–90% are asymptomatic. It affects older people of British or northern European ancestry (Lancashire), M:F 3:2, and incidence is falling. Genetics: SQSTM1 (p62) in 20–50% of familial cases, RANK, OPTN, VCP (multisystem proteinopathy). Sites: pelvis, spine, femur, skull, tibia. X-ray signs: "blade of grass" lytic front, osteoporosis circumscripta, cotton-wool skull, picture-frame and ivory vertebrae, thickened iliopectineal line. Complications: fractures (banana-type), secondary OA (the commonest cause of pain), deafness (30–50% with skull disease), basilar invagination, spinal stenosis, high-output cardiac failure, hypercalcaemia on immobilisation, osteosarcoma (<0.5%). Zoledronate 5 mg IV once (most durable effect). Alternatives: risedronate 30 mg daily for 2 months, alendronate 40 mg daily for 6 months, pamidronate. Replete vitamin D first and give calcium and vitamin D for about 10 days afterwards. Monitor ALP (or P1NP) at 3–6 months, then yearly. Retreat for recurrent pain with a rising ALP. Calcitonin is no longer recommended. Supportive care: analgesia, heel raises, hearing aids, arthroplasty (more blood loss). Prophylactic zoledronate in SQSTM1 carriers reduced new lesions (ZiPP) but is not routine.

question: A 48-year-old man has bone pain, proximal weakness and rib fractures. Phosphate is low with renal phosphate wasting, calcium normal and FGF23 raised; there is no family history. Which investigation is most likely to find the cause?

options.A: X-linked hypophosphataemia; burosumab
options.B: MRI of both hips
options.C: Osteomalacia due to vitamin D deficiency
options.D: 68Ga-DOTATATE PET/CT
options.E: Macrophage 1-alpha-hydroxylase; glucocorticoids, fluids, stop vitamin D

explanation: Adult-onset FGF23-mediated hypophosphataemia suggests tumour-induced osteomalacia. These small mesenchymal tumours express somatostatin receptors, so 68Ga-DOTATATE PET/CT is the most sensitive localisation test, followed by anatomical imaging. Complete resection is curative. TIO tumours are small benign phosphaturic mesenchymal tumours (in bone, soft tissue, sinuses or skin) that secrete FGF23, causing a low TmP/GFR and low or inappropriately normal 1,25(OH)2D. It is often misdiagnosed as fibromyalgia or SpA. Localise with Ga-68 DOTATATE PET/CT, then MRI, with venous sampling for FGF23 if needed. Before surgery, or if the tumour is unresectable, give oral phosphate plus calcitriol or burosumab. Other acquired causes: IV ferric carboxymaltose (recheck phosphate), fibrous dysplasia, epidermal naevus syndrome.

question: A 78-year-old man with long-standing Paget's disease of the femur develops increasing, constant pain with a tender soft-tissue swelling over the femur. ALP is rising despite recent zoledronic acid. What must be excluded first?

options.A: Replete vitamin D (and correct calcium) first, then give the drug and recheck calcium afterwards; in advanced CKD consider CKD-mineral bone disorder before choosing an antiresorptive
options.B: Osteosarcoma arising in pagetic bone
options.C: ANA positivity alone does not establish SLE or another connective tissue disease
options.D: Raised ALP with normal calcium and phosphate is the activity marker; a single zoledronic acid infusion treats pagetic bone pain, but asymptomatic disease is monitored rather than treated to normalise ALP
options.E: 68Ga-DOTATATE PET/CT

explanation: Sarcomatous change occurs in under 1% of patients with Paget's disease but carries a poor prognosis. New severe pain, swelling or a pathological fracture with rising ALP after treatment needs urgent MRI and biopsy. New severe constant pain, swelling, a lytic lesion or a pathological fracture in pagetic bone, with ALP rising despite treatment: urgent MRI, CT staging and biopsy at a sarcoma centre. Giant cell tumour is a rarer complication (skull and facial bones; may respond to dexamethasone).

question: A 58-year-old man presents with two thoracic vertebral fragility fractures. DXA shows a lumbar spine Z-score of -2.9. Which set of investigations is most important to identify secondary causes?

options.A: Macrophage 1-alpha-hydroxylase; glucocorticoids, fluids, stop vitamin D
options.B: 68Ga-DOTATATE PET/CT
options.C: Hypophosphatasia; avoid bisphosphonates; check pyridoxal-5'-phosphate and ALPL genetics
options.D: Testosterone, myeloma screen, coeliac serology, calcium/PTH and vitamin D
options.E: Do not stop without follow-on therapy; plan a bisphosphonate (often zoledronate) about 6 months after the last dose

explanation: Up to half of men with osteoporosis have a secondary cause, including hypogonadism, myeloma, glucocorticoids, alcohol, coeliac disease and hyperparathyroidism. Myeloma must be excluded in any patient with vertebral fractures and a low Z-score. Treatment should not wait for a further DXA. Secondary causes in men (about 50% have one): hypogonadism (including ADT), alcohol, GC, myeloma or MGUS, coeliac disease, hyperparathyroidism, hyperthyroidism, Cushing's, mastocytosis (urticaria pigmentosa, raised tryptase), hypercalciuria, HIV, anticonvulsants, COPD, homocystinuria, haemochromatosis, OI (blue sclerae). Bisphosphonates, denosumab and teriparatide or abaloparatide are effective in men. Treat hypogonadism (testosterone if indicated). Men have higher post-fracture mortality.

question: A 45-year-old woman has asymptomatic hypercalcaemia (adjusted calcium 2.75 mmol/L) with a PTH in the upper part of the reference range. Her 25(OH)D is replete. The calcium:creatinine clearance ratio is 0.006. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.A: 68Ga-DOTATATE PET/CT
options.B: Familial hypocalciuric hypercalcaemia
options.C: Hypophosphatasia; avoid bisphosphonates; check pyridoxal-5'-phosphate and ALPL genetics
options.D: Osteomalacia due to vitamin D deficiency
options.E: Macrophage 1-alpha-hydroxylase; glucocorticoids, fluids, stop vitamin D

explanation: A calcium:creatinine clearance ratio below 0.01 strongly suggests FHH (usually a CASR variant), and parathyroidectomy does not help. Values above 0.02 favour primary hyperparathyroidism, and intermediate values warrant genetic testing. Vitamin D should be replete before the test is interpreted. Hypercalcaemia with non-suppressed PTH: primary hyperparathyroidism, FHH (CASR, GNA11, AP2S1), lithium, thiazides (unmasking), tertiary hyperparathyroidism (CKD), MEN1 or 2A. Hypercalcaemia with suppressed PTH: malignancy (PTHrP, lytic metastases, myeloma), granulomatous disease (raised 1,25D; sarcoid, TB, lymphoma), vitamin D toxicity, milk-alkali syndrome, thyrotoxicosis, immobilisation (Paget's), Addison's, vitamin A, theophylline. Calcium:creatinine clearance ratio = (urine Ca × serum Cr) / (serum Ca × urine Cr). Below 0.01 suggests FHH; above 0.02 suggests PHPT. FHH: reassurance, no surgery; family screening; genetic confirmation. PHPT surgical criteria: calcium >0.25 mmol/L above ULN, osteoporosis or fragility fracture, eGFR <60, stones or hypercalciuria, age <50.

question: A woman in the third trimester of pregnancy develops progressive hip pain. MRI shows diffuse marrow oedema of the femoral head and neck without a subchondral fracture line. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.A: Transient osteoporosis of the hip
options.B: Femoroacetabular impingement (cam type)
options.C: Familial hypocalciuric hypercalcaemia
options.D: Osteomalacia due to vitamin D deficiency
options.E: MRI of both hips

explanation: Transient osteoporosis of the hip affects women in late pregnancy and middle-aged men. Diffuse marrow oedema without the focal subchondral line of osteonecrosis is typical. It is self-limiting over months; management is analgesia and protected weight-bearing to prevent fracture. Diffuse marrow oedema of the hip: transient osteoporosis or bone marrow oedema syndrome (reversible) vs osteonecrosis (focal, double-line sign), subchondral insufficiency fracture, stress fracture, septic arthritis or osteomyelitis, early inflammatory arthritis, pigmented villonodular synovitis, tumour. Pregnancy- and lactationassociated osteoporosis presents with vertebral fractures post-partum. Analgesia and protected weight-bearing (crutches) until resolution (6–12 months). Bisphosphonates (or iloprost) may hasten recovery outside pregnancy. Avoid bisphosphonates in pregnancy. Early MRI to exclude fracture.

question: A 30-year-old woman with SLE who received high-dose prednisolone last year has 6 weeks of groin pain on weight-bearing. Hip radiographs are normal. What is the most sensitive investigation for the likely diagnosis?

options.A: Transient osteoporosis of the hip
options.B: 68Ga-DOTATATE PET/CT
options.C: All patients unless contraindicated, at no more than 5 mg/kg actual body weight per day, so 300 mg daily for 60 kg
options.D: Femoroacetabular impingement (cam type)
options.E: MRI of both hips

explanation: Glucocorticoid-associated osteonecrosis of the femoral head is often bilateral and is common in SLE. MRI detects it before radiographic change, when joint-preserving measures such as core decompression are most likely to help. Both hips should be imaged. Groin pain in SLE: AVN vs septic arthritis (immunosuppressed), insufficiency fracture (GIOP), lupus arthritis, iliopsoas haematoma or abscess, hernia, referred lumbar pain. Risk in SLE is about 5–10%, linked to GC dose (especially >20 mg/day early, and pulses), aPL, Cushingoid habitus, vasculitis and Raynaud's. Femoral head disease is bilateral in about 50%. Other sites: femoral condyles, humeral head, talus. ARCO staging (I–IV). Before collapse: protected weightbearing, reduce GC, core decompression with or without graft or cells. Bisphosphonates and anticoagulation (if thrombophilic) have mixed evidence. After collapse or with secondary OA: arthroplasty. Large weight-bearing lesions usually collapse within 2–3 years.

question: A 7-year-old girl has precocious puberty, large irregular café-au-lait patches and expansile 'ground-glass' lesions in several long bones. What is the genetic basis, and which metabolic complication can occur?

options.A: A postzygotic activating GNAS mutation; lesions may secrete FGF23
options.B: Osteosarcoma arising in pagetic bone
options.C: MRI of both hips
options.D: ANA positivity alone does not establish SLE or another connective tissue disease
options.E: Do not stop without follow-on therapy; plan a bisphosphonate (often zoledronate) about 6 months after the last dose

explanation: McCune-Albright syndrome combines polyostotic fibrous dysplasia, 'coast of Maine' café-au-lait macules and endocrine hyperfunction. The GNAS mutation is somatic and mosaic, and a germline mutation would be lethal. Growth hormone excess worsens craniofacial fibrous dysplasia, and phosphate wasting should be checked. FD/MAS is caused by a post-zygotic GNAS activating mutation (mosaic). Fibrous dysplasia is monostotic in about 70%, at craniofacial sites, the proximal femur ("shepherd's crook"), ribs and tibia, with "ground-glass" lesions. Caféau-lait macules have "coast of Maine" borders and often respect the midline. Endocrine features: peripheral precocious puberty (commonest), hyperthyroidism, GH excess, neonatal Cushing's, FGF23 phosphate wasting. Analgesia; IV bisphosphonates for pain (they do not heal lesions; oral forms are ineffective); denosumab is investigational (rebound hypercalcaemia). Treat endocrinopathies, especially GH excess. Correct phosphate and vitamin D. Intramedullary rodding for deformity. Malignant transformation is <1% (risk rises with GH excess or radiation). Compare neurofibromatosis type 1, where café-au-lait macules have smooth "coast of California" borders.

question: A 52-year-old man with pulmonary sarcoidosis has an adjusted calcium of 3.0 mmol/L, suppressed PTH, a low-normal 25(OH)D and a raised 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D. What is the mechanism and the most appropriate treatment?

options.A: 68Ga-DOTATATE PET/CT
options.B: Familial hypocalciuric hypercalcaemia
options.C: Macrophage 1-alpha-hydroxylase; glucocorticoids, fluids, stop vitamin D
options.D: X-linked hypophosphataemia; burosumab
options.E: Osteomalacia due to vitamin D deficiency

explanation: Granuloma macrophages convert 25(OH)D to calcitriol without feedback control. Hypercalcaemia and hypercalciuria respond to glucocorticoids; hydroxychloroquine is an alternative. Vitamin D and calcium supplements should be avoided, and renal function and nephrocalcinosis monitored. 1,25(OH)2D-mediated hypercalcaemia: sarcoidosis, TB, fungal infection, lymphoma, granulomatosis with polyangiitis, berylliosis, silicone or paraffin granulomas, Crohn's disease, CYP24A1 mutations (loss of 24hydroxylase; idiopathic infantile hypercalcaemia, stones). Hydration, stop calcium and vitamin D supplements, sun avoidance, prednisolone 20–40 mg (calcium normalises within days to weeks). Hydroxychloroquine or ketoconazole are steroid-sparing options. Monitor renal function, urine calcium and nephrocalcinosis.

question: What are the entry criterion and minimum score for the 2019 EULAR/ACR SLE classification criteria? Also tested as: Under the 2019 SLE classification criteria, what is the minimum total weighted score required, provided at least one clinical criterion is present?

options.A: All patients unless contraindicated, at no more than 5 mg/kg actual body weight per day, so 300 mg daily for 60 kg
options.B: They are classification criteria and do not replace clinical diagnosis; she scores 5 points and does not yet meet the criteria
options.C: It is used off-label for refractory organ-threatening disease, such as haematological, neuropsychiatric or renal involvement
options.D: ANA at a titre of 1:80 or higher on HEp-2 cells (or an equivalent test) at any time, then 10 or more weighted points with at least one clinical criterion
options.E: Anti-Sm

explanation: Criteria count only if not better explained by another condition, need not occur simultaneously, and only the highestweighted item in each domain counts. Renal and neuropsychiatric domains carry high weights; biopsy-proven class III or IV lupus nephritis alone scores 10. Classification criteria do not replace clinical diagnosis. Domain Items (points) fever >38.3 °C (2) Constitutional leucopenia <4 (3); thrombocytopenia Haematological <100 (4); AIHA (4) delirium (2); psychosis (3); seizure (5) Neuropsychiatric non-scarring alopecia (2); oral ulcers Mucocutaneous (2); SCLE or DLE (4); ACLE (6) effusion (5); acute pericarditis (6) Serosal joint involvement (6) Musculoskeletal proteinuria >0.5 g/24 h (4); class II or V Renal (8); class III or IV (10) any (2) aPL low C3 or C4 (3); both low (4) Complement SLE-specific Ab anti-dsDNA or anti-Sm (6) Sensitivity about 96%, specificity about 93%. SLICC criteria (≥4 with ≥1 clinical and ≥1 immunological, or biopsy nephritis plus ANA or dsDNA) remain valid. About 10–20% of patients with clinician-diagnosed early lupus do not meet the criteria. Treat them anyway (HCQ).

question: A 32-year-old woman with arthralgia has an ANA of 1:160 but no other clinical features of connective tissue disease. What is the best interpretation?

options.A: ANA positivity alone does not establish SLE or another connective tissue disease
options.B: MRI of both hips
options.C: Osteosarcoma arising in pagetic bone
options.D: Osteomalacia due to vitamin D deficiency
options.E: All patients unless contraindicated, at no more than 5 mg/kg actual body weight per day, so 300 mg daily for 60 kg

explanation: ANA is sensitive but non-specific and occurs in healthy people and other conditions. A negative ANA makes SLE much less likely. ANA positivity without SLE: healthy people (about 13% at 1:80, 3–5% at ≥1:160), older age, relatives, autoimmune thyroid or liver disease, other CTDs, infection (EBV, HCV, HIV, TB, endocarditis), malignancy, drugs. A DFS70 (dense fine speckled) pattern alone argues against systemic autoimmune disease. ANA sensitivity is 95–98% on HEp-2 IIF. Rare ANA-negative SLE occurs with anti-Ro on substrates lacking Ro60 or heavy proteinuria; if suspicion is high, test anti-Ro or ENA directly. Do not repeat ANA to monitor activity. Do not order ANA without clinical suspicion. Investigate further (ENA, dsDNA, complement, urinalysis, FBC) only with compatible features.

question: Which antibody is most specific for SLE?

options.A: Anti-Sm
options.B: 5 mg/day prednisolone equivalent or less, withdrawn when possible
options.C: All patients unless contraindicated, at no more than 5 mg/kg actual body weight per day, so 300 mg daily for 60 kg
options.D: It is used off-label for refractory organ-threatening disease, such as haematological, neuropsychiatric or renal involvement
options.E: Infection (including opportunistic infection) and pulmonary embolism

explanation: Anti-Sm is highly specific but insensitive (about 10-30%). Anti-dsDNA is also highly specific and tracks activity, particularly nephritis. Antibody Frequency Associations 60–70% nephritis; tracks activity; dsDNA Crithidia or Farr assays most specific 10–30% about 99% specific; does Sm not track activity U1-RNP 25–40% Raynaud's, myositis, MCTD; possibly less nephritis Ro (Ro60, 30–40% SCLE, photosensitivity, Ro52) Sjögren's, neonatal lupus and CHB, cytopenias 10–15% with Ro; neonatal lupus La 10–20% psychosis, depression, Ribosomal P lupus hepatitis 50–70% non-specific Histone (>95% in DIL) C1q 30–60% active proliferative LN; negative result has high NPV 60–80% nephritis; may be positive Nucleosome when dsDNA is negative 30–40% thrombosis, obstetric aPL events, livedo, low platelets, valves

question: Which serological pattern predicts an impending renal flare in quiescent SLE, and how should a modest isolated rise in anti-dsDNA without clinical change be managed? Also tested as: A patient with clinically quiescent SLE has a modest rise in anti-dsDNA but no new symptoms, signs, urine abnormality or organ change. What is the best approach?

options.A: High-dose glucocorticoids including IV methylprednisolone pulses, with IVIG
options.B: Anti-Sm
options.C: It is used off-label for refractory organ-threatening disease, such as haematological, neuropsychiatric or renal involvement
options.D: Rising anti-dsDNA with falling C3 and C4 predicts flare; isolated serological activity warrants closer monitoring (including urinalysis), not treatment escalation
options.E: Infection (including opportunistic infection) and pulmonary embolism

explanation: Rising anti-dsDNA with falling complement reflects immune-complex activity, particularly nephritis. Serological activity supports closer monitoring, but treatment escalation should follow clinical or organ activity rather than isolated serology. A markedly raised CRP in SLE should prompt a search for infection or serositis. About 10–15% of patients are serologically active but clinically quiescent; continue HCQ. Persistently low C4 with normal C3 may reflect inherited partial C4 deficiency (low copy number). A CH50 near zero suggests congenital early classical-pathway deficiency. Cell-bound C4d panels may help diagnose ANA-positive patients with an uncertain picture. Shorten the review interval (urinalysis, UPCR, FBC, C3/C4, dsDNA every 4–8 weeks). Check HCQ adherence (wholeblood levels <200 ng/mL suggest non-adherence).

question: Who should take hydroxychloroquine in SLE, and what is the correct dose for a 60 kg woman? Also tested as: A 38-year-old woman with SLE weighs 60 kg. What is the appropriate daily dose of hydroxychloroquine?

options.A: Methotrexate (or azathioprine or mycophenolate) first; then add belimumab or anifrolumab if disease remains active or glucocorticoids cannot be tapered to 5 mg/day or less
options.B: It may reduce thrombotic risk as background therapy but does not replace anticoagulation in confirmed thrombotic APS
options.C: It is used off-label for refractory organ-threatening disease, such as haematological, neuropsychiatric or renal involvement
options.D: All patients unless contraindicated, at no more than 5 mg/kg actual body weight per day, so 300 mg daily for 60 kg
options.E: MRI of both hips

explanation: Hydroxychloroquine reduces flares, damage accrual and thrombosis and improves survival. It is continued in pregnancy and breastfeeding. At 5 mg/kg actual body weight, 60 kg gives 300 mg/day, which can be achieved with alternating doses; 400 mg daily would be about 6.7 mg/kg/day and increase retinal toxicity risk. If HCQ is not tolerated: chloroquine (more retinotoxic) or mepacrine (skin; yellow skin discoloration; no retinal toxicity). Rare HCQ toxicities: cardiomyopathy and conduction disease, QT prolongation, neuromyopathy (curvilinear bodies), hypoglycaemia, pigmentation, psoriasis flare. HCQ benefits: flares fall by about 50%; it reduces nephritis progression, thrombosis, seizures, CV events, CHB recurrence and pre-eclampsia, and improves lipids and glucose. Retinal toxicity is about 1% at 5 years and 10–20% at 20 years. Reduce the dose if eGFR is <30. Whole-blood levels >750–1150 ng/mL are linked to fewer flares, but do not exceed 5 mg/kg.

question: What is the target for maintenance glucocorticoid dosing in SLE?

options.A: It is used off-label for refractory organ-threatening disease, such as haematological, neuropsychiatric or renal involvement
options.B: Continue mycophenolate-based therapy (with belimumab, a calcineurin inhibitor or obinutuzumab where used) for at least 3 years, with hydroxychloroquine and glucocorticoid withdrawal
options.C: All patients unless contraindicated, at no more than 5 mg/kg actual body weight per day, so 300 mg daily for 60 kg
options.D: 5 mg/day prednisolone equivalent or less, withdrawn when possible
options.E: Anti-Sm

explanation: Glucocorticoids are useful for rapid control, including IV methylprednisolone pulses in organ-threatening disease, but maintenance should be minimised. Early addition of immunosuppressants or biologics facilitates tapering. GC strategy: IV methylprednisolone 250–1000 mg for 1–3 days allows a lower oral start (≤0.5 mg/kg/day, maximum about 40 mg) and a faster taper. Reach ≤5 mg/day within about 6 months, then try to withdraw. Damage accrues even at 5–7.5 mg/day and rises sharply above 7.5 mg/day. Start a steroid-sparing agent early rather than waiting for steroid dependence.

question: A patient with SLE has persistent arthritis, rash or cutaneous lupus (without major organ involvement) despite hydroxychloroquine, with or without azathioprine, and cannot reduce prednisolone below 10 mg daily. What are the steroid-sparing options? Also tested as: A 33-year-old woman with SLE has persistent arthritis, rash and fatigue on hydroxychloroquine and azathioprine, and cannot reduce prednisolone below 10 mg daily. There is no renal or CNS involvement. Which addition is most appropriate? | A 45-year-old man with SLE has active cutaneous lupus despite hydroxychloroquine and topical treatment. There is no organ-threatening disease. Which is an appropriate second-line systemic option?

options.A: Infection (including opportunistic infection) and pulmonary embolism
options.B: Urgent assessment and treatment for neutropenic sepsis, with review of drug toxicity
options.C: Methotrexate (or azathioprine or mycophenolate) first; then add belimumab or anifrolumab if disease remains active or glucocorticoids cannot be tapered to 5 mg/day or less
options.D: Assess and address sleep, mood, anaemia, thyroid disease, vitamin D, pain and deconditioning, as well as disease activity
options.E: All patients unless contraindicated, at no more than 5 mg/kg actual body weight per day, so 300 mg daily for 60 kg

explanation: For non-organ-threatening disease not controlled by hydroxychloroquine, methotrexate, azathioprine or mycophenolate are options, chosen by organ phenotype, toxicity and pregnancy plans. Belimumab or anifrolumab are added when there is inadequate response or glucocorticoids cannot be tapered to 5 mg/day or less. The 2026 BSR guideline suggests anifrolumab may be more appropriate than belimumab in non-renal SLE, and names it the preferred first-line biologic for refractory cutaneous lupus; belimumab requires autoantibody positivity with high activity. Rituximab is an option when other choices are less suitable, particularly in organ-threatening disease. Smoking cessation and photoprotection are essential, and smoking reduces hydroxychloroquine efficacy. Things that look like refractory lupus but are not: fibromyalgia (in 20–30%), OA, damage (Jaccoud's), steroid myopathy, hypothyroidism, non-adherence, drug rash, rosacea or seborrhoeic dermatitis (malar rash mimics), dermatomyositis (knuckle involvement, heliotrope, raised CK), tinea or psoriasis (SCLE mimics). Severity Treatment Mild (skin, HCQ, topicals, NSAIDs, short low-dose GC; joints, methotrexate if persistent mucosa) HCQ + methotrexate, azathioprine or MMF Moderate with a GC bridge; add belimumab or anifrolumab pulse GC + MMF or cyclophosphamide (± Severe a third agent in LN); rituximab if refractory; IVIG or PLEX as rescue Erosive rhupus: treat like RA (methotrexate, abatacept, rituximab). Ultrasound helps separate true synovitis from fibromyalgia.

question: What are the mechanisms of anifrolumab and belimumab, and which adverse effect is increased with anifrolumab? Also tested as: What is the mechanism of action of belimumab?

options.A: Macrophage 1-alpha-hydroxylase; glucocorticoids, fluids, stop vitamin D
options.B: A CTLA-4-immunoglobulin fusion protein that blocks CD80/86–CD28 co-stimulation of T cells
options.C: Anti-histone
options.D: All patients unless contraindicated, at no more than 5 mg/kg actual body weight per day, so 300 mg daily for 60 kg
options.E: Anifrolumab blocks the type I interferon receptor (IFNAR1) and increases herpes zoster; belimumab inhibits soluble BLyS/BAFF

explanation: Anifrolumab reduced disease activity and glucocorticoid use in moderate-to-severe non-renal SLE. Belimumab reduces B-cell survival; it reduces flares and glucocorticoid use in autoantibody-positive SLE and improves renal outcomes when added to standard lupus nephritis treatment. Anifrolumab: 300 mg IV every 4 weeks (a weekly SC autoinjector is licensed in the US after TULIP-SC). In TULIP- 2, BICLA response was 48% vs 32%. It works especially for skin and joints and is effective regardless of IFN signature (more so if IFN-high). Zoster is 6–7% vs 1–2%; there are also more URTIs and bronchitis. Not established in severe LN (IRIS ongoing) or NPSLE. Belimumab: IV 10 mg/kg (weeks 0, 2, 4, then every 4 weeks) or SC 200 mg weekly; licensed from age 5 (IV). Works best in serologically active disease. Watch for a depression and suicidality signal. In BEAT-LUPUS, belimumab after rituximab reduced severe flares (it counters the postrituximab BAFF rebound). Give recombinant zoster vaccine before anifrolumab. Ask about mood on belimumab. Neither has been studied in severe active NPSLE.

question: What is the role of rituximab in SLE?

options.A: It is used off-label for refractory organ-threatening disease, such as haematological, neuropsychiatric or renal involvement
options.B: All patients unless contraindicated, at no more than 5 mg/kg actual body weight per day, so 300 mg daily for 60 kg
options.C: Anti-Sm
options.D: Urgent assessment and treatment for neutropenic sepsis, with review of drug toxicity
options.E: 5 mg/day prednisolone equivalent or less, withdrawn when possible

explanation: Randomised trials missed their primary endpoints, but real-world evidence supports rituximab in refractory disease. Immunoglobulins and HBV status should be checked beforehand. EXPLORER (non-renal) and LUNAR (LN) missed their primary endpoints, but observational data and NHS commissioning support use. Typical dose: 1 g × 2, two weeks apart, with methylprednisolone, often with cyclophosphamide or MMF. Serum sickness is more common in SLE. Indications: refractory LN, AIHA, ITP, TTP, NPSLE or myelitis, rhupus, CAPS. Before treatment: HBV, immunoglobulins, vaccines ≥2 weeks earlier. Obinutuzumab (type II anti-CD20) is licensed for LN.

question: When is a kidney biopsy indicated in SLE: for example new proteinuria, haematuria and rising creatinine, or a UPCR of 65 mg/mmol on two occasions with a bland sediment and normal creatinine in a patient who feels well? Also tested as: A woman with SLE has a urine protein:creatinine ratio of 65 mg/mmol on two occasions, a bland sediment and normal creatinine. What is the most appropriate next step? | Which finding warrants prompt assessment for lupus nephritis even in a patient who feels well?

options.A: Blood pressure control with ACE inhibitor or ARB for proteinuria, lipid management, and an SGLT2 inhibitor where appropriate
options.B: Biopsy (if safe) for persistent proteinuria of 0.5 g/day or more (UPCR about 50 mg/mmol or more), an active glomerular sediment or an unexplained fall in eGFR, so both need a biopsy
options.C: Familial hypocalciuric hypercalcaemia
options.D: All patients unless contraindicated, at no more than 5 mg/kg actual body weight per day, so 300 mg daily for 60 kg
options.E: Class IV

explanation: Biopsy defines the histological class, activity and chronicity and guides treatment, subject to bleeding risk. It is advised for persistent proteinuria of 0.5 g/day or more, especially with glomerular haematuria or casts. Clinically silent nephritis is well recognised, so regular urinalysis, protein quantification, renal function and blood pressure checks are essential. LN mimics: hypertensive or diabetic nephropathy; drug toxicity (NSAIDs, PPI interstitial nephritis, CNI); aPL nephropathy or TMA, TTP, aHUS; pre-eclampsia; renal vein thrombosis; post-infectious, IgA or ANCA GN; anti-GBM; MGRS; lupus podocytopathy (MCD or FSGS-like, nephrotic with class I/II). LN affects 40–50% of adults and 50–70% of children, usually within 5 years. Risk is higher with Black, Hispanic or Asian ancestry, male sex, young age, anti-dsDNA, low complement and anti-C1q. 10–30% of proliferative LN progresses to kidney failure within 10–15 years. Screen: urinalysis, UPCR, BP and eGFR every 6–12 months if stable, and every 3 months if high-risk or active. Spot UPCR is preferred to 24-hour collection. Consider repeat biopsy for refractory disease, suspected class change, or before stopping maintenance (residual activity predicts relapse).

question: Renal biopsy in lupus nephritis shows endocapillary proliferation with subendothelial deposits involving at least 50% of glomeruli. What is the ISN/RPS class?

options.A: Class IV
options.B: Blood pressure control with ACE inhibitor or ARB for proteinuria, lipid management, and an SGLT2 inhibitor where appropriate
options.C: Continue mycophenolate-based therapy (with belimumab, a calcineurin inhibitor or obinutuzumab where used) for at least 3 years, with hydroxychloroquine and glucocorticoid withdrawal
options.D: Transient osteoporosis of the hip
options.E: Infection (including opportunistic infection) and pulmonary embolism

explanation: Class III is focal (under 50% of glomeruli) and class IV diffuse (50% or more) proliferative nephritis. Class V is membranous; class VI is advanced sclerosis (90% or more of glomeruli). Class Histology Usual approach I minimal mesangial treat extrarenal disease only usually none; if proteinuria >3 II mesangial g, consider podocytopathy proliferative (GC ± CNI) focal (<50% of III induction then maintenance glomeruli), subendothelial deposits diffuse (≥50%) as III; most aggressive IV V membranous immunosuppress if nephrotic (subepithelial) or >1 g/day despite RAAS blockade; III/IV + V is treated as III/IV ≥90% globally VI no immunosuppression for the kidney; prepare for RRT sclerosed and transplant The 2018 revision dropped the A/C and S/G sub-labels in favour of a modified NIH activity index (0–24) and chronicity index (0–12). A chronicity index ≥4 predicts poor renal survival. Always report podocytopathy and TMA.

question: What is the initial therapy for class IV lupus nephritis (proteinuria 3.2 g/day, creatinine 98 µmol/L), and what is the low-dose (Euro-Lupus) cyclophosphamide regimen? Also tested as: Which regimen describes low-dose (Euro-Lupus) intravenous cyclophosphamide?

options.A: IV methylprednisolone then a planned oral taper, with hydroxychloroquine and mycophenolate combined with belimumab, a calcineurin inhibitor or obinutuzumab; Euro-Lupus is 500 mg IV every 2 weeks for 6 doses (total 3 g), followed by maintenance
options.B: Continue mycophenolate-based therapy (with belimumab, a calcineurin inhibitor or obinutuzumab where used) for at least 3 years, with hydroxychloroquine and glucocorticoid withdrawal
options.C: All patients unless contraindicated, at no more than 5 mg/kg actual body weight per day, so 300 mg daily for 60 kg
options.D: Class IV
options.E: Blood pressure control with ACE inhibitor or ARB for proteinuria, lipid management, and an SGLT2 inhibitor where appropriate

explanation: Current EULAR (2025) and BSR (2026) recommendations favour combination therapy for class III/IV nephritis: mycophenolate plus belimumab, plus a calcineurin inhibitor (voclosporin or tacrolimus) or plus obinutuzumab, on a background of hydroxychloroquine and glucocorticoids (IV pulses then a taper to 5 mg/day or less by about 4–6 months). Mycophenolate alone or Euro-Lupus cyclophosphamide (with or without belimumab) are alternatives with lower efficacy. The low-dose regimen has similar efficacy to high-dose cyclophosphamide with less gonadal and infection toxicity, and is followed by maintenance with azathioprine or mycophenolate. Targets are a 25% fall in uPCR by 3 months, 50% by 6 months and uPCR below 70 mg/mmol by 12 months. Add-on Trial Best for BLISS-LN proteinuria <3 g, Belimumab (43% vs frequent extrarenal 32%) flares; less effective with cyclophosphamide AURORA (CR heavy proteinuria, mixed Voclosporin or 41% vs 23%) class V; avoid if eGFR tacrolimus ≤45 fewer flares, steroid Obinutuzumab REGENCY (CR about sparing; watch IgG 46% vs 33% at week 76) MMF 2–3 g/day (preferred in Black and Hispanic patients and women of childbearing age). High-dose NIH cyclophosphamide is reserved for crescentic or rapidly progressive GN. The EULAR course defines complete response as UPCR <50 mg/mmol with stable eGFR on ≤5 mg/day prednisolone by 12 months. Proteinuria may take 18–24 months to settle. Not on track: check adherence (MPA and HCQ levels), switch induction agent, add a third agent or anti-CD20, consider re-biopsy. Pure class V: RAAS blockade; if nephrotic or >1 g/day, MMF plus CNI. Consider anticoagulation in nephrotic class V with albumin <20–25 g/L.

question: After successful induction for lupus nephritis, what is the recommended maintenance strategy?

options.A: Continue mycophenolate-based therapy (with belimumab, a calcineurin inhibitor or obinutuzumab where used) for at least 3 years, with hydroxychloroquine and glucocorticoid withdrawal
options.B: Rituximab maintenance for 24-48 months after remission induction
options.C: Blood pressure control with ACE inhibitor or ARB for proteinuria, lipid management, and an SGLT2 inhibitor where appropriate
options.D: 5 mg/day prednisolone equivalent or less, withdrawn when possible
options.E: Class IV

explanation: Maintenance should continue for at least 3 years. The 2026 BSR guideline prefers continuing the induction combination (mycophenolate with obinutuzumab, belimumab or a calcineurin inhibitor), using mycophenolate alone if combinations are unsuitable, and azathioprine if mycophenolate is not tolerated or pregnancy is planned. Full glucocorticoid withdrawal should be attempted. Renal function, proteinuria, sediment, complement and anti-dsDNA are monitored. Use mycophenolate at the lowest effective dose (about 1–2 g/day), and continue belimumab, voclosporin or obinutuzumab if used in induction. Continue for ≥3–5 years after response, then withdraw slowly. Switch to azathioprine for pregnancy. Continue HCQ indefinitely. Monitor every 2–4 weeks during induction and every 3 months once stable (BP, eGFR, UPCR, sediment, FBC, albumin, C3/C4, dsDNA, IgG on anti-CD20). Persistent proteinuria >0.7–0.8 g/day at 12 months predicts poor renal outcome.

question: Which measures complement immunosuppression in lupus nephritis?

options.A: Infection (including opportunistic infection) and pulmonary embolism
options.B: Switch to azathioprine (with or without tacrolimus), stopping mycophenolate at least 6 weeks before conception, and confirm stable disease before conceiving
options.C: Blood pressure control with ACE inhibitor or ARB for proteinuria, lipid management, and an SGLT2 inhibitor where appropriate
options.D: Continue mycophenolate-based therapy (with belimumab, a calcineurin inhibitor or obinutuzumab where used) for at least 3 years, with hydroxychloroquine and glucocorticoid withdrawal
options.E: Class IV

explanation: Renoprotection reduces proteinuria and progression but does not replace treatment of active proliferative nephritis.
