EULAR 2025 suggests adding an SGLT2 inhibitor if proteinuria persists after 12 months of treatment. Potassium and renal function need monitoring. Renoprotection checklist: HCQ (reduce if eGFR <30); ACE inhibitor or ARB with BP <130/80 (systolic <120 if tolerated); SGLT2 inhibitor once stable with eGFR ≥20 (evidence from CKD trials, not LN-specific); statin; avoid NSAIDs; sodium restriction; PJP prophylaxis with high-dose GC; bone protection; vaccination; fertility preservation if using cyclophosphamide. In kidney failure, transplantation is preferred (recurrence <5–10%), with anticoagulation if APS is present.

question: A woman with SLE has isolated severe thrombocytopenia (12 x 10I/L) with mucosal bleeding. What is the most appropriate initial treatment?

options.A: High-dose glucocorticoids including IV methylprednisolone pulses, with IVIG
options.B: Assess and address sleep, mood, anaemia, thyroid disease, vitamin D, pain and deconditioning, as well as disease activity
options.C: Urgent assessment and treatment for neutropenic sepsis, with review of drug toxicity
options.D: All patients unless contraindicated, at no more than 5 mg/kg actual body weight per day, so 300 mg daily for 60 kg
options.E: Assess urgently and in parallel for infection, thrombotic microangiopathy, catastrophic APS macrophage activation syndrome and severe lupus activity

explanation: Acute severe immune thrombocytopenia is treated with high-dose glucocorticoids and IVIG when bleeding or a rapid rise is needed. Maintenance agents include MMF, azathioprine or ciclosporin; rituximab, thrombopoietin receptor agonists or splenectomy are later options. Thrombocytopenia in SLE: immune (ITP-like), TTP or TMA (schistocytes, high LDH, low haptoglobin, ADAMTS13 <10%), aPL-associated or catastrophic APS, HLH or MAS, drugs (azathioprine, MMF, heparin-induced thrombocytopenia, co-trimoxazole), hypersplenism, marrow infiltration, Evans syndrome, pseudothrombocytopenia (EDTA clumping). Maintenance options: MMF, azathioprine, ciclosporin, rituximab, TPO receptor agonists (eltrombopag, romiplostim), splenectomy. Aspirin can still be used in aPL thrombocytopenia once platelets are >50.

question: A patient with active generalised SLE develops seizures and psychosis. Infection, metabolic causes and drugs have been excluded. What is the most appropriate treatment?

options.A: Urgent assessment and treatment for neutropenic sepsis, with review of drug toxicity
options.B: It is used off-label for refractory organ-threatening disease, such as haematological, neuropsychiatric or renal involvement
options.C: Infection (including opportunistic infection) and pulmonary embolism
options.D: Assess urgently and in parallel for infection, thrombotic microangiopathy, catastrophic APS macrophage activation syndrome and severe lupus activity
options.E: High-dose glucocorticoids (including pulses) with cyclophosphamide

explanation: Inflammatory neuropsychiatric lupus is treated with high-dose glucocorticoids and cyclophosphamide (or rituximab if refractory), plus symptomatic therapy. Thrombotic events related to aPL are managed with anticoagulation. NP events in SLE are attributable to SLE in only about a third. Mimics: infection (LP, cultures; PML on rituximab), steroid psychosis (first 1–2 weeks at >40 mg/day), metabolic disturbance (uraemia, hyponatraemia, hypoglycaemia), PRES (hypertension, CNIs), TTP, aPL thrombosis, drugs, primary psychiatric disease, NMOSD (AQP4-IgG), MOG antibody disease, MS. The ACR nomenclature lists 19 syndromes (12 CNS, 7 PNS). Attribution weighs timing (within 6 months of diagnosis), event type, confounders and supportive features (activity, MRI, CSF, anti-ribosomal P, aPL). Mechanisms: thrombotic or ischaemic (focal) vs inflammatory or antibody-mediated (diffuse: anti-NMDA NR2, anti-ribosomal P). Investigations: MRI with contrast, DWI, FLAIR and SWI; CSF (mainly to exclude infection); aPL, anti-ribosomal P, AQP4 and MOG; EEG; NCS; neuropsychological tests. Transverse myelitis is an emergency: pulse GC and cyclophosphamide within hours, plus PLEX if poor response; treat as NMOSD if AQP4-positive. Seizures: antiepileptics; long-term treatment may be unnecessary after a single provoked seizure with normal MRI and EEG. Cognition: treat vascular risk, mood and sleep; do not escalate immunosuppression. Chorea: usually aPL-related; antithrombotics. Maintenance: MMF or azathioprine. Refractory disease: rituximab, IVIG, PLEX.

question: A patient with SLE on immunosuppression develops fever and pleuritic chest pain. What must be considered before attributing this to a lupus flare?

options.A: Urgent assessment and treatment for neutropenic sepsis, with review of drug toxicity
options.B: Assess urgently and in parallel for infection, thrombotic microangiopathy, catastrophic APS macrophage activation syndrome and severe lupus activity
options.C: Infection (including opportunistic infection) and pulmonary embolism
options.D: Pulmonary embolism, alongside other acute cardiopulmonary causes
options.E: Blood pressure control with ACE inhibitor or ARB for proteinuria, lipid management, and an SGLT2 inhibitor where appropriate

explanation: Infection is a leading cause of death in SLE and can mimic or coexist with a flare. Thromboembolism must also be considered, especially with aPL. Feature Infection Flare rigors, high low-grade Fever neutrophilia, leucopenia, lymphopenia WCC left shift >50 mg/L CRP normal or mild rise (except serositis or arthritis) >0.5 Procalcitonin normal rising dsDNA, falling Serology unchanged C3/C4 If in doubt, treat both: cultures and antibiotics, with senior review of lupus therapy. Consider opportunistic organisms (PJP, CMV, TB, fungi, Nocardia, Listeria, zoster). Do a CTPA for pleuritic pain with aPL. Risk factors for serious infection: activity, GC (even 5–10 mg), cyclophosphamide or B-cell depletion, lymphopenia, hypogammaglobulinaemia, LN, low albumin, hyposplenism. HCQ is protective.

question: A patient with SLE on mycophenolate and prednisolone develops fever with a neutrophil count of 0.3 x 10I/L. What should happen?

options.A: Take part in cervical screening, with consideration of more frequent screening and HPV vaccination because of increased risk
options.B: A drug interaction causing additive antifolate marrow toxicity
options.C: Urgent assessment and treatment for neutropenic sepsis, with review of drug toxicity
options.D: Infection (including opportunistic infection) and pulmonary embolism
options.E: Assess urgently and in parallel for infection, thrombotic microangiopathy, catastrophic APS macrophage activation syndrome and severe lupus activity

explanation: Fever with neutropenia is a medical emergency requiring prompt cultures and empirical antibiotics. Neutropenic sepsis pathway: cultures and broad-spectrum antibiotics within 1 hour, withhold myelotoxic drugs (MMF, azathioprine, cyclophosphamide, co-trimoxazole), and consider G-CSF. Isolated asymptomatic lupus leucopenia or lymphopenia does not need immunosuppression. Check TPMT and NUDT15 before azathioprine.

question: A patient with SLE develops fever, confusion, thrombocytopenia and worsening renal function. What is the key immediate principle?

options.A: Infection (including opportunistic infection) and pulmonary embolism
options.B: Anticoagulation plus high-dose glucocorticoids plus plasma exchange and/or IVIG
options.C: Assess urgently and in parallel for infection, thrombotic microangiopathy, catastrophic APS macrophage activation syndrome and severe lupus activity
options.D: High-dose glucocorticoids (including pulses) with cyclophosphamide
options.E: Urgent assessment and treatment for neutropenic sepsis, with review of drug toxicity

explanation: Fever, confusion, thrombocytopenia and renal decline in SLE can reflect several life-threatening processes at once. A blood film for schistocytes, ADAMTS13, ferritin, fibrinogen, cultures and aPL testing help distinguish infection, thrombotic microangiopathy, catastrophic APS, MAS and severe lupus activity. Process Key tests schistocytes, ADAMTS13 <10%, high LDH, TTP low haptoglobin ≥3 organs within a week, microthrombi, Catastrophic aPL (often LA, triple-positive) APS ferritin >5,000–10,000, falling ESR, HLH or MAS fibrinogen and platelets, raised triglycerides, sCD25, haemophagocytosis on marrow cultures, procalcitonin, prolonged PT and Sepsis or DIC APTT, low fibrinogen dsDNA, C3/C4, active sediment Lupus flare Treat in parallel: plasma exchange for TTP (with caplacizumab where indicated); anticoagulation plus GC plus PLEX and/or IVIG for CAPS; GC plus anakinra or ciclosporin for MAS; antibiotics.

question: A patient with SLE reports severe fatigue. Disease activity indices are low. What is the most appropriate approach?

options.A: Long-term warfarin; DOACs are avoided after arterial events in APS
options.B: Urgent assessment and treatment for neutropenic sepsis, with review of drug toxicity
options.C: High-dose glucocorticoids including IV methylprednisolone pulses, with IVIG
options.D: Assess and address sleep, mood, anaemia, thyroid disease, vitamin D, pain and deconditioning, as well as disease activity
options.E: Infection (including opportunistic infection) and pulmonary embolism

explanation: Fatigue in SLE is multifactorial. Exercise, sleep and psychological approaches are useful. Fatigue occurs in 80–90% and correlates poorly with activity. Screen and treat depression and anxiety (25–40%), sleep disorders, fibromyalgia, anaemia, hypothyroidism, vitamin D deficiency and deconditioning. Graded aerobic exercise and psychological interventions are most effective. Anifrolumab and belimumab modestly improve fatigue.

question: Which preventive measures are recommended in SLE, what cutaneous advice suits photosensitive patients, and how should the excess cardiovascular risk be managed? Also tested as: Which cutaneous advice is appropriate for photosensitive SLE? | How does SLE affect cardiovascular risk, and how should this be managed?

options.A: It may reduce thrombotic risk as background therapy but does not replace anticoagulation in confirmed thrombotic APS
options.B: It is used off-label for refractory organ-threatening disease, such as haematological, neuropsychiatric or renal involvement
options.C: The SAV3E framework: sun protection (broad-spectrum sunscreen year-round), antimalarial for all vitamin D and bone health, vaccination, vascular risk management, and evaluation of organ involvement; CV risk is
options.D: Drug-induced subacute cutaneous lupus erythematosus
options.E: Assess and address sleep, mood, anaemia, thyroid disease, vitamin D, pain and deconditioning, as well as disease activity

explanation: 2–3× increased, so review traditional and lupus-specific risk factors regularly SLE confers excess cardiovascular and infection risk; annual cardiovascular risk review and vaccination are part of routine care. Ultraviolet light can trigger cutaneous and systemic flares, so regular broad-spectrum sunscreen and avoidance of excessive UV exposure are advised throughout the year. Myocardial infarction and stroke risk is roughly two- to three-fold increased; management combines disease control, glucocorticoid minimisation, attention to aPL and treatment of traditional risk factors. CV drivers: traditional risk factors plus activity, LN and CKD, aPL, GC, IFN-driven endothelial damage and proinflammatory HDL. Standard calculators underestimate risk; multiply by about 2 or use carotid plaque imaging. UVA passes through window glass and some fluorescent or LED lighting. Sun: SPF ≥50 broad-spectrum sunscreen and UVprotective clothing; replace vitamin D. BP: <130/80, with ACE inhibitor or ARB if proteinuric. Lipids: statins by upgraded risk category; LN, CKD or APS often place patients at high or very high risk. Other: aspirin for high-risk aPL profiles; minimise GC; continue HCQ; stop smoking; exercise. Vaccines: influenza, pneumococcal (PCV20 or PCV15 + PPSV23), COVID-19, HPV (to 45), recombinant zoster (before anifrolumab or JAKi), hepatitis B. Annual checks: lipids, HbA1c, CV risk, SDI, bone health, cervical screening.

question: A 62-year-old man taking hydralazine develops arthralgia, serositis and a positive ANA. Anti-dsDNA is negative and complement is normal. Which antibody is most typical?

options.A: Long-term warfarin; DOACs are avoided after arterial events in APS
options.B: Low-dose aspirin (75-100 mg daily)
options.C: Blood pressure control with ACE inhibitor or ARB for proteinuria, lipid management, and an SGLT2 inhibitor where appropriate
options.D: Drug-induced subacute cutaneous lupus erythematosus
options.E: Anti-histone

explanation: Drug-induced lupus (hydralazine, procainamide, isoniazid, minocycline) typically has anti-histone antibodies, rarely involves the kidney or CNS, and resolves after withdrawal. TNF inhibitor-induced lupus more often features antidsDNA. Type Drugs Serology Features procainamide, anti-histone arthralgia, Classic >95%; myalgia, fever, DIL hydralazine (slow serositis; dsDNA and acetylators), low kidney and isoniazid, complement CNS rare minocycline (prare ANCA, hepatitis), quinidine, methyldopa, chlorpromazine, sulfasalazine, terbinafine Antiinfliximab, rash, arthritis, dsDNA TNFetanercept, about 90%, serositis induced adalimumab low (ATIL) complement about 50% Drug- PPIs, thiazides, anti-Ro annular CCBs, ACE induced photosensitive inhibitors, SCLE rash terbinafine, taxanes, TNFi, ICIs IFN-α, ICIs, JAK Other variable can unmask and other true SLE targeted agents Stop the drug; symptoms settle within weeks, though ANA can persist for months to years. Use NSAIDs, short lowdose GC or HCQ if symptoms persist. If features persist beyond about 6 months, reconsider true SLE. Do not rechallenge. Hydralazine can also cause ANCA vasculitis (MPO, often with anti-histone and anti-elastase).

question: A 49-year-old woman develops annular, polycyclic, photosensitive plaques on her upper back and arms 6 weeks after starting terbinafine. Anti-Ro is positive. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.A: Low-dose aspirin plus prophylactic-dose LMWH
options.B: Long-term warfarin; DOACs are avoided after arterial events in APS
options.C: Low-dose aspirin (75-100 mg daily)
options.D: Anti-histone
options.E: Drug-induced subacute cutaneous lupus erythematosus

explanation: SCLE causes non-scarring annular or papulosquamous lesions and is strongly associated with anti-Ro. Triggers include terbinafine, PPIs, thiazides, calcium-channel blockers and checkpoint inhibitors. Annular photosensitive lesions: SCLE vs tinea corporis (scrape for fungus), granuloma annulare, erythema annulare centrifugum, psoriasis, polymorphic light eruption, dermatomyositis, Sjögren's annular erythema (Asian patients), neonatal lupus. Stop the trigger (lesions resolve over weeks to months), photoprotection, topical steroids, HCQ. Look for systemic SLE (about 50% of SCLE meets criteria, usually mild). In women of childbearing age, anti-Ro has implications for future pregnancy (CHB).

question: Which set of conditions defines remission in SLE according to the DORIS definition?

options.A: Infection (including opportunistic infection) and pulmonary embolism
options.B: Assess and address sleep, mood, anaemia, thyroid disease, vitamin D, pain and deconditioning, as well as disease activity
options.C: Urgent assessment and treatment for neutropenic sepsis, with review of drug toxicity
options.D: Clinical SLEDAI 0, physician global assessment below 0.5, prednisolone 5 mg/day or less, with stable antimalarials, immunosuppressants and biologics allowed
options.E: It may reduce thrombotic risk as background therapy but does not replace anticoagulation in confirmed thrombotic APS

explanation: Serology is ignored in clinical SLEDAI. Lupus low disease activity state (SLEDAI 4 or less, prednisolone 7.5 mg/day or less) is an alternative target. LLDAS: SLEDAI-2K ≤4 with no major-organ activity, no haemolysis or GI activity, no new features, PGA ≤1, prednisolone ≤7.5 mg/day, with standard immunosuppressants and biologics tolerated. Spending ≥50% of follow-up in LLDAS halves damage, flares and mortality. Reaching a target on high-dose GC does not count. Treat-to-target: assess activity at every visit and damage yearly. Aim for remission or LLDAS within 6–12 months with prednisolone ≤5 mg. Escalate if the target is not met by 3–6 months, after checking adherence (up to 50% are nonadherent) and excluding non-lupus causes. Flare predictors: young onset, prior LN, CNS disease or vasculitis, persistently active serology, stopping HCQ, rapid GC withdrawal, pregnancy, UV, infection.

question: Which laboratory tests form the antiphospholipid antibody criteria, and why must positive results be repeated? Also tested as: Why must positive antiphospholipid antibodies be repeated before diagnosing APS?

options.A: Long-term warfarin with target INR 2–3; avoid DOACs such as rivaroxaban
options.B: Lupus anticoagulant, anticardiolipin and anti-beta2-glycoprotein I antibodies, repeated at least 12 weeks apart, because transient antibodies are common
options.C: Low-dose aspirin (75-100 mg daily)
options.D: Switch to therapeutic-dose LMWH with low-dose aspirin before 6 weeks' gestation, continuing through pregnancy and postpartum
options.E: DOACs can cause false-positive lupus anticoagulant results; repeat off anticoagulation or with DOACremoval techniques, and confirm persistence

explanation: Positivity must be persistent on two occasions at least 12 weeks apart, with moderate to high titres for solid-phase assays. Transient aPL occur with infection, drugs and other conditions, and low-titre results have little clinical significance. Triple positivity identifies the highest-risk profile. Causes of transient or non-pathogenic aPL: infections (syphilis, HIV, HCV, EBV, parvovirus, COVID-19, leprosy), drugs (chlorpromazine, procainamide, hydralazine, phenytoin, quinidine), malignancy (lymphoma), older age, other autoimmune diseases. Other prothrombotic states to consider: factor V Leiden, prothrombin G20210A, protein C, protein S or antithrombin deficiency, PNH (flow cytometry), myeloproliferative neoplasm (JAK2), HIT, malignancy, nephrotic syndrome, Behçet's. LA is the strongest single predictor of thrombosis. Testing is unreliable during acute thrombosis and on anticoagulants (see next entry). Do a dRVVT plus an LA-sensitive APTT (two tests).

question: A patient with a recent pulmonary embolism started apixaban before antiphospholipid testing. Lupus anticoagulant is reported as positive. How should this be interpreted?

options.A: Low-dose aspirin (75-100 mg daily)
options.B: Long-term warfarin; DOACs are avoided after arterial events in APS
options.C: DOACs can cause false-positive lupus anticoagulant results; repeat off anticoagulation or with DOACremoval techniques, and confirm persistence
options.D: Lupus anticoagulant, anticardiolipin and anti-beta2-glycoprotein I antibodies, repeated at least 12 weeks apart, because transient antibodies are common
options.E: Long-term warfarin with target INR 2–3; avoid DOACs such as rivaroxaban

explanation: DOACs, heparin and VKAs interfere with clotting-based LA assays, whereas solid-phase assays for anticardiolipin and anti-beta2-glycoprotein I are unaffected. Options: retest LA ≥2 days after stopping a DOAC (if clinically safe); use DOAC-removal agents (DOAC-Stop) before LA testing; switch to LMWH (with anti-Xaneutralising reagents); rely on solid-phase assays and antiβ2GPI, which are unaffected; or use the Taipan or Ecarin ratio (insensitive to VKAs). Confirm persistence at 12 weeks. Pre-test counselling matters, because finding highrisk APS changes the choice of anticoagulant (a DOAC is not appropriate).

question: Which obstetric complications meet the clinical criteria for APS?

options.A: Three or more unexplained consecutive miscarriages before 10 weeks, unexplained fetal death at or beyond 10 weeks, or delivery before 34 weeks for severe pre-eclampsia or placental insufficiency
options.B: Anticoagulation plus high-dose glucocorticoids plus plasma exchange and/or IVIG
options.C: Lupus anticoagulant, anticardiolipin and anti-beta2-glycoprotein I antibodies, repeated at least 12 weeks apart, because transient antibodies are common
options.D: Low-dose aspirin (75-100 mg daily)
options.E: Switch to therapeutic-dose LMWH with low-dose aspirin before 6 weeks' gestation, continuing through pregnancy and postpartum

explanation: These are the revised Sapporo (Sydney) clinical criteria. Maternal anatomical and hormonal causes and parental chromosomal abnormalities should be excluded for recurrent early loss. The 2023 ACR/EULAR APS classification criteria weight obstetric items differently: recurrent early losses score lowest, while severe pre-eclampsia or placental insufficiency before 34 weeks score highest. Recurrent miscarriage work-up: parental karyotype (balanced translocation), uterine anomalies (3D ultrasound), thyroid disease, diabetes, PCOS, hyperprolactinaemia, inherited thrombophilia (limited relevance), cervical insufficiency (second-trimester loss), infection, maternal age. Sydney clinical obstetric criteria: - ≥3 unexplained consecutive miscarriages before 10 weeks - ≥1 unexplained fetal death at or beyond 10 weeks - ≥1 delivery before 34 weeks for severe pre-eclampsia, eclampsia or placental insufficiency The 2023 criteria give the most weight to severe early preeclampsia or placental insufficiency before 34 weeks.

question: A 30-year-old woman has triple-positive antiphospholipid antibodies but no history of thrombosis or pregnancy complications. What is the recommended prophylaxis?

options.A: Lupus anticoagulant, anticardiolipin and anti-beta2-glycoprotein I antibodies, repeated at least 12 weeks apart, because transient antibodies are common
options.B: It may reduce thrombotic risk as background therapy but does not replace anticoagulation in confirmed thrombotic APS
options.C: Long-term warfarin; DOACs are avoided after arterial events in APS
options.D: Low-dose aspirin (75-100 mg daily)
options.E: Long-term warfarin with target INR 2–3; avoid DOACs such as rivaroxaban

explanation: Asymptomatic carriers with a high-risk aPL profile are offered low-dose aspirin, along with management of other thrombotic risk factors. Hydroxychloroquine is added in SLE. Low-dose aspirin for a high-risk aPL profile (and consider it for low-risk profiles in SLE), plus HCQ in SLE. Manage CV risk factors. Avoid oestrogen-containing contraception and HRT. Use thromboprophylaxis (LMWH) in high-risk situations such as surgery, immobilisation, the post-partum period and long-haul travel.

question: A woman with persistent antiphospholipid antibodies has a first unprovoked DVT. What is the recommended long-term anticoagulation, and which anticoagulant should be avoided if she is triple-positive? Also tested as: A 42-year-old woman with triple-positive antiphospholipid antibodies has her first unprovoked DVT. Which anticoagulant should be avoided?

options.A: Lupus anticoagulant, anticardiolipin and anti-beta2-glycoprotein I antibodies, repeated at least 12 weeks apart, because transient antibodies are common
options.B: Long-term warfarin with target INR 2–3; avoid DOACs such as rivaroxaban
options.C: Low-dose aspirin plus prophylactic-dose LMWH
options.D: DOACs can cause false-positive lupus anticoagulant results; repeat off anticoagulation or with DOACremoval techniques, and confirm persistence
options.E: Low-dose aspirin (75-100 mg daily)

explanation: A first unprovoked venous event in APS warrants long-term vitamin K antagonist therapy with INR 2–3. Rivaroxaban was associated with more thrombotic events than warfarin in triple-positive APS (TRAPS trial), so DOACs are avoided in high-risk APS. They may be considered only in selected lower-risk (single- or double-positive) venous APS when a VKA is not feasible or a stable INR cannot be achieved. Other trials: ASTRO-APS (apixaban, more strokes) and Ordi-Rimola (rivaroxaban, more arterial events). Point-ofcare INR may be inaccurate when LA is strongly positive; check against laboratory INR. Recurrence despite INR 2–3: check adherence and time in therapeutic range, then increase the target to 3–4, add lowdose aspirin, or switch to therapeutic LMWH. Add HCQ (and possibly a statin) as adjuncts. Provoked VTE with a low-risk profile can be considered for 3–6 months of treatment only after specialist review.

question: A young adult (with or without SLE) has an ischaemic stroke with persistently positive lupus anticoagulant, anticardiolipin and anti-beta2-glycoprotein I antibodies. What is the most appropriate long-term treatment? Also tested as: A 36-year-old woman with SLE has an acute ischaemic stroke. Lupus anticoagulant and anti-beta2glycoprotein I antibodies are persistently positive, and lupus activity is otherwise low. What is the most appropriate long-term treatment?

options.A: Long-term warfarin; DOACs are avoided after arterial events in APS
options.B: Low-dose aspirin plus prophylactic-dose LMWH
options.C: Anti-centromere: limited cutaneous disease, calcinosis and late PAH. Anti-Scl-70: diffuse disease and
options.D: Assess and address sleep, mood, anaemia, thyroid disease, vitamin D, pain and deconditioning, as well as disease activity
options.E: DOACs can cause false-positive lupus anticoagulant results; repeat off anticoagulation or with DOACremoval techniques, and confirm persistence

explanation: Arterial thrombosis with persistent aPL is managed with a vitamin K antagonist: INR 2–3 or 3–4 (balancing bleeding and recurrence), or INR 2–3 plus low-dose aspirin. This applies whether lupus activity is high or low. Young stroke differential: cardioembolism (PFO with paradoxical embolism, AF, Libman–Sacks or infective endocarditis), arterial dissection, vasculitis (primary CNS, Takayasu, Behçet's, SLE), RCVS, CADASIL, Fabry disease, sickle cell disease, moyamoya, DADA2 (lacunar strokes, livedo), drugs (cocaine, amphetamines), inherited thrombophilia (venous events more than arterial), Sneddon's syndrome, homocystinuria. Investigate with MRI and MRA, echo (TOE for vegetations), Holter and a thrombophilia screen. Manage BP, lipids and smoking. Continue HCQ in SLE.

question: A woman with known APS develops renal failure, livedo, confusion and thrombocytopenia over 5 days, with microthrombi on skin biopsy. What is the first-line treatment?

options.A: Mycophenolate mofetil (or methotrexate or rituximab)
options.B: Assess urgently and in parallel for infection, thrombotic microangiopathy, catastrophic APS macrophage activation syndrome and severe lupus activity
options.C: Switch to therapeutic-dose LMWH with low-dose aspirin before 6 weeks' gestation, continuing through pregnancy and postpartum
options.D: Anticoagulation plus high-dose glucocorticoids plus plasma exchange and/or IVIG
options.E: HRCT chest with full PFTs (FVC and DLCO) in every patient at baseline; mycophenolate is first-line for significant or progressive SSc-ILD

explanation: Catastrophic APS (multi-organ small-vessel thrombosis within a week) has high mortality. Triple therapy is first-line and triggers such as infection are treated; rituximab or eculizumab are used for refractory disease. TTP (ADAMTS13 <10%), aHUS (complement), HIT (heparin exposure; PF4 antibodies), DIC (sepsis), HELLP, malignant hypertension, scleroderma renal crisis, sepsis. CAPS: thrombosis in ≥3 organs within a week, histological small-vessel occlusion, and aPL. Mortality is about 30– 50%. Common organs: kidney, lung (ARDS, DAH), brain, heart, skin, adrenals (haemorrhage), liver. About half have a trigger: infection, surgery, stopping anticoagulation, SLE flare, pregnancy or the puerperium. Triple therapy: therapeutic heparin, high-dose GC (pulses) and PLEX and/or IVIG. Treat the trigger. For refractory disease: rituximab or eculizumab (complement C5 inhibition). Intensive care.

question: A 32-year-old woman with three consecutive unexplained miscarriages before 10 weeks has persistent medium-high titre anticardiolipin antibodies. She is newly pregnant. What is the most appropriate treatment?

options.A: Drug-induced subacute cutaneous lupus erythematosus
options.B: Switch to therapeutic-dose LMWH with low-dose aspirin before 6 weeks' gestation, continuing through pregnancy and postpartum
options.C: Long-term warfarin with target INR 2–3; avoid DOACs such as rivaroxaban
options.D: Long-term warfarin; DOACs are avoided after arterial events in APS
options.E: Low-dose aspirin plus prophylactic-dose LMWH

explanation: Obstetric APS without prior thrombosis is treated with low-dose aspirin and prophylactic LMWH, continuing LMWH for 6 weeks postpartum. Live birth rates in treated obstetric APS are about 70–80%. HCQ added to standard therapy is under study (HYPATIA) and is often used for refractory cases. Start aspirin before conception (or from a positive test) and LMWH from a positive pregnancy test or the fetal heart. Monitor with uterine artery Doppler at 20–24 weeks and serial growth scans. Refractory obstetric APS: add HCQ, consider increasing LMWH to intermediate or therapeutic dose, add low-dose prednisolone in the first trimester, or IVIG (expert centre). Women with aPL-positivity but no events: aspirin, plus postpartum LMWH for 6 weeks if highrisk or other risk factors.

question: How should thrombotic APS be managed in pregnancy, including in a woman on warfarin who finds she is 5 weeks pregnant? Also tested as: A woman on warfarin for thrombotic APS discovers she is 5 weeks pregnant. What is the most appropriate action?

options.A: Low-dose aspirin (75-100 mg daily)
options.B: Drug-induced subacute cutaneous lupus erythematosus
options.C: Switch to therapeutic-dose LMWH with low-dose aspirin before 6 weeks' gestation, continuing through pregnancy and postpartum
options.D: Anticoagulation plus high-dose glucocorticoids plus plasma exchange and/or IVIG
options.E: Low-dose aspirin plus prophylactic-dose LMWH

explanation: Thrombotic APS needs therapeutic anticoagulation throughout pregnancy and postpartum. Warfarin is teratogenic (embryopathy risk is greatest between 6 and 12 weeks) and DOACs are not used in pregnancy. Warfarin is compatible with breastfeeding postpartum. Warfarin embryopathy: nasal hypoplasia, stippled epiphyses (chondrodysplasia punctata). Later exposure carries fetal intracranial haemorrhage risk. Peri-delivery: plan neuraxial anaesthesia timing (stop prophylactic LMWH 12 hours before, therapeutic 24 hours before). Restart LMWH after delivery and bridge back to warfarin. Use a monitored anti-Xa level in extremes of weight or renal impairment. Women on warfarin should be counselled before conception and do early pregnancy tests.

question: What is the role of hydroxychloroquine in thrombosis in SLE?

options.A: Long-term warfarin; DOACs are avoided after arterial events in APS
options.B: Assess and address sleep, mood, anaemia, thyroid disease, vitamin D, pain and deconditioning, as well as disease activity
options.C: Low-dose aspirin (75-100 mg daily)
options.D: It may reduce thrombotic risk as background therapy but does not replace anticoagulation in confirmed thrombotic APS
options.E: All patients unless contraindicated, at no more than 5 mg/kg actual body weight per day, so 300 mg daily for 60 kg

explanation: Hydroxychloroquine is part of background SLE therapy and may add benefit in aPL-positive patients. HCQ reduces thrombosis in aPL-positive SLE (observational data). Mechanisms include reduced aPL binding to phospholipid bilayers, reduced platelet activation and improved lipids. Continue HCQ in all SLE patients. It is adjunctive only: confirmed thrombotic APS still needs a VKA. HCQ is also used in refractory obstetric APS. Statins are an adjunct in recurrent thrombosis.

question: A patient meets the systemic sclerosis classification criteria. What is the minimum total score required?

options.A: Pulmonary complications: interstitial lung disease and pulmonary arterial hypertension
options.B: ANA at a titre of 1:80 or higher on HEp-2 cells (or an equivalent test) at any time, then 10 or more weighted points with at least one clinical criterion
options.C: Hand physiotherapy and occupational therapy, stretching, skin care and joint protection
options.D: It is considered for selected patients with rapidly progressive diffuse disease at risk of organ failure, at experienced centres

explanation: Skin thickening of the fingers of both hands extending proximal to the MCP joints scores 9 and is sufficient alone. Otherwise weighted items (puffy fingers, sclerodactyly, fingertip lesions, telangiectasia, abnormal nailfold capillaries, PAH or ILD, Raynaud's, SSc-specific antibodies) are summed. Item Points 9 Bilateral finger skin thickening proximal to (sufficient) the MCPs Puffy fingers / sclerodactyly distal to the 2 / 4 MCPs Digital ulcers / pitting scars 2 / 3 2 Telangiectasia 2 Abnormal nailfold capillaries PAH and/or ILD 2 Raynaud's 3 ACA, Scl-70 or RNA pol III 3 Sensitivity about 91%, specificity about 92%. The criteria do not apply if skin thickening spares the fingers or a mimic explains the features better.

question: A woman has a year of Raynaud's and puffy fingers, a centromere-pattern ANA and giant capillaries with haemorrhages on nailfold capillaroscopy. How should this be interpreted, and how does the scleroderma capillaroscopy pattern evolve? Also tested as: Which nailfold capillaroscopy finding is most typical of early systemic sclerosis?

options.A: Pulmonary complications: interstitial lung disease and pulmonary arterial hypertension
options.B: Anti-histone
options.C: It is considered for selected patients with rapidly progressive diffuse disease at risk of organ failure, at experienced centres
options.D: Very early systemic sclerosis (VEDOSS) requiring monitoring for organ involvement; the pattern evolves from early (giant capillaries, microhaemorrhages) through active to late (capillary loss, avascular areas, ramified capillaries)
options.E: Anti-centromere: limited cutaneous disease, calcinosis and late PAH. Anti-Scl-70: diffuse disease and

explanation: Raynaud's with puffy fingers, SSc-specific antibodies and a scleroderma capillaroscopy pattern indicates very early SSc, so baseline and serial screening for ILD, PAH and other organ involvement is needed. Primary Raynaud's has normal capillaroscopy and negative autoantibodies. The capillaroscopic stage correlates with digital ulcer risk. Secondary Raynaud's: SSc, SLE, MCTD, Sjögren's, myositis (especially antisynthetase), UCTD; vibration white finger (hand-arm vibration syndrome); hypothenar hammer syndrome; thoracic outlet syndrome (unilateral); atherosclerosis or Buerger's disease (smokers); cryoglobulinaemia, cold agglutinins, paraprotein; drugs (βblockers, ergots, sympathomimetics, chemotherapy such as bleomycin and cisplatin, interferon); hypothyroidism. Feature Primary Secondary (SSc) Raynaud's teens to 20s usually after 30 Onset mild, severe, painful, may Severity symmetrical be asymmetric Ulcers, pitting, no yes gangrene Capillaroscopy normal scleroderma pattern positive, SSc- ANA negative or low titre specific Abnormal capillaroscopy plus an SSc antibody gives a >60–80% chance of progression to SSc. Refer anyone with Raynaud's plus puffy fingers, a positive ANA or abnormal capillaroscopy. A handheld dermatoscope works for clinic capillaroscopy.

question: What does the modified Rodnan skin score measure?

options.A: Skin thickness at 17 body sites scored 0-3 (maximum 51)
options.B: Mycophenolate mofetil (or methotrexate or rituximab)
options.C: Systemic disease activity across 12 organ domains
options.D: Hand physiotherapy and occupational therapy, stretching, skin care and joint protection
options.E: Anticoagulation plus high-dose glucocorticoids plus plasma exchange and/or IVIG

explanation: The mRSS is the main skin outcome in diffuse SSc trials and correlates with disease severity and mortality. The mRSS scores 17 sites from 0 to 3 (total 0–51). Skin progresses over the first 1–3 years in dcSSc, then often softens. Early rapid progression predicts organ involvement and mortality.

question: Which clinical phenotypes are associated with anti-centromere, anti-Scl-70 and anti-RNA polymerase III antibodies? Also tested as: What is the significance of anti-RNA polymerase III antibodies in systemic sclerosis?

options.A: Anti-centromere: limited cutaneous disease, calcinosis and late PAH. Anti-Scl-70: diffuse disease and
options.B: Hand physiotherapy and occupational therapy, stretching, skin care and joint protection

question: A 44-year-old woman with limited cutaneous SSc has frequent painful Raynaud's attacks despite keeping warm. What is the first-line drug?

options.A: Gastric antral vascular ectasia (GAVE)
options.B: Rotating or intermittent courses of antibiotics for small intestinal bacterial overgrowth
options.C: Mycophenolate mofetil (or methotrexate or rituximab)
options.D: PPI therapy with reflux measures, assessment of dysmotility and aspiration risk, and prokinetics or dilatation where indicated
options.E: A dihydropyridine calcium-channel blocker such as nifedipine

explanation: CCBs are first-line, with PDE5 inhibitors as an alternative or addition. IV iloprost is used for severe attacks. Betablockers may worsen vasospasm. General: whole-body warmth, stop smoking, avoid vasoconstrictors (β-blockers, sympathomimetics, decongestants, triptans). First line: a dihydropyridine CCB (nifedipine MR, amlodipine) and/or a PDE5 inhibitor (sildenafil, tadalafil). Alternatives: losartan, fluoxetine, topical nitrates. Severe or refractory: IV iloprost. Refractory: botulinum toxin to the palm, digital sympathectomy, fat grafting.

question: A patient with SSc has a painful digital ulcer despite nifedipine; another has five new ulcers this year despite nifedipine and sildenafil, which heal with iloprost. What is used for healing, and what reduces new ulcers? Also tested as: A patient with diffuse SSc has developed five new digital ulcers this year despite nifedipine and sildenafil. Ulcers heal with iloprost. Which drug reduces the number of new ulcers?

options.A: Initial combination therapy with a PDE5 inhibitor and an endothelin receptor antagonist
options.B: PPI therapy with reflux measures, assessment of dysmotility and aspiration risk, and prokinetics or dilatation where indicated
options.C: Mycophenolate mofetil (or methotrexate or rituximab)
options.D: A dihydropyridine calcium-channel blocker such as nifedipine
options.E: Wound care, assessment for infection, and a PDE5 inhibitor and/or IV iloprost for healing; bosentan reduces the number of new digital ulcers but does not speed healing

explanation: PDE5 inhibitors and IV prostanoids help ulcer healing. Infected ulcers need antibiotics, and critical ischaemia needs urgent vascular assessment. Bosentan requires monthly LFTs and effective contraception. Digital ulcer types and mimics: ischaemic fingertip ulcers vs ulcers over calcinosis or extensor surfaces (traction, mechanical), infection or osteomyelitis (probe to bone; Xray or MRI), macrovascular occlusion (ulnar artery occlusion is common in SSc; also emboli, thoracic outlet syndrome), vasculitis, cholesterol emboli, cryoglobulinaemia, Buerger's disease. Critical ischaemia: admit for IV iloprost, analgesia and consider 24–72 hours of anticoagulation plus aspirin. Arrange urgent vascular and hand surgery review. Do duplex or angiography for macrovascular disease.

question: Which patients are at greatest risk of scleroderma renal crisis, how is renal crisis treated (for example BP 186/104, rising creatinine and microangiopathic haemolysis in early diffuse SSc on glucocorticoids), and what is the role of prophylactic ACE inhibition? Also tested as: A 48-year-old woman with early diffuse SSc on glucocorticoids has BP 186/104 mmHg, headache, creatinine rising from 70 to 160 micromol/L over a week and microangiopathic haemolysis. What is the most appropriate treatment? | What is the role of ACE inhibitors in systemic sclerosis?

options.A: HRCT chest with full PFTs (FVC and DLCO) in every patient at baseline; mycophenolate is first-line for significant or progressive SSc-ILD
options.B: Highest risk: early (under 4 years) rapidly progressive diffuse disease, anti-RNA polymerase III, tendon friction rubs and prednisolone above about 15 mg/day. Treat with an ACE inhibitor such as captopril titrated to
options.C: Mycophenolate mofetil (or methotrexate or rituximab)
options.D: Pulmonary complications: interstitial lung disease and pulmonary arterial hypertension
options.E: It is considered for selected patients with rapidly progressive diffuse disease at risk of organ failure, at experienced centres

explanation: blood pressure, continued even on dialysis. ACE inhibitors are not given prophylactically ACE inhibitors are the mainstay of renal crisis and are continued even if dialysis is needed, as recovery can occur over months. CCBs can be added for blood pressure control. Prophylactic ACE inhibition has not prevented renal crisis and may be associated with worse outcomes. Creatinine may rise initially during treatment, which should not prompt withdrawal. AKI in SSc: renal crisis vs ANCA (MPO) GN (consider Dpenicillamine history), drug nephrotoxicity (NSAIDs, CNIs), TTP, aHUS, hypovolaemia (GI loss), pre-eclampsia, obstructive uropathy. Renal crisis is a TMA emergency: new accelerated hypertension (often >150/85, or a systolic rise ≥30 mmHg) with AKI, schistocytes, thrombocytopenia, headache, visual disturbance, seizures, heart failure and pericardial effusion. Normotensive SRC occurs in about 10% and carries a worse prognosis. Incidence is 2–5% overall and 10–15% in early diffuse disease. Ciclosporin also raises risk. Captopril 6.25–12.5 mg, increased every 4–8 hours, aiming for a fall of 10–20 mmHg per day without hypotension. Then add a CCB, then an α-blocker, then IV prostacyclin. 20–50% need dialysis; recovery can continue for up to 2 years, so delay transplant listing. Eculizumab for refractory TMA. One-year mortality is 10–20%. Prevention: home BP monitoring, avoid high-dose GC, and keep prednisolone ≤10–15 mg with BP checks.

question: A woman with newly diagnosed anti-Scl-70-positive diffuse SSc needs baseline assessment; another patient has ILD involving 25% of the lungs with FVC 68% and declining. What is the key baseline investigation, and what is first-line treatment? Also tested as: A patient with systemic sclerosis has ILD involving 25% of the lungs on HRCT, with FVC 68% predicted and declining. What is the most appropriate first-line treatment?

options.A: HRCT chest with full PFTs (FVC and DLCO) in every patient at baseline; mycophenolate is first-line for significant or progressive SSc-ILD
options.B: Initial combination therapy with a PDE5 inhibitor and an endothelin receptor antagonist
options.C: Anti-centromere: limited cutaneous disease, calcinosis and late PAH. Anti-Scl-70: diffuse disease and
options.D: Pulmonary complications: interstitial lung disease and pulmonary arterial hypertension
options.E: Hand physiotherapy and occupational therapy, stretching, skin care and joint protection

explanation: HRCT is advised at baseline in all patients with SSc, with PFTs including FVC and DLCO and regular follow-up PFTs, especially in early disease. MMF, cyclophosphamide or rituximab are used for SSc-ILD, with MMF commonly first. Nintedanib is added for progressive fibrosis, and tocilizumab may be considered in early ILD with raised acute-phase reactants. High-dose glucocorticoids risk renal crisis. Breathlessness in SSc: ILD, PAH, cardiac disease (diastolic dysfunction, myocarditis), aspiration from reflux, anaemia (GAVE), chest wall restriction from truncal skin, myositis (respiratory muscles), drug pneumonitis (methotrexate, cyclophosphamide), infection, lung cancer (higher in SSc- ILD). ILD is present on HRCT in 50–65%, and 25–30% develop clinically progressive disease. It is the leading cause of death (30–35%). The usual pattern is NSIP. Risk factors: dcSSc, Scl-70, Th/To, U3-RNP, Ro52, male sex, African ancestry, early disease, raised CRP. Extent >20% on HRCT (Goh staging) predicts progression. Significant progression means FVC falls ≥10%, or 5–9% with DLCO ≥15%. Trial evidence: SLS-II (MMF ≈ cyclophosphamide, better tolerated); SLS-I (cyclophosphamide); RECITAL and DESIRES (rituximab); focuSSced (tocilizumab preserved FVC); SENSCIS (nintedanib slowed FVC decline by 40– 45%, including on MMF). Selected rapid progressors: AHSCT. End stage: oxygen, pulmonary rehabilitation, lung transplant (needs reflux control). Monitoring: PFTs every 3–6 months in early disease, at least yearly otherwise; treat reflux.

question: A 40-year-old man has early diffuse cutaneous SSc with rapidly progressive skin thickening (mRSS 28) and no significant organ involvement. Which treatment is most appropriate for the skin disease?

options.A: Gastric antral vascular ectasia (GAVE)
options.B: Skin thickness at 17 body sites scored 0-3 (maximum 51)
options.C: A dihydropyridine calcium-channel blocker such as nifedipine
options.D: Anticoagulation plus high-dose glucocorticoids plus plasma exchange and/or IVIG
options.E: Mycophenolate mofetil (or methotrexate or rituximab)

explanation: Methotrexate, MMF or rituximab are used for skin fibrosis. Autologous stem cell transplantation is considered in selected rapidly progressive patients at experienced centres. Early dcSSc skin: methotrexate or MMF (preferred if ILD is present), or rituximab. Tocilizumab when CRP is raised (benefit mainly in lung preservation). GC only at ≤10–15 mg. Symptomatic care: emollients and antihistamines for itch, laser for telangiectasia, surgical removal of calcinosis (drug evidence for sodium thiosulfate, diltiazem or bisphosphonates is weak), physiotherapy for contractures, mouth exercises for microstomia. Emerging: CAR-T, anifrolumab.

question: What is the role of autologous haematopoietic stem cell transplantation in systemic sclerosis?

options.C: Hand physiotherapy and occupational therapy, stretching, skin care and joint protection
options.D: Pulmonary complications: interstitial lung disease and pulmonary arterial hypertension
options.E: It is considered for selected patients with rapidly progressive diffuse disease at risk of organ failure, at experienced centres

explanation: Trials show survival benefit in selected patients, balanced against substantial treatment-related mortality. Careful cardiopulmonary screening is required. ASTIS, SCOT and ASSIST trials showed event-free and overall survival benefit despite 5–10% treatment-related mortality. It suits selected patients under 65 with rapidly progressive dcSSc and without severe cardiac disease or advanced organ failure (cardiac MRI and right heart catheterisation screening).

question: A woman with limited SSc has progressive breathlessness with FVC 92%, DLCO 41% (FVC/DLCO 2.2) and a raised tricuspid regurgitant velocity. How is PAH screened for and confirmed? Also tested as: How should patients with systemic sclerosis be screened for pulmonary arterial hypertension?

options.A: Pulmonary complications: interstitial lung disease and pulmonary arterial hypertension
options.B: HRCT chest with full PFTs (FVC and DLCO) in every patient at baseline; mycophenolate is first-line for significant or progressive SSc-ILD
options.C: Screen at least annually (PAH is often asymptomatic early and a normal echo does not exclude it) by combining symptoms, DLCO, NT-proBNP, echocardiography and algorithms such as DETECT; confirm by right heart catheterisation
options.D: Hand physiotherapy and occupational therapy, stretching, skin care and joint protection
options.E: A dihydropyridine calcium-channel blocker such as nifedipine

explanation: Isolated low DLCO with a high FVC/DLCO ratio suggests PAH. Diagnosis needs right heart catheterisation: mean PAP above 20 mmHg, PAWP 15 mmHg or less, and PVR above 2 Wood units. PH groups in SSc (often coexisting): 1, PAH including pulmonary veno-occlusive disease (PVOD worsens on vasodilators: suspect it with septal lines, ground glass, lymphadenopathy or a very low DLCO); 2, left heart disease (diastolic dysfunction); 3, ILD with hypoxia; 4, CTEPH (V/Q scan). PAH affects 8–12% of patients. Risk factors: limited cutaneous disease, ACA, U3-RNP, Th/To, long duration, many telangiectasias, FVC/DLCO >1.6, raised NT-proBNP. DETECT applies to disease >3 years with DLCO <60%. Screening detects milder disease and improves survival. Echo, PFTs and NT-proBNP yearly; RHC if suspected; refer to a PH centre.

question: A patient with SSc has newly diagnosed PAH (WHO functional class III) on right heart catheterisation, with low to intermediate risk. Which approach is most appropriate?

options.A: HRCT chest with full PFTs (FVC and DLCO) in every patient at baseline; mycophenolate is first-line for significant or progressive SSc-ILD
options.B: Anticholinergic drugs, sedating antihistamines and tricyclic antidepressants
options.C: Anti-centromere: limited cutaneous disease, calcinosis and late PAH. Anti-Scl-70: diffuse disease and
options.D: PPI therapy with reflux measures, assessment of dysmotility and aspiration risk, and prokinetics or dilatation where indicated
options.E: Initial combination therapy with a PDE5 inhibitor and an endothelin receptor antagonist

explanation: Initial combination therapy is standard. IV prostacyclin is added for high-risk patients. Vasoreactivity-guided CCB therapy does not apply to connective tissue disease-associated PAH. Initial dual therapy: an ERA (ambrisentan, macitentan) plus a PDE5 inhibitor (tadalafil, sildenafil), or riociguat in place of the PDE5 inhibitor. High risk: add parenteral prostacyclin (epoprostenol, treprostinil) or selexipag. Sotatercept (activin signalling inhibitor) is licensed as add-on therapy. Supportive care: diuretics, oxygen, rehabilitation, transplant referral. Anticoagulation is not routine (GAVE bleeding risk). Pregnancy is strongly advised against (ERAs are teratogenic). Three-year survival is 50–60% in older series and is improving.

question: A woman with SSc has diarrhoea, bloating and weight loss. A glucose hydrogen breath test is positive. What is the most appropriate treatment?

options.A: B-cell targeted therapy with rituximab plus glucocorticoids, adding plasma exchange for lifethreatening disease
options.B: 4; she is classified as having Sjögren's
options.C: Mycophenolate mofetil (or methotrexate or rituximab)
options.D: PPI therapy with reflux measures, assessment of dysmotility and aspiration risk, and prokinetics or dilatation where indicated
options.E: Rotating or intermittent courses of antibiotics for small intestinal bacterial overgrowth

explanation: Small bowel dysmotility predisposes to bacterial overgrowth and malabsorption. Prokinetics help dysmotility, and nutritional screening with dietetic input is important. Rotate antibiotics (rifaximin, doxycycline, metronidazole, co-amoxiclav). Prokinetics (prucalopride, low-dose erythromycin, domperidone). Octreotide for pseudoobstruction. Correct B12 (often low from SIBO), vitamin D, iron and fat-soluble vitamins. Screen nutrition with MUST, BMI and albumin; parenteral nutrition for intestinal failure. Malnutrition predicts mortality. Pneumatosis intestinalis is often benign but needs surgical assessment if there is peritonism.

question: A patient with SSc has severe reflux and dysphagia. What is the most appropriate management?

options.A: Initial combination therapy with a PDE5 inhibitor and an endothelin receptor antagonist
options.B: PPI therapy with reflux measures, assessment of dysmotility and aspiration risk, and prokinetics or dilatation where indicated
options.C: Mycophenolate mofetil (or methotrexate or rituximab)
options.D: Preservative-free artificial tears and gels with lid hygiene first; for refractory disease, topical ciclosporin
options.E: Rotating or intermittent courses of antibiotics for small intestinal bacterial overgrowth

explanation: Oesophageal dysmotility with reflux is near-universal in SSc. Aspiration can contribute to lung disease. High-dose PPI (often twice daily) with H2 blocker add-on at night; raise the head of the bed; small meals; prokinetics. Endoscopy for dysphagia, alarm features or Barrett's surveillance; dilatation for strictures. Treat reflux aggressively in ILD (aspiration) and before lung transplant. GI involvement occurs in about 90% (mouth to anus).

question: A 63-year-old woman with limited cutaneous SSc for 18 years has anaemia and melaena. Endoscopy shows linear red stripes in the gastric antrum. What is the diagnosis?

options.A: Gastric antral vascular ectasia (GAVE)
options.B: A dihydropyridine calcium-channel blocker such as nifedipine
options.C: Mycophenolate mofetil (or methotrexate or rituximab)
options.D: PPI therapy with reflux measures, assessment of dysmotility and aspiration risk, and prokinetics or dilatation where indicated
options.E: Rotating or intermittent courses of antibiotics for small intestinal bacterial overgrowth

explanation: GAVE ("watermelon stomach") causes chronic GI bleeding in SSc and is treated endoscopically (argon plasma coagulation) with iron replacement. Iron-deficiency anaemia in SSc: GAVE, oesophagitis, telangiectasia bleeding anywhere in the GI tract, malabsorption (SIBO, coeliac overlap), NSAIDs, anticoagulants. Other causes of anaemia: renal crisis (MAHA), anaemia of chronic disease, B12 deficiency. Iron (often IV), endoscopic argon plasma coagulation (repeated) or band ligation. Transfusion if severe. GAVE is associated with anti-RNA pol III and early diffuse disease.

question: What is the leading cause of death in systemic sclerosis?

options.A: Pulmonary complications: interstitial lung disease and pulmonary arterial hypertension
options.B: About 30–40% are ANCA-positive (usually MPO); cardiac involvement is a leading cause of death mepolizumab (or benralizumab) treats relapsing, steroid-dependent disease
options.C: It is considered for selected patients with rapidly progressive diffuse disease at risk of organ failure, at experienced centres
options.D: Anti-centromere: limited cutaneous disease, calcinosis and late PAH. Anti-Scl-70: diffuse disease and
options.E: Hand physiotherapy and occupational therapy, stretching, skin care and joint protection

explanation: Since ACE inhibitors transformed renal crisis outcomes, ILD and PAH are the main causes of SSc-related death. SSc-related deaths are about 55% of the total. Causes: ILD (commonest), PAH, cardiac disease; renal crisis is now uncommon. Non-SSc deaths: cancer, infection, atherosclerotic CVD. Poor prognostic factors: older onset, male sex, diffuse disease with high or rapidly rising mRSS, friction rubs, FVC <70%, PAH, cardiac involvement, renal crisis, raised CRP, anaemia.

question: Which measures help hand function in systemic sclerosis?

options.A: Anti-centromere: limited cutaneous disease, calcinosis and late PAH. Anti-Scl-70: diffuse disease and
options.B: It is considered for selected patients with rapidly progressive diffuse disease at risk of organ failure, at experienced centres
options.C: Hand physiotherapy and occupational therapy, stretching, skin care and joint protection
options.D: Pulmonary complications: interstitial lung disease and pulmonary arterial hypertension
options.E: HRCT chest with full PFTs (FVC and DLCO) in every patient at baseline; mycophenolate is first-line for significant or progressive SSc-ILD

explanation: Rehabilitation helps maintain range of movement and function. Hand OT and physiotherapy, splints, paraffin wax baths, stretching, skin care (emollients), and protecting the digits from cold and trauma. Mouth-stretching exercises and dental hygiene for microstomia. Treat calcinosis and contractures surgically where needed. Psychological support (body image, depression).

question: What are the cardinal features of Sjögren's disease?

options.A: Systemic disease activity across 12 organ domains
options.B: B-cell targeted therapy with rituximab plus glucocorticoids, adding plasma exchange for lifethreatening disease
options.C: Dry eyes and dry mouth due to lymphocytic infiltration of exocrine glands
options.D: Anticholinergic drugs, sedating antihistamines and tricyclic antidepressants
options.E: Preservative-free artificial tears and gels with lid hygiene first; for refractory disease, topical ciclosporin

explanation: Sjögren's can also affect joints, skin, lungs, kidneys, nerves and blood, and carries an increased lymphoma risk. Sicca causes: - Drugs (the commonest cause): anticholinergics, TCAs, SSRIs, antihistamines, diuretics, βblockers, opioids, antipsychotics, ICIs. - Age and lifestyle: ageing, menopause, mouth breathing, smoking, anxiety, dehydration. - Infection: HCV, HIV (DILS), HTLV-1, EBV. - Infiltrative: IgG4-RD, sarcoid, amyloid, lymphoma, haemochromatosis. - Other: head and neck radiation, GVHD, diabetes, fibromyalgia, blepharitis or meibomian gland dysfunction, contact lenses, prior LASIK. Oral: red, fissured, depapillated tongue; "cracker sign"; cervical (gum-line) caries; candidiasis and angular cheilitis. Eyes: grittiness, mucus strands, punctate erosions, filamentary keratitis. Also nasal crusting, dry cough (xerotrachea), xerosis, vaginal dryness. Fatigue (70–80%) is the most disabling symptom.

question: A 52-year-old woman has dry eyes and mouth. Anti-Ro/SSA is positive and Schirmer's test is 4 mm in 5 minutes in both eyes. Lip biopsy has not been performed. How does she score on the 2016 Sjögren's classification criteria?

options.A: Diffuse infiltrative lymphocytosis syndrome (DILS)
options.B: Systemic disease activity across 12 organ domains
options.C: Preservative-free artificial tears and gels with lid hygiene first; for refractory disease, topical ciclosporin
options.D: 4; she is classified as having Sjögren's
options.E: Dry eyes and dry mouth due to lymphocytic infiltration of exocrine glands

explanation: Weighted items: labial gland focus score 1 or more (3), anti-Ro/SSA (3), ocular staining score 5 or more (1), Schirmer 5 mm/5 min or less (1), unstimulated salivary flow 0.1 mL/min or less (1). A score of 4 or more classifies, provided inclusion criteria are met and exclusions are absent. Anti-La alone does not score. Entry requires ocular or oral dryness symptoms, or suspected SjD from an ESSDAI domain. Exclusions: head and neck radiation, active HCV (PCR-positive), AIDS, sarcoidosis, amyloidosis, GVHD, IgG4-RD. Either a positive biopsy or anti-Ro is needed, because the minor items total only 3. Stop anticholinergic drugs before testing. Investigations: Schirmer I, ocular staining score, tear breakup time, unstimulated sialometry, salivary ultrasound, labial biopsy if seronegative. Also anti-Ro and anti-La, RF, immunoglobulins, C3/C4, cryoglobulins, SPEP and FLC, FBC, urinalysis, U&E and bicarbonate.

question: What does the ESSDAI measure in Sjögren's disease?

options.A: Dry eyes and dry mouth due to lymphocytic infiltration of exocrine glands
options.B: Anticholinergic drugs, sedating antihistamines and tricyclic antidepressants
options.C: Skin thickness at 17 body sites scored 0-3 (maximum 51)
options.D: Preservative-free artificial tears and gels with lid hygiene first; for refractory disease, topical ciclosporin
options.E: Systemic disease activity across 12 organ domains

explanation: The ESSDAI guides systemic treatment. The patient-reported ESSPRI captures dryness, fatigue and pain. ESSDAI domains: constitutional, lymphadenopathy, glandular, articular, cutaneous, pulmonary, renal, muscular, PNS, CNS, haematological and biological. It is the primary outcome in trials.

question: Which medication class commonly worsens dryness in Sjögren's disease?

options.A: B-cell targeted therapy with rituximab plus glucocorticoids, adding plasma exchange for lifethreatening disease
options.B: Anticholinergic drugs, sedating antihistamines and tricyclic antidepressants
options.C: Preservative-free artificial tears and gels with lid hygiene first; for refractory disease, topical ciclosporin
options.D: Systemic disease activity across 12 organ domains
options.E: Dry eyes and dry mouth due to lymphocytic infiltration of exocrine glands

explanation: Medication review is an important part of managing sicca symptoms. Review and switch drying drugs: anticholinergic bladder drugs (try mirabegron), sedating antihistamines (use nonsedating), TCAs (alternative analgesics), diuretics, opioids, antipsychotics. Also avoid caffeine, alcohol and smoking.

question: What is the stepwise management of dry eyes in Sjögren's disease, including severe dry eye with corneal damage despite frequent tears? Also tested as: A woman with Sjögren's has severe dry eye with corneal damage despite frequent preservative-free tears and gels. What is the most appropriate next ocular treatment?

options.A: Systemic disease activity across 12 organ domains
options.B: Dry eyes and dry mouth due to lymphocytic infiltration of exocrine glands
options.C: Preservative-free artificial tears and gels with lid hygiene first; for refractory disease, topical ciclosporin
options.D: 4; she is classified as having Sjögren's
options.E: B-cell targeted therapy with rituximab plus glucocorticoids, adding plasma exchange for lifethreatening disease

explanation: (or lifitegrast) with ophthalmology input, plus autologous serum drops, punctal plugs or short topical steroid courses Ocular lubricants are foundational; use preservative-free drops if more than 4 times daily, and gels or ointments at night. Refractory disease is managed under ophthalmology care with topical immunomodulatory drops, autologous serum drops or punctal plugs. Short courses of topical steroid may be used with care. Avoid dry environments and screen glare, and use wraparound glasses. Scleral lenses for severe disease. Oral pilocarpine also helps the eyes. Watch for corneal ulceration or melt.

question: How is xerostomia managed according to residual gland function, and which dental complication is particularly important? Also tested as: A 47-year-old woman with Sjögren's has troublesome oral dryness despite saliva substitutes. Salivary flow testing shows residual gland function. What is the most appropriate next treatment? | Which dental complication is particularly important in Sjögren's disease?

options.A: B-cell targeted therapy with rituximab plus glucocorticoids, adding plasma exchange for lifethreatening disease
options.B: Anticholinergic drugs, sedating antihistamines and tricyclic antidepressants
options.C: Tailor to gland function: non-pharmacological stimulation for mild dysfunction; pilocarpine or cevimeline when residual function remains; saliva substitutes when there is none. Rapidly progressive dental caries is the key complication
options.D: Systemic disease activity across 12 organ domains
options.E: Dry eyes and dry mouth due to lymphocytic infiltration of exocrine glands

explanation: Muscarinic agonists stimulate residual function; sweating and urinary frequency are common adverse effects. Immunosuppressants do not improve dryness. Regular dental review, fluoride and treatment of oral candidiasis are essential. General measures: frequent sips of water, sugar-free gum or xylitol lozenges, a humidifier. Dental: high-fluoride toothpaste (5000 ppm), fluoride varnish, review every 3–6 months, treat candida. Substitutes: gels, sprays, oxygenated glycerol triester. Pilocarpine 5 mg 3–4 times daily (contraindicated in asthma, narrow-angle glaucoma and uncontrolled cardiac disease).

question: What is the role of systemic treatment in Sjögren's disease with fatigue and arthralgia but no organ involvement, and with mild inflammatory arthritis? Also tested as: A patient with Sjögren's has inflammatory arthralgia and mild arthritis without major organ involvement. What is the most appropriate first-line systemic treatment?

options.A: Colchicine with topical treatments first; for refractory ulcers, apremilast (randomised trial evidence) or a
options.B: Fatigue alone does not warrant immunosuppression (assess reversible causes and use symptomdirected care); for arthritis, hydroxychloroquine with short-term glucocorticoids if needed, and methotrexate for persistent arthritis
options.C: Systemic disease activity across 12 organ domains
options.D: Dry eyes and dry mouth due to lymphocytic infiltration of exocrine glands
options.E: Anticholinergic drugs, sedating antihistamines and tricyclic antidepressants

explanation: Fatigue, pain and dryness respond poorly to immunosuppression; exercise, sleep and treatment of comorbidity are central. The BSR guideline allows a 6–12 month trial of hydroxychloroquine for significant fatigue and systemic symptoms, but not routine immunosuppressants. Hydroxychloroquine is used for musculoskeletal and cutaneous features. Fatigue contributors: hypothyroidism (15–30% have autoimmune thyroiditis), anaemia, coeliac disease, depression, poor sleep (nocturia, dry mouth), fibromyalgia, PBC, RTA with hypokalaemia. Arthritis in SjD is symmetrical, non-erosive and intermittent (Jaccoud-type is possible). Erosions or anti-CCP suggest RA overlap.

question: A woman with Sjögren's has severe refractory systemic disease, such as cryoglobulinaemic vasculitis with palpable purpura, neuropathy and glomerulonephritis (HCV-negative, type II cryoglobulins). What is the most appropriate treatment? Also tested as: A 61-year-old woman with Sjögren's has palpable purpura, peripheral neuropathy and glomerulonephritis. Type II mixed cryoglobulins are present and hepatitis C testing is negative. What is the most appropriate treatment?

options.A: Development of MALT lymphoma
options.B: Preservative-free artificial tears and gels with lid hygiene first; for refractory disease, topical ciclosporin
options.C: Small-fibre neuropathy
options.D: Direct-acting antiviral therapy for hepatitis C
options.E: B-cell targeted therapy with rituximab plus glucocorticoids, adding plasma exchange for lifethreatening disease

explanation: Rituximab is used for severe refractory systemic disease, particularly cryoglobulinaemic vasculitis, which is a severe fatigue (TEARS and TRACTISS trials). By manifestation: | Manifestation | Treatment | |---|---| | Cutaneous vasculitis or purpura | GC; rituximab if cryoglobulinaemic | | ILD | GC + MMF or azathioprine; rituximab; nintedanib if progressive | | Cryoglobulinaemic GN, vasculitic neuropathy | pulse GC + rituximab or cyclophosphamide; PLEX | | Sensory ganglionopathy | often refractory: IVIG, rituximab | | Small-fibre neuropathy | neuropathic agents; IVIG in selected cases | | Cytopenias | GC, rituximab, IVIG | | CNS or myelitis | pulse GC + cyclophosphamide or rituximab | Belimumab is used off-label in some cases.

question: A 58-year-old woman with Sjögren's has persistent unilateral parotid enlargement for 6 months, palpable purpura, low C4 and mixed cryoglobulins. What is the most important concern?

options.A: Small-fibre neuropathy
options.B: Direct-acting antiviral therapy for hepatitis C
options.C: Distal (type 1) renal tubular acidosis due to tubulointerstitial nephritis
options.D: B-cell targeted therapy with rituximab plus glucocorticoids, adding plasma exchange for lifethreatening disease
options.E: Development of MALT lymphoma

explanation: Lymphoma risk (about 5-10% lifetime, mostly MALT) is higher with persistent gland enlargement, purpura, low C4, cryoglobulinaemia, monoclonal gammopathy and lymphopenia. Ultrasound and biopsy of the gland are warranted. Parotid enlargement: - Bilateral: SjD, IgG4-RD (Mikulicz), sarcoid (Heerfordt's: parotitis, uveitis, facial palsy, fever), HIV (DILS, lymphoepithelial cysts), HCV, diabetes, alcohol, bulimia, malnutrition, amyloid, mumps, drugs (iodine). - Unilateral or firm: MALT lymphoma, pleomorphic adenoma, Warthin's tumour, parotid carcinoma, bacterial parotitis or stones. Lymphoma predictors: persistent parotid enlargement, palpable purpura, low C4 (and C3), cryoglobulins, monoclonal component, raised β2-microglobulin and FLC, CD4 lymphopenia, neutropenia, lymphadenopathy, splenomegaly, high ESSDAI, young onset, male sex, focus score ≥3, germinal centres. High-risk patients: review every 3–6 months with parotid ultrasound, and biopsy any persistent mass (core or open). MALT lymphoma: rituximab-based regimens (± chemotherapy) with haematology. Gastric MALT may need H. pylori eradication.

question: A 39-year-old woman with Sjögren's has weakness, serum potassium 2.6 mmol/L, a normal anion gap metabolic acidosis and urine pH 6.5. What is the most likely cause?

options.A: B-cell targeted therapy with rituximab plus glucocorticoids, adding plasma exchange for lifethreatening disease
options.B: Small-fibre neuropathy
options.C: Anti-HMGCR immune-mediated necrotising myopathy; immunosuppression such as glucocorticoids with IVIG and/or methotrexate
options.D: Development of MALT lymphoma
options.E: Distal (type 1) renal tubular acidosis due to tubulointerstitial nephritis

explanation: Tubulointerstitial nephritis typically causes distal RTA, with inability to acidify urine, hypokalaemia and nephrocalcinosis. Glomerulonephritis is less common and often related to cryoglobulinaemia. Normal anion gap acidosis with hypokalaemia: distal (type 1) RTA (urine pH >5.5; SjD, SLE, PBC, amphotericin, lithium, toluene); proximal (type 2) RTA (bicarbonate wasting, Fanconi syndrome: myeloma, tenofovir, ifosfamide, Wilson's); diarrhoea (urine anion gap negative); ureteric diversion; acetazolamide. TIN with distal RTA can cause hypokalaemic periodic paralysis, nephrocalcinosis, stones and osteomalacia. Nephrogenic diabetes insipidus and Fanconi syndrome also occur. TIN occurs early; GN (MPGN from cryoglobulins) occurs later and signals lymphoma risk. Potassium citrate or bicarbonate. GC (± MMF, rituximab) for active TIN with declining eGFR. Renal biopsy if eGFR is falling or there is proteinuria or haematuria.

question: A woman with Sjögren's has burning feet with normal nerve conduction studies. Which diagnosis is most likely?

options.A: Small-fibre neuropathy
options.B: Referral for surgical carpal tunnel decompression
options.C: Development of MALT lymphoma
options.D: Distal (type 1) renal tubular acidosis due to tubulointerstitial nephritis
options.E: B-cell targeted therapy with rituximab plus glucocorticoids, adding plasma exchange for lifethreatening disease

explanation: Small-fibre neuropathy is a recognised extraglandular feature and is confirmed by skin biopsy for intraepidermal nerve fibre density. Sensory ganglionopathy also occurs. Burning feet: small-fibre neuropathy (SjD, sarcoid, diabetes or prediabetes, alcohol, HIV, amyloid, Fabry disease, B12 deficiency, coeliac disease, chemotherapy) vs large-fibre length-dependent neuropathy (abnormal NCS), tarsal tunnel syndrome, erythromelalgia (myeloproliferative), sensory ganglionopathy (non-length-dependent, ataxic). Sensory ganglionopathy is characteristic of SjD: asymmetric sensory ataxia with pseudoathetosis and areflexia, from dorsal root ganglion injury. Exclude paraneoplastic anti-Hu ganglionopathy (small cell lung cancer) and cisplatin. Other neurology: trigeminal neuropathy, mononeuritis multiplex (cryoglobulins), autonomic neuropathy, myelitis or NMOSD (AQP4-IgG), white matter lesions. Small-fibre neuropathy: confirm with skin biopsy (reduced intraepidermal nerve fibre density) or QSART; treat with neuropathic analgesia, with IVIG in selected immune cases. Ganglionopathy responds poorly (IVIG, rituximab).

question: What are the typical clinical features of inflammatory myopathy, and which rash is characteristic of dermatomyositis? Also tested as: Gottron's papules and a heliotrope rash are characteristic of which condition?

options.A: Subacute, symmetrical proximal weakness with raised muscle enzymes; Gottron's papules and a heliotrope rash are characteristic of dermatomyositis
options.B: Anti-NXP2
options.C: Anti-MDA5
options.D: Enhanced malignancy screening, including CT of the chest, abdomen and pelvis, with age-and sexappropriate tests
options.E: Dry eyes and dry mouth due to lymphocytic infiltration of exocrine glands

explanation: Extramuscular involvement includes ILD, dysphagia, myocarditis and arthritis. Skin disease may precede or dominate muscle involvement (clinically amyopathic dermatomyositis). DM rash mimics: SLE (spares the knuckles), psoriasis (scalp), seborrhoeic dermatitis, rosacea, contact dermatitis, drug eruption (hydroxyurea DM-like eruption), photosensitivity reactions, flagellate erythema from bleomycin or shiitake mushrooms. Pathognomonic DM signs: Gottron's papules and sign, heliotrope rash. Characteristic: V-sign, shawl and holster signs, facial erythema, flagellate erythema, itchy scalp, inverse Gottron's (palmar), periungual erythema with ragged cuticles. Late: poikiloderma, calcinosis. Skin can precede weakness by 3–6 months. Prominent myalgia suggests another diagnosis. Use CDASI to measure skin activity. Photoprotection matters (UV triggers skin and muscle flares).

question: A patient with suspected inflammatory myositis has a normal CK. Does this exclude myositis?

options.A: Without visual symptoms: prednisolone 40–60 mg daily immediately with urgent fast-track referral.
options.B: A normal CK does not exclude myositis; review weakness, other enzymes, MRI, EMG, antibodies and biopsy
options.C: MRI of the thighs with STIR (fat-suppressed) sequences
options.D: Muscle strength, CK, lung function and HRCT, swallowing, cardiac involvement and malignancy risk
options.E: They indicate overlap connective tissue disease features rather than a specific myositis subtype

explanation: Clinically amyopathic dermatomyositis (especially anti-MDA5) and longstanding disease may have normal CK. CK is normal in about 20% of DM. Aldolase can be raised with a normal CK in perimysial or fascial disease. AST and ALT are usually muscle-derived, so check GGT before blaming methotrexate. EMG shows a myopathic pattern with fibrillations; a normal EMG does not exclude IIM. CK is reliable for activity in IMNM, partly in ASyS, and not in DM or IBM.

question: A patient with suspected inflammatory myositis needs a muscle biopsy. Which investigation best guides biopsy site selection?

options.A: Muscle strength, CK, lung function and HRCT, swallowing, cardiac involvement and malignancy risk
options.B: A normal CK does not exclude myositis; review weakness, other enzymes, MRI, EMG, antibodies and biopsy
options.C: MRI of the thighs with STIR (fat-suppressed) sequences
options.D: Proceed urgently with ultrasound and/or biopsy (never withhold treatment to preserve test sensitivity) biopsy ideally within 2 weeks of starting glucocorticoids, with a specimen of at least 1 cm
options.E: Troponin I

explanation: STIR MRI shows active muscle oedema and avoids sampling end-stage or unaffected muscle. If EMG is used, the contralateral muscle should be biopsied to avoid needle artefact. Target an affected but not end-stage muscle (deltoid, biceps, vastus lateralis), avoiding recently needled muscles. A biopsy is not always needed: a typical clinical picture plus an MSA (DM rash with anti-TIF1γ; anti-HMGCR with typical IMNM) may suffice. Biopsy when antibodies are negative or discordant, when IBM, dystrophy or metabolic myopathy is possible, or when the response is poor. Sarcoplasmic MxA is highly specific for DM (ENMC criteria).

question: At diagnosis of inflammatory myositis, what should be assessed?

options.A: MRI of the thighs with STIR (fat-suppressed) sequences
options.B: A normal CK does not exclude myositis; review weakness, other enzymes, MRI, EMG, antibodies and biopsy
options.C: Muscle strength, CK, lung function and HRCT, swallowing, cardiac involvement and malignancy risk
options.D: They indicate overlap connective tissue disease features rather than a specific myositis subtype
options.E: Small-fibre neuropathy

explanation: Extramuscular disease drives prognosis, and antibody profile guides risk stratification. At diagnosis: MMT-8, CK, PFTs with DLCO plus HRCT (for all), swallowing assessment (SLT), troponin I, ECG and echo (CMR if suspected), an extended myositis antibody panel, cancer screening stratified by risk, bone health, CV risk and vaccination. Severe features: MRC <3 proximally, dysphagia or aspiration, falling FVC or nocturnal hypoventilation, rapid progression, rhabdomyolysis, cardiac involvement.

question: A 45-year-old woman has Gottron's papules, periungual erythema, painful palmar papules, digital ulcers and rapidly worsening breathlessness. CK is normal and HRCT shows rapidly progressive ground-glass change and consolidation. Which antibody is most likely?

options.A: Anti-Jo-1
options.B: Anti-SRP
options.C: Anti-MDA5
options.D: Anti-HMGCR immune-mediated necrotising myopathy; immunosuppression such as glucocorticoids with IVIG and/or methotrexate
options.E: Subacute, symmetrical proximal weakness with raised muscle enzymes; Gottron's papules and a heliotrope rash are characteristic of dermatomyositis

explanation: Anti-MDA5 dermatomyositis is often clinically amyopathic with cutaneous ulceration and carries a high risk of rapidly progressive ILD with high mortality. Early intensive combination immunosuppression is used. RP-ILD in a CTD: anti-MDA5, ASyS with acute exacerbation, SLE pneumonitis or DAH, PJP, CMV, COVID-19, drug pneumonitis, acute exacerbation of fibrotic ILD. Anti-MDA5 skin clues: palmar papules, painful digital ulcers or skin necrosis, alopecia, oral ulcers, arthritis, little weakness. Ferritin and KL-6 are raised. Pathogenesis involves intense type I IFN, macrophage activation and lung vasculopathy. Early mortality from RP-ILD is 30–60%. An emergency: pulse GC plus two more agents immediately (the Japanese triple regimen of high-dose GC, tacrolimus and IV cyclophosphamide; or rituximab, MMF, IVIG or tofacitinib). Add PLEX if refractory. Monitor for CMV and PJP (give prophylaxis). Track ferritin and KL-6. Refer early for lung transplant.

question: A 49-year-old woman has proximal weakness, non-erosive arthritis, cracked hyperkeratotic skin on the radial borders of her fingers, Raynaud's phenomenon and basal crackles. Which antibody is most likely?

options.A: Anti-HMGCR immune-mediated necrotising myopathy; immunosuppression such as glucocorticoids with IVIG and/or methotrexate
options.B: Anti-MDA5
options.C: Anti-SRP
options.D: Anti-Jo-1
options.E: Enhanced malignancy screening, including CT of the chest, abdomen and pelvis, with age-and sexappropriate tests

explanation: Antisynthetase syndrome (anti-Jo-1, PL-7, PL-12 and others) features myositis, ILD, mechanic's hands, Raynaud's, arthritis and fever. ILD determines prognosis and may dominate. Antisynthetase antibodies: Jo-1 (commonest; myositis plus ILD), PL-7 and PL-12 (lung-dominant, little myositis), EJ, OJ, KS, Zo, Ha. Arthritis occurs in up to 90%, is symmetric and non-erosive, and can sublux ("floppy thumb" in about 19% of Jo-1). ACPA, RF and Ro52 can be positive. ILD is usually NSIP or OP. The model is lung-first (smoking or inhaled triggers in HLA-DRB1*03:01 carriers). Test the extended myositis panel in any "seronegative RA" with ILD, mechanic's hands or raised CK. Treatment is driven by the lung: GC plus MMF, azathioprine or tacrolimus; methotrexate for arthritis without significant ILD; rituximab or IV cyclophosphamide for severe or progressive ILD (RECITAL showed similar efficacy, with fewer adverse events for rituximab).
