question: A 67-year-old man presents with a heliotrope rash, shawl sign and proximal weakness. Anti-TIF1-gamma is positive. What is the most important next step?

options.A: Anti-SRP
options.B: Subacute, symmetrical proximal weakness with raised muscle enzymes; Gottron's papules and a heliotrope rash are characteristic of dermatomyositis
options.C: Anti-HMGCR immune-mediated necrotising myopathy; immunosuppression such as glucocorticoids with IVIG and/or methotrexate
options.D: Anti-Jo-1
options.E: Enhanced malignancy screening, including CT of the chest, abdomen and pelvis, with age-and sexappropriate tests

explanation: Anti-TIF1-gamma and anti-NXP2 in adult dermatomyositis confer high cancer risk. Screening is repeated over the first 3 years, when risk is greatest. Cancer risk by group: | Group | Cancer risk | |---|---| | Anti- TIF1γ (adult DM) | very high (20–50%) | | Anti-NXP2 (adult) | moderate to high | | Seronegative DM or IMNM | high | | SAE, Mi-2 | intermediate | | HMGCR | uncertain or modest | | SRP, ASyS, overlap, MDA5 (Western) | low | | IBM, juvenile | not raised | About a quarter of adults with IIM develop cancer within 3 years either side of onset (up to 30% in DM). High-risk features: age >40, male sex, dysphagia, skin necrosis or ulceration, rapid onset, refractoriness, TIF1γ, NXP2, seronegative disease. Lower risk: ILD, Raynaud's, arthritis, antisynthetase antibodies. Tumours can express mutated TIF1 genes, making the myositis paraneoplastic. IMACS screening: a basic panel for standard risk; basic plus enhanced (CT neck, chest, abdomen and pelvis; tumour markers; mammography; pelvic and TV ultrasound; FOB) for moderate risk; enhanced panel annually for 3 years for high risk, with FDG-PET if negative. Nasoendoscopy for South-East Asian patients (nasopharyngeal carcinoma). Re-screen at flare or refractoriness. Treat the cancer first. IVIG spares GC without oncological concern.

question: In juvenile dermatomyositis, which antibody is most strongly associated with calcinosis?

options.A: Anti-NXP2
options.B: Anti-SRP
options.C: They indicate overlap connective tissue disease features rather than a specific myositis subtype
options.D: Anti-Jo-1
options.E: PR3-ANCA (c-ANCA) in GPA; GPA more often has granulomatous ENT or lung disease with PR3-ANCA whereas MPA usually has MPO-ANCA without granulomas

explanation: Anti-NXP2 is associated with calcinosis and more severe muscle disease. Early, effective disease control reduces calcinosis risk. JDM accounts for up to 4 per million children per year. Antibodies include TIF1γ (the commonest in JDM, but not cancer-associated in children), NXP2 (calcinosis, severe weakness, GI vasculopathy), MDA5 (ILD, arthritis, ulcers) and Mi-2. Calcinosis occurs in 20–40% overall, more with delayed treatment. Aggressive early control: pulse methylprednisolone with methotrexate (first line), then IVIG, MMF, rituximab or JAK inhibitors. Calcinosis has no validated treatment (options: intensify immunosuppression, sodium thiosulfate, bisphosphonates, diltiazem, surgery). Photoprotection.

question: A 70-year-old man on atorvastatin for 3 years has progressive proximal weakness. CK is 8,500 U/L and weakness persists 3 months after stopping the statin. Biopsy shows necrotic fibres with minimal inflammation. What is the most likely diagnosis and management?

options.A: Anti-SRP
options.B: This is likely inclusion body myositis, which responds poorly to immunosuppression; management is supportive
options.C: Enhanced malignancy screening, including CT of the chest, abdomen and pelvis, with age-and sexappropriate tests
options.D: Anti-HMGCR immune-mediated necrotising myopathy; immunosuppression such as glucocorticoids with IVIG and/or methotrexate
options.E: Anti-Jo-1

explanation: Anti-HMGCR myopathy persists after statin withdrawal and needs immunosuppression; IVIG is particularly effective. Statins should be avoided thereafter. Statin-related muscle disease: toxic self-limited myopathy (improves within weeks of stopping; HMGCR negative) vs anti-HMGCR IMNM (persists or progresses after stopping; HMGCR positive; HLA-DRB1*11:01). Also hypothyroidism (which raises statin myopathy risk), interacting drugs (fibrates, macrolides, ciclosporin), and an unmasked metabolic myopathy. Stop statins and never restart. Use PCSK9 inhibitors or ezetimibe for lipids. GC plus IVIG at induction, plus methotrexate or another DMARD. IVIG can be used early or even first-line. CK tracks activity and guides tapering. Younger anti-HMGCR patients recover more slowly and may mimic a dystrophy. Zilucoplan failed in phase 2; FcRn blockers are under study.

question: A 38-year-old woman has rapidly progressive severe proximal weakness, dysphagia, CK 15,000 U/L and an arrhythmia. Biopsy shows necrotising myopathy with minimal inflammation. Which antibody is most likely?

options.A: Anti-HMGCR immune-mediated necrotising myopathy; immunosuppression such as glucocorticoids with IVIG and/or methotrexate
options.B: Anti-Jo-1
options.C: This is likely inclusion body myositis, which responds poorly to immunosuppression; management is supportive
options.D: Anti-SRP
options.E: Anti-MDA5

explanation: Anti-SRP is associated with severe necrotising myopathy, dysphagia and cardiac involvement, often needing early combination therapy. Anti-SRP (about 5% of IIM): acute aggressive proximal weakness, very high CK, early atrophy, dysphagia, cardiac involvement and sometimes ILD; no rash or arthritis. It is often steroid-refractory. IMNM antibodies are directly pathogenic (complement-mediated), and titres track CK and strength. Aggressive early therapy: GC plus IVIG plus early rituximab, then MMF or tacrolimus; PLEX in case reports. Cardiac monitoring.

question: A 72-year-old man has 3 years of slowly progressive finger flexor and quadriceps weakness, falls, dysphagia, a mildly raised CK and positive anti-cN1A antibodies. What is the likely diagnosis and how does it respond to treatment?

options.A: Anti-HMGCR immune-mediated necrotising myopathy; immunosuppression such as glucocorticoids with IVIG and/or methotrexate
options.B: GCA can present with large-vessel (extracranial) disease without cranial symptoms
options.C: Enhanced malignancy screening, including CT of the chest, abdomen and pelvis, with age-and sexappropriate tests
options.D: This is likely inclusion body myositis, which responds poorly to immunosuppression; management is supportive
options.E: Anti-SRP

explanation: IBM typically affects people over 50 with asymmetric deep finger flexor and quadriceps weakness. Biopsy shows rimmed vacuoles. Exercise, falls prevention and swallowing management are key. Distal or asymmetric weakness: ALS (fasciculations, UMN signs), myotonic dystrophy, distal myopathies, FSHD (scapular winging, facial weakness), multifocal motor neuropathy, CIDP, sporadic late-onset nemaline myopathy (paraprotein). IBM: over 45, male; insidious asymmetric weakness of the deep finger flexors and quadriceps; falls in 40–70%; dysphagia (cricopharyngeal) in 40–60%; CK <15× ULN. Diagnosis is often delayed by 3–5 years. Anti-cN1A is present in 30–50% but also occurs in Sjögren's and SLE. It is associated with T-LGL leukaemia and Sjögren's. Strength falls by 3.5–17% per year, but life expectancy is near normal. There is no approved disease-modifying drug. Use exercise, falls prevention, orthoses (knee brace, AFO), OT, SLT, and IVIG, cricopharyngeal dilatation or myotomy for dysphagia. Avoid long-term GC (they lower CK but do not help strength). Failed trials: bimagrumab, arimoclomol, ulviprubart (anti-KLRG1). A sirolimus trial is ongoing.

question: What is the first-line treatment for active dermatomyositis or polymyositis, and how does it change with severe weakness and dysphagia with aspiration risk? Also tested as: A 56-year-old woman with dermatomyositis has severe weakness and dysphagia with aspiration risk. What is the most appropriate initial regimen?

options.A: Anti-NXP2
options.B: Anti-SRP
options.C: This is likely inclusion body myositis, which responds poorly to immunosuppression; management is supportive
options.D: High-dose glucocorticoids with an early steroid-sparing agent (methotrexate, azathioprine or mycophenolate); for severe disease, IV methylprednisolone pulses then high-dose oral glucocorticoids with IVIG
options.E: Anti-HMGCR immune-mediated necrotising myopathy; immunosuppression such as glucocorticoids with IVIG and/or methotrexate

explanation: and an early steroid-sparing agent IVIG, rituximab or calcineurin inhibitors are used for refractory or severe disease, and cyclophosphamide for severe ILD. IVIG has proven efficacy in dermatomyositis and is useful for dysphagia. Speech and language therapy swallowing assessment is essential, and respiratory muscle weakness needs monitoring. Prednisolone 0.5–1 mg/kg/day (40–60 mg), tapering after about 6 weeks according to response, to 10–20 mg by 6 months and ideally ≤5 mg. Continue a DMARD for ≥2 years after remission. Methotrexate is not contraindicated in ILD, but MMF or tacrolimus is preferred when ILD dominates. IVIG (2 g/kg every 4 weeks) carries a thromboembolism risk, so hydrate and infuse slowly. Supportive: PJP prophylaxis with high-dose GC plus a second agent (especially in ILD or anti-MDA5); specialist exercise programme (safe even in active disease); bone health; vaccination. Skin: photoprotection, topical steroids or tacrolimus, HCQ (drug rash is more common in DM), methotrexate, MMF, IVIG, JAK inhibitors. Refractory disease: rituximab (RIM trial missed its primary endpoint, but most patients improved), abatacept, cyclophosphamide, JAKi or brepocitinib, CAR-T trials. Failure to improve at 4–6 months: consider wrong diagnosis (dystrophy, Pompe), IBM, steroid myopathy (normal CK, no MRI oedema), damage (fat on MRI), hidden cancer, non-adherence.

question: A patient with active polymyositis has a raised troponin T without chest pain or ECG change. Which test best distinguishes cardiac from skeletal muscle origin?

options.A: Troponin I
options.B: GCA can present with large-vessel (extracranial) disease without cranial symptoms
options.C: Anti-MDA5
options.D: Ultrasound of the temporal and axillary arteries
options.E: MRI of the thighs with STIR (fat-suppressed) sequences

explanation: Troponin T and CK-MB can be released from regenerating skeletal muscle, whereas troponin I is cardiac-specific. A raised troponin I warrants assessment for myocarditis. A raised troponin I warrants ECG, echo and CMR (T2 oedema, LGE), with Holter monitoring. Treat myocarditis with intensified immunosuppression (pulse GC, IVIG) and cardiology input. Screen all adults with troponin I, ECG and echo; IIM also raises atherosclerotic risk.

question: What is the significance of myositis-associated antibodies (such as anti-PM/Scl, anti-Ku and anti-U1-RNP) compared with myositis-specific antibodies?

options.A: Muscle strength, CK, lung function and HRCT, swallowing, cardiac involvement and malignancy risk
options.B: Pulmonary arterial hypertension and interstitial lung disease
options.C: Anti-centromere: limited cutaneous disease, calcinosis and late PAH. Anti-Scl-70: diffuse disease and
options.D: A normal CK does not exclude myositis; review weakness, other enzymes, MRI, EMG, antibodies and biopsy
options.E: They indicate overlap connective tissue disease features rather than a specific myositis subtype

explanation: Myositis-specific antibodies (Jo-1, MDA5, SRP, HMGCR, TIF1-gamma, Mi-2, NXP2) define clinical phenotypes, whereas associated antibodies suggest overlap syndromes. MAA associations: anti-PM/Scl (SSc overlap, ILD, calcinosis, mechanic's hands; good muscle response); anti-Ku (SSc or SLE overlap, arthritis); anti-U1-RNP (MCTD); anti-Ro52 (worse ILD when combined with Jo-1 or MDA5). Overlap myositis is treated by the dominant organ: IVIG and GC for muscle, MMF or rituximab for ILD, methotrexate or biologics for erosive arthritis, CCBs and PDE5 inhibitors for Raynaud's.

question: A patient has suspected GCA: new temporal headache, jaw claudication, scalp tenderness and CRP 82 mg/L without visual symptoms, or transient monocular visual loss in the past 24 hours. What is the immediate glucocorticoid regimen? Also tested as: An 80-year-old man with suspected GCA has had transient monocular visual loss in the past 24 hours. What is the most appropriate initial glucocorticoid regimen?

options.A: Urgent assessment for GCA, with high-dose glucocorticoids if it is suspected
options.B: GCA can present with large-vessel (extracranial) disease without cranial symptoms
options.C: Without visual symptoms: prednisolone 40–60 mg daily immediately with urgent fast-track referral.
options.D: Ultrasound of the temporal and axillary arteries
options.E: Proceed urgently with ultrasound and/or biopsy (never withhold treatment to preserve test sensitivity) biopsy ideally within 2 weeks of starting glucocorticoids, with a specimen of at least 1 cm

explanation: With evolving visual loss or amaurosis fugax: IV methylprednisolone 500 mg–1 g daily for up to 3 days, then highdose oral prednisolone, with same-day ophthalmology High-dose glucocorticoids are started the same day when GCA is strongly suspected, without waiting for investigations; specialist assessment should follow within days, and ultrasound and biopsy remain informative early in treatment. If IV treatment is not immediately available for visual symptoms, oral prednisolone 60 mg should be given at once. Established blindness rarely recovers, so protecting the other eye is the goal. New headache over 50: GCA vs intracranial mass or haemorrhage, cervicogenic headache, migraine (new over 50 is atypical), TMJ disorder or dental pain, trigeminal neuralgia, glaucoma, herpes zoster (pre-eruptive), sinusitis, AAV involving the temporal artery, crowned dens syndrome, medication-overuse headache, hypertension or PRES. Visual loss with a swollen disc and normal CRP suggests non-arteritic AION. Symptoms improve within 24–72 hours of GC. CRP normalises in 1–2 weeks (ESR in 2–4 weeks). Routine pulses without ischaemic features are not recommended. Avoid more than 60 mg/day.

question: A patient with suspected GCA was started on glucocorticoids yesterday. What should happen to diagnostic testing, and when and how should temporal artery biopsy be done? Also tested as: When should temporal artery biopsy be performed in suspected GCA, and how large should the specimen be?

options.A: MRI of the thighs with STIR (fat-suppressed) sequences
options.B: Proceed urgently with ultrasound and/or biopsy (never withhold treatment to preserve test sensitivity) biopsy ideally within 2 weeks of starting glucocorticoids, with a specimen of at least 1 cm
options.C: Without visual symptoms: prednisolone 40–60 mg daily immediately with urgent fast-track referral.
options.D: GCA can present with large-vessel (extracranial) disease without cranial symptoms
options.E: Ultrasound of the temporal and axillary arteries

explanation: Sensitivity declines with time on steroids but remains useful in the first days. Confirming the diagnosis matters because treatment is prolonged and toxic. Skip lesions cause false negatives, so an adequate length is needed, and a negative biopsy does not exclude GCA, particularly large-vessel disease. Biopsy sensitivity is 60–80% (it shrinks to about 0.7 cm after fixation; still useful up to 4 weeks). Contralateral biopsy adds little. Steroids reduce ultrasound yield after 1–2 weeks and PET yield after a few days. High probability plus positive imaging needs no further test. Low probability plus negative imaging makes GCA unlikely. Use biopsy when imaging is unavailable, equivocal, or negative despite high suspicion.

question: In a fast-track GCA clinic, what is the first-line imaging test for suspected cranial GCA?

options.A: Ultrasound of the temporal and axillary arteries
options.B: Not routinely; antiplatelet therapy is reserved for other established indications
options.C: Without visual symptoms: prednisolone 40–60 mg daily immediately with urgent fast-track referral.
options.D: Proceed urgently with ultrasound and/or biopsy (never withhold treatment to preserve test sensitivity) biopsy ideally within 2 weeks of starting glucocorticoids, with a specimen of at least 1 cm
options.E: GCA can present with large-vessel (extracranial) disease without cranial symptoms

explanation: A non-compressible halo sign supports GCA, with accuracy comparable to biopsy in experienced hands. FDG-PET, CT or MR angiography assess large-vessel involvement. Halo sign mimics: atherosclerosis (calcified plaques, older people), AAV involving the temporal artery, amyloid, and operator error (excess compression or gain). FDG-PET/CT is best for large-vessel and aortic disease and PUO; modern scanners also detect cranial arteries. Highresolution cranial MRI shows mural enhancement. CTA or MRA images the aorta and its branches.

question: A 72-year-old woman has arm claudication, constitutional upset and a raised CRP, but no headache or jaw claudication and normal temporal arteries. Could this be GCA?

options.A: Without visual symptoms: prednisolone 40–60 mg daily immediately with urgent fast-track referral.
options.B: Urgent assessment for GCA, with high-dose glucocorticoids if it is suspected
options.C: GCA can present with large-vessel (extracranial) disease without cranial symptoms
options.D: This is likely inclusion body myositis, which responds poorly to immunosuppression; management is supportive
options.E: Ultrasound of the temporal and axillary arteries

explanation: Large-vessel GCA causes limb claudication, bruits, pulse or blood pressure asymmetry and aortitis. Imaging of the aorta and branches (ultrasound, PET-CT, CT or MR angiography) is used. Aortitis and large-vessel vasculitis: GCA, Takayasu (<40), IgG4-related periaortitis, Behçet's, Cogan's syndrome, relapsing polychondritis, SpA (aortic root), sarcoid, Erdheim–Chester ("coated aorta"), infection (syphilis, TB, Salmonella, Staphylococcus: mycotic aneurysm), isolated aortitis (found at surgery), radiation. Atherosclerosis can mimic it on imaging. Baseline aortic imaging (CT, MRA or PET) in all patients with GCA, and surveillance every 1–2 years with largevessel involvement or risk factors. Control BP and stop smoking.

question: How should glucocorticoids be tapered once GCA is controlled, and what is added for a patient who relapses twice below 15 mg daily? Also tested as: Once GCA is controlled, what is the target glucocorticoid taper?

options.A: Not routinely; antiplatelet therapy is reserved for other established indications
options.B: Ultrasound of the temporal and axillary arteries
options.C: Prednisolone 15 mg daily (up to 25 mg if needed); reduce to 10 mg/day within about 2 months, then by about 1 mg every 4 weeks, aiming to stop within about a year if remission is maintained
options.D: Without visual symptoms: prednisolone 40–60 mg daily immediately with urgent fast-track referral.
options.E: Taper to 15–20 mg/day within 2–3 months, aiming to stop within 12–18 months; for relapsing disease (or high toxicity risk) add tocilizumab with a glucocorticoid taper, with upadacitinib or methotrexate as alternatives

explanation: Initial prednisolone 40–60 mg/day is tapered to 15–20 mg/day within 2–3 months. The 2025 EULAR recommendations aim to stop glucocorticoids within 12–18 months (the 2018 version targeted 5 mg/day or less after 1 year). Tocilizumab increases sustained remission and reduces cumulative glucocorticoid dose. The 2025 EULAR recommendations reserve adjunctive therapy (tocilizumab, or the JAK inhibitor upadacitinib) for relapsing or refractory disease or high glucocorticoid-toxicity risk, with methotrexate as an alternative. TNF inhibitors are ineffective in GCA. Relapses occur in 40–60%, usually below 10–15 mg or within 2 years, most often as PMR or headache. A rising CRP alone is not a relapse. Tocilizumab and upadacitinib suppress CRP and ESR, so judge activity clinically and by imaging. With tocilizumab or upadacitinib, a 26-week taper to zero is standard. Tocilizumab is usually given for 1 year (sometimes 2), and relapse after stopping is common. Minor relapse: return to the last effective dose (or add 5–10 mg), then taper again; add or switch a steroid-sparing agent. Major relapse (ischaemic symptoms or progressive aortitis): 40–60 mg (pulses if visual), plus tocilizumab or upadacitinib. Remember JAKi cautions in older patients with CV or VTE risk. GC toxicity affects about 85% of those on long courses.

question: A 74-year-old woman with newly diagnosed GCA has no history of cardiovascular or cerebrovascular disease. Should low-dose aspirin be started?

options.A: Without visual symptoms: prednisolone 40–60 mg daily immediately with urgent fast-track referral.
options.B: Ultrasound of the temporal and axillary arteries
options.C: GCA can present with large-vessel (extracranial) disease without cranial symptoms
options.D: Anti-SRP
options.E: Not routinely; antiplatelet therapy is reserved for other established indications

explanation: Evidence of benefit is limited and bleeding risk is increased on glucocorticoids. Gastroprotection and bone protection should be considered. Use aspirin only for usual CV indications, adding a PPI if combined with GC. Some clinicians use short-term aspirin for critical cranial ischaemia. Other measures: bone protection from day 1, BP, glucose, eye and mood checks, PJP prophylaxis with high doses plus other immunosuppression, vaccination, a steroid card. Follow up at weeks 0, 1–2, 3 and 6, then months 3, 6, 9 and 12.

question: A patient being treated for PMR develops jaw claudication. What is the most appropriate response?

options.A: Offer a bisphosphonate unless contraindicated
options.B: Urgent assessment for GCA, with high-dose glucocorticoids if it is suspected
options.C: Reconsider the diagnosis and investigate mimics: late-onset RA, infection (including endocarditis) malignancy, large-vessel GCA, and, when there is true weakness with a raised CK, inflammatory myopathy,
options.D: GCA can present with large-vessel (extracranial) disease without cranial symptoms
options.E: Without visual symptoms: prednisolone 40–60 mg daily immediately with urgent fast-track referral.

explanation: Patients with PMR should be asked about headache, scalp tenderness, jaw or tongue claudication and visual symptoms at every review. At every PMR review, ask about headache, scalp tenderness, jaw or tongue claudication, visual symptoms and limb claudication. Poor response or relapse of PMR should prompt imaging for large-vessel GCA (ultrasound of axillary arteries, PET-CT).

question: What initial glucocorticoid dose is recommended for PMR (new bilateral shoulder and hip girdle pain, 90 minutes of stiffness, ESR 58, no GCA features), and how should it be tapered after a complete response? Also tested as: A patient with PMR responded completely to prednisolone 15 mg daily. How should glucocorticoids be tapered?

options.A: Without visual symptoms: prednisolone 40–60 mg daily immediately with urgent fast-track referral.
options.B: Prednisolone 15 mg daily (up to 25 mg if needed); reduce to 10 mg/day within about 2 months, then by about 1 mg every 4 weeks, aiming to stop within about a year if remission is maintained
options.C: Reconsider the diagnosis and investigate mimics: late-onset RA, infection (including endocarditis) malignancy, large-vessel GCA, and, when there is true weakness with a raised CK, inflammatory myopathy,
options.D: Urgent assessment for GCA, with high-dose glucocorticoids if it is suspected
options.E: Taper to 15–20 mg/day within 2–3 months, aiming to stop within 12–18 months; for relapsing disease (or high toxicity risk) add tocilizumab with a glucocorticoid taper, with upadacitinib or methotrexate as alternatives

explanation: The 2025 EULAR recommendations advise 15–25 mg/day initially, and the 2026 BSR guideline describes a typical starting dose of 15 mg, increased to a maximum of 25 mg if response is inadequate. Very low (≤7.5 mg) or very high (>30 mg) starting doses are avoided. A brisk response is expected within 1–2 weeks; EULAR advises that a steroid trial should not be used as a diagnostic test. EULAR advises tapering to 10 mg/day within the first 2 months and aiming to stop within a year, while the 2026 BSR guideline describes a standard taper over 9–12 months, with faster options for those at high toxicity risk under closer review. Expect ≥70% global improvement within 1 week and a normal CRP within 3–4 weeks. Use the lower end of the dose range with comorbidity or diabetes and the higher end with high relapse risk. A single IM methylprednisolone injection (e.g. 120 mg every 3 weeks, tapering) is an alternative. NSAIDs have little role. The EULAR course notes typical duration is 1–2 years, with about a third needing longer low-dose treatment.

question: Under the 2026 BSR PMR guideline, what bone-protection principle applies to people starting glucocorticoids?

options.A: Rituximab with glucocorticoids, with methotrexate or mycophenolate as alternatives
options.B: Offer a bisphosphonate unless contraindicated
options.C: Urgent assessment for GCA, with high-dose glucocorticoids if it is suspected
options.D: Antigen-specific immunoassays for PR3-ANCA and MPO-ANCA as the primary test
options.E: Prednisolone 15 mg daily (up to 25 mg if needed); reduce to 10 mg/day within about 2 months, then by about 1 mg every 4 weeks, aiming to stop within about a year if remission is maintained

explanation: The 2026 BSR guideline recommends bone protection for all people with PMR starting glucocorticoids, with bone health review (and DXA) at diagnosis. A bisphosphonate is the usual choice unless contraindicated, guided by individual fracture risk and local pathways. Bone protection: calcium, vitamin D and a bisphosphonate (per BSR, for all starting GC unless contraindicated). DXA at diagnosis where available. Monitor BP, glucose, weight, mood and cataracts. Give a steroid card and sick-day rules.

question: Which features are required to classify polymyalgia rheumatica, and what does shoulder ultrasound typically show? Also tested as: Shoulder ultrasound in polymyalgia rheumatica typically shows which finding?

options.A: Age 50 or over, bilateral shoulder aching and raised CRP and/or ESR, plus sufficient additional points ultrasound typically shows subdeltoid bursitis, biceps tenosynovitis and glenohumeral synovitis
options.B: By the predominant size of vessel involved, with additional aetiological categories
options.C: Achilles tendinopathy and tendon rupture
options.D: Recurrent oral ulceration at least 3 times in 12 months, plus two of: genital ulcers, eye lesions, skin lesions or positive pathergy test
options.E: Anti-SRP

explanation: Additional points come from morning stiffness over 45 minutes, hip pain or limited movement, absence of RF/ACPA, absence of other joint involvement and characteristic ultrasound findings. Ultrasound findings add to classification and help distinguish PMR from mimics. The 2025 EULAR recommendations stress that classification criteria should not be used to diagnose individual patients. 2012 EULAR/ACR scoring: morning stiffness >45 minutes, 2 points; hip pain or limited range, 1; absence of RF and ACPA, 2; no other joint pain, 1; ultrasound (≥1 shoulder plus ≥1 hip abnormal), 1; both shoulders abnormal, 1. The threshold is ≥4 without ultrasound (sensitivity 68%, specificity 78%) or ≥5 with ultrasound. Distal features occur in 25–50% (peripheral synovitis, CTS, RS3PE-like oedema). PET shows interspinous bursae, ischial tuberosities and shoulders. Work-up: FBC, U&E, LFTs, bone profile, CK, TSH, glucose, SPEP and FLC, RF and ACPA, vitamin D, urinalysis, chest radiograph. A normal CRP should prompt reconsideration.

question: A patient with PMR relapses during taper, sometimes repeatedly (for example a 66-year-old woman with peripheral arthritis and ESR 70 at diagnosis who has relapsed twice). How should relapse be managed, and what steroid-sparing treatment is appropriate? Also tested as: A 66-year-old woman with PMR, peripheral arthritis and ESR 70 mm/h at diagnosis has relapsed twice on taper. Which additional treatment is most appropriate?

options.A: Plasma exchange
options.B: Return to the last effective dose and taper again more slowly; for repeated relapse or high relapse risk add methotrexate 7.5–10 mg weekly, with an IL-6 receptor inhibitor (sarilumab or tocilizumab) for refractory disease
options.C: Prednisolone 15 mg daily (up to 25 mg if needed); reduce to 10 mg/day within about 2 months, then by about 1 mg every 4 weeks, aiming to stop within about a year if remission is maintained
options.D: Urgent assessment for GCA, with high-dose glucocorticoids if it is suspected
options.E: Offer a bisphosphonate unless contraindicated

explanation: Relapses are common, especially in the first year. Return to the last effective dose and taper over 4–8 weeks back to the dose at which relapse occurred. The 2026 BSR guideline advises discussing a relapse with rheumatology and referring after a second relapse or 18 months of glucocorticoids. Repeated relapse should prompt steroid-sparing therapy and reassessment of the diagnosis. Methotrexate is considered early in those at high relapse risk, with relapse or with glucocorticoid toxicity. For people who cannot taper glucocorticoids, both the 2026 BSR and 2025 EULAR recommendations support an IL-6 receptor antagonist; EULAR prefers sarilumab for relapsing or refractory PMR (NHS access depends on commissioning). TNF inhibitors are not effective. Relapse affects 30–50%. High-risk features: female sex, ESR >40, peripheral arthritis. SAPHYR: sarilumab gave higher sustained remission with a 14-week taper than placebo with a 52-week taper. SEMAPHORE and PMR- SPARE: tocilizumab improved GC-free remission, including in early PMR. JAK inhibitors are under study. Treat symptoms, not an isolated CRP rise. Look for largevessel GCA in relapsing PMR.

question: A patient labelled as PMR has an atypical course: partial response to prednisolone 15 mg with wrist and MCP synovitis; very high inflammatory markers with weight loss and a poor steroid response; or true proximal weakness with CK 2,400 U/L. What should be done? Also tested as: A patient with presumed PMR has shoulder pain, very high inflammatory markers and weight loss, with a poor response to prednisolone. What is the best next step? | A 69-year-old woman thought to have PMR has shoulder girdle pain but also true proximal weakness and a CK of 2,400 U/L. What is the most important next step?

options.A: Reconsider the diagnosis and investigate mimics: late-onset RA, infection (including endocarditis) malignancy, large-vessel GCA, and, when there is true weakness with a raised CK, inflammatory myopathy,
options.B: Anti-HMGCR immune-mediated necrotising myopathy; immunosuppression such as glucocorticoids with IVIG and/or methotrexate
options.C: Prednisolone 15 mg daily (up to 25 mg if needed); reduce to 10 mg/day within about 2 months, then by about 1 mg every 4 weeks, aiming to stop within about a year if remission is maintained
options.D: Urgent assessment for GCA, with high-dose glucocorticoids if it is suspected
options.E: Offer a bisphosphonate unless contraindicated

explanation: hypothyroidism and drug-induced myopathy An incomplete response, age under 60, prominent peripheral arthritis or systemic features should prompt reconsideration of the diagnosis. PMR causes pain and stiffness, not true weakness, and CK is normal; weakness with a raised CK points to myopathy. PMR mimics include malignancy, infection (including endocarditis), late-onset RA, CPPD, myopathy and endocrine disease. Category Mimics elderly-onset RA (especially Inflammatory seronegative), RS3PE, SpA, CPPD (pseudo-PMR), myositis, vasculitis (LV- GCA, AAV), ICI-PMR myeloma, lymphoma, paraneoplastic Malignancy solid tumours septic arthritis, endocarditis, spinal Infection infection, TB hypothyroidism, hyperparathyroidism, Endocrine and osteomalacia, statin myopathy metabolic bilateral cuff disease, adhesive capsulitis, Mechanical cervical spondylosis, OA, fibromyalgia (normal CRP) Parkinson's disease (rigidity) Neurological Red flags: age <60, chronic onset, no shoulder involvement, normal or extremely high markers, prominent systemic features or weight loss, erosive peripheral arthritis, neurological signs, poor response to 15–25 mg within 1–2 weeks. Tests: RF and ACPA, ultrasound of the hands; SPEP and FLC, CT or PET-CT for malignancy and LV-GCA; blood cultures and echo; CK, TSH and myositis antibodies; vitamin D, calcium and PTH. Refer to specialist care if atypical, under 60, steroid-dependent or refractory.

question: A young woman has left arm claudication, a 30 mmHg inter-arm systolic difference, a subclavian bruit, raised CRP and MRA showing subclavian wall thickening and stenosis. What distinguishes Takayasu arteritis from GCA, and what treatment is recommended alongside glucocorticoids? Also tested as: What distinguishes Takayasu arteritis from giant cell arteritis?

options.A: Without visual symptoms: prednisolone 40–60 mg daily immediately with urgent fast-track referral.
options.B: Takayasu affects the aorta and major branches in younger patients, usually women under 40 (age at onset is the main distinction from GCA); add a glucocorticoid-sparing agent such as methotrexate, azathioprine or mycophenolate from the outset
options.C: Troponin I
options.D: GCA can present with large-vessel (extracranial) disease without cranial symptoms
options.E: Ultrasound of the temporal and axillary arteries

explanation: Both are granulomatous large-vessel vasculitides. Takayasu arteritis needs combined therapy; tocilizumab or TNF inhibitors are used for refractory disease. Elective revascularisation is performed in remission unless ischaemia is critical. Subclavian or aortic stenosis in a young person: Takayasu vs fibromuscular dysplasia, thoracic outlet syndrome (positional, cervical rib), atherosclerosis (risk factors), radiation arteritis, IgG4-related disease, Behçet's, Cogan's, sarcoid, infection (TB, syphilis), congenital coarctation, mid-aortic syndrome (NF1, Williams syndrome), Marfan or Loeys-Dietz (aneurysmal). Numano types I–V describe distribution (from arch branches to the whole aorta). Pulmonary artery involvement and coronary ostial lesions occur. Hypertension is common and often missed because of subclavian stenosis. Induction: prednisolone 40–60 mg/day, tapered, plus methotrexate, azathioprine, MMF or leflunomide. Refractory: tocilizumab, TNFi (infliximab, adalimumab); JAKi are emerging. CV protection: aspirin or statin per risk; strict BP control (measure on an unaffected limb). Revascularisation: stent or bypass in inactive disease (restenosis is higher when active); bypass lasts longer than stenting. Monitoring: MRA, CTA or PET (markers can be normal when active).

question: A 29-year-old man of Turkish origin has recurrent oral and genital ulcers and erythema nodosum-like lesions. What is required for classification of Behçet's disease under the International Study Group criteria?

options.A: Colchicine with topical treatments first; for refractory ulcers, apremilast (randomised trial evidence) or a
options.B: Rituximab with glucocorticoids, with methotrexate or mycophenolate as alternatives
options.C: Recurrent oral ulceration at least 3 times in 12 months, plus two of: genital ulcers, eye lesions, skin lesions or positive pathergy test
options.D: Glucocorticoids with an immunosuppressant (preferably a monoclonal anti-TNF antibody, or azathioprine); anticoagulation may be added only if bleeding risk is low
options.E: Not routinely; antiplatelet therapy is reserved for other established indications

explanation: Recurrent oral ulceration is mandatory in this classification. Behçet's is a variable-vessel vasculitis affecting eyes, vessels, nervous system and gut. ICBD criteria (≥4 points, more sensitive): oral ulcers 2, genital ulcers 2, ocular lesions 2; skin, neurological, vascular and pathergy 1 each. Oral ulcers are not mandatory under ICBD. Pathergy is positive in up to 60% in Turkey, the Middle East and Japan, but rarely in northern Europeans. HLA-B*51 is present in 50–60% (vs about 15% of controls) and supports but does not establish the diagnosis. There is no diagnostic test, so the diagnosis is clinical. Check FBC (cyclic neutropenia), B12, folate, ferritin, coeliac serology, HSV swabs, syphilis serology and HLA-B*51. Ophthalmology screening and a vascular assessment if symptomatic.

question: A patient with Behçet's has recurrent oral and genital ulcers without major organ involvement. What is the first-line treatment, and what is used if oral ulcers persist despite topical treatment and colchicine? Also tested as: A 34-year-old woman with Behçet's has recurrent painful oral ulcers despite topical treatment and colchicine, with no major organ involvement. Which treatment has randomised trial evidence for oral ulcers?

options.A: Avacopan
options.B: Rituximab with glucocorticoids, with methotrexate or mycophenolate as alternatives
options.C: Colchicine with topical treatments first; for refractory ulcers, apremilast (randomised trial evidence) or a
options.D: Recurrent oral ulceration at least 3 times in 12 months, plus two of: genital ulcers, eye lesions, skin lesions or positive pathergy test
options.E: Not routinely; antiplatelet therapy is reserved for other established indications

explanation: TNF inhibitor Colchicine prevents recurrent mucocutaneous lesions, especially erythema nodosum and genital ulcers. Apremilast reduced oral ulcers in a randomised trial (RELIEF), and the 2025 EULAR recommendations advise apremilast or a TNF inhibitor when mucocutaneous disease is refractory to, or intolerant of, colchicine. Chronic systemic glucocorticoids should be avoided. Topicals: steroid mouthwash and creams, sucralfate, local anaesthetics. Further escalation: azathioprine, interferon-α, TNFi; thalidomide as a last resort (teratogenic, neuropathy). Arthritis: colchicine first, then IA steroid, then azathioprine, IFN-α or TNFi. Other points: stopping smoking can paradoxically worsen oral ulcers. Pregnancy often improves Behçet's, and colchicine can continue. Emerging: IL-17 or IL-23 blockade (secukinumab, ustekinumab) for mucocutaneous disease; tocilizumab for refractory eye or neurological disease; JAKi.

question: How should Behçet's posterior uveitis or retinal vasculitis be treated, and how does management change when it is sight-threatening? Also tested as: A 32-year-old woman with Behçet's disease develops sight-threatening posterior uveitis. What is the most appropriate approach?

options.A: Glucocorticoids with an immunosuppressant (preferably a monoclonal anti-TNF antibody, or azathioprine); anticoagulation may be added only if bleeding risk is low
options.B: Recurrent oral ulceration at least 3 times in 12 months, plus two of: genital ulcers, eye lesions, skin lesions or positive pathergy test
options.C: Colchicine with topical treatments first; for refractory ulcers, apremilast (randomised trial evidence) or a
options.D: All Behçet's uveitis needs systemic immunosuppression and glucocorticoids should never be used alone: azathioprine with glucocorticoids, or ciclosporin, interferon-alpha or a monoclonal anti-TNF agent; for sight- threatening disease, high-dose glucocorticoids with a monoclonal anti-TNF antibody (preferably infliximab) combined with another immunosuppressant
options.E: Levamisole-adulterated cocaine

explanation: Sight-threatening posterior segment disease needs urgent ophthalmology-led treatment. The 2025 EULAR update increasingly favours monoclonal anti-TNF antibodies (especially infliximab) for eye involvement, both for induction and maintenance. Azathioprine, ciclosporin or interferon-alpha remain options for less severe posterior disease. Retinal vasculitis: Behçet's (occlusive, veins and arteries, hypopyon), sarcoid (periphlebitis, "candle-wax drippings"), TB (Eales disease), syphilis, toxoplasmosis, CMV or ARN (herpes viruses; exclude before immunosuppression), SLE or APS, GPA, PAN, Susac syndrome (BRAO, deafness, corpus callosum lesions), MS (intermediate uveitis, periphlebitis), intraocular lymphoma masquerade. Isolated anterior uveitis can be treated topically, with systemic azathioprine in young men with poor-prognosis features. Avoid ciclosporin in neuro-Behçet's (it is neurotoxic and can induce neuro-BD). Arrange regular ophthalmology review. Adalimumab is licensed for noninfectious posterior uveitis (VISUAL I/II).

question: A 31-year-old man with Behçet's disease develops an acute femoral DVT. Pulmonary artery aneurysm has been excluded. What is the most appropriate management?

options.A: Recurrent oral ulceration at least 3 times in 12 months, plus two of: genital ulcers, eye lesions, skin lesions or positive pathergy test
options.B: Glucocorticoids with an immunosuppressant (preferably a monoclonal anti-TNF antibody, or azathioprine); anticoagulation may be added only if bleeding risk is low
options.C: Urgent assessment for GCA, with high-dose glucocorticoids if it is suspected
options.D: Urgent assessment and treatment of active vasculitic neuropathy, because prompt therapy may prevent permanent deficit
options.E: Colchicine with topical treatments first; for refractory ulcers, apremilast (randomised trial evidence) or a

explanation: Thrombosis in Behçet's is driven by vessel wall inflammation. The 2025 EULAR recommendations advise glucocorticoids with immunosuppressives, preferably anti-TNF antibodies, continued as maintenance. Anticoagulants may be added only if bleeding risk is low and pulmonary artery aneurysms have been excluded, because rupture can be fatal. Thrombosis in Behçet's is inflammatory, with an adherent thrombus, so immunosuppression prevents recurrence and anticoagulation alone adds little. Venous disease is the commonest vascular form (superficial thrombophlebitis, DVT, Budd–Chiari, IVC thrombosis, CVST). Pulmonary artery aneurysms present with haemoptysis and are lethal. Arterial or pulmonary artery aneurysm: high-dose GC plus cyclophosphamide, infliximab if refractory. Embolisation is preferred to open surgery. Operate urgently on symptomatic peripheral aneurysms under immunosuppression (anastomotic aneurysm risk). Parenchymal neuro-BD: high-dose GC plus azathioprine or TNFi (preferred for severe disease). GI disease: 5-ASA or azathioprine; TNFi or thalidomide for severe disease; surgery for perforation or bleeding. CVST: GC with short anticoagulation (after excluding PAA). Mortality comes mainly from PAA, Budd–Chiari, CNS and major vessel disease in young men. vasculitis

question: How does the Chapel Hill consensus nomenclature primarily classify vasculitis?

options.A: Levamisole-adulterated cocaine
options.B: Urgent surgical and medical assessment for mesenteric ischaemia, alongside vasculitis treatment
options.C: By the predominant size of vessel involved, with additional aetiological categories
options.D: Antigen-specific immunoassays for PR3-ANCA and MPO-ANCA as the primary test
options.E: Direct-acting antiviral therapy for hepatitis C

explanation: Large-vessel (Takayasu, GCA), medium-vessel (PAN, Kawasaki), small-vessel (ANCA-associated and immunecomplex) and variable-vessel (Behçet's, Cogan's) categories are recognised. Category Diseases GCA (>50), Takayasu (<50) Large PAN (no GN, ANCA-negative), Kawasaki Medium Small: ANCA MPA, GPA, EGPA Small: anti-GBM, cryoglobulinaemic, IgA vasculitis, HUV immune complex Behçet's, Cogan's Variable Single-organ cutaneous leucocytoclastic angiitis, PACNS, isolated aortitis lupus, rheumatoid, sarcoid, RP vasculitis Systemic disease HCV cryoglobulinaemia, HBV-PAN, Probable syphilitic aortitis, drug-associated cause (hydralazine, PTU, levamisole), cancer Chapel Hill is a nomenclature, not diagnostic criteria. Large and medium vessels do not involve capillaries or venules.

question: A patient with suspected small-vessel vasculitis needs ANCA testing. Which approach is most appropriate?

options.A: ANCA alone neither diagnoses vasculitis nor justifies escalation; assess the clinical phenotype and alternative causes, and in remission monitor more closely with clinical, urine and renal assessment
options.B: MRI of the thighs with STIR (fat-suppressed) sequences
options.C: Antigen-specific immunoassays for PR3-ANCA and MPO-ANCA as the primary test
options.D: Urgent surgical and medical assessment for mesenteric ischaemia, alongside vasculitis treatment
options.E: Levamisole-adulterated cocaine

explanation: High-quality PR3 and MPO immunoassays are the preferred screening tests. Test only with compatible features (pulmonary–renal syndrome, RPGN, mononeuritis, ENT destruction, scleritis, palpable purpura). Use high-quality PR3 and MPO immunoassays; IIF is optional. Request anti-GBM in parallel for RPGN or DAH.

question: Which ANCA specificity is most strongly associated with GPA, and which features best distinguish GPA from MPA? Also tested as: Which feature best distinguishes GPA from MPA?

options.A: Urgent airway assessment with ENT and respiratory input, alongside disease-directed treatment
options.B: Glucocorticoids (IV pulses then the reduced-dose PEXIVAS taper) with rituximab or cyclophosphamide rituximab was non-inferior to cyclophosphamide and superior in relapsing disease (RAVE)
options.C: Rituximab with glucocorticoids, with methotrexate or mycophenolate as alternatives
options.D: Rituximab maintenance for 24-48 months after remission induction
options.E: PR3-ANCA (c-ANCA) in GPA; GPA more often has granulomatous ENT or lung disease with PR3-ANCA whereas MPA usually has MPO-ANCA without granulomas

explanation: MPO-ANCA (p-ANCA) predominates in MPA, renal-limited vasculitis and ANCA-positive EGPA. These are patterns rather than absolute rules, and both cause pauci-immune necrotising glomerulonephritis and alveolar haemorrhage. Destructive midline nasal disease: GPA vs cocaine-induced midline destructive lesion (often PR3 or anti-elastase positive), NK/T-cell lymphoma, invasive fungal sinusitis, TB, leprosy, leishmaniasis, syphilis, sarcoidosis, IgG4-RD, relapsing polychondritis (cartilage only, no mucosal destruction). GPA: PR3 in 65–75%, MPO in 10–20%, ANCA-negative in about 10% (more often limited ENT disease). MPA: MPO in 60–80%, PR3 in about 10%, negative in 10–20%. EGPA: ANCA-positive in 30–40% (MPO).

question: How should a low-positive MPO-ANCA without vasculitic features, or a rise in ANCA in a patient with vasculitis in remission (asymptomatic, normal urinalysis), be interpreted? Also tested as: A patient with MPO-ANCA vasculitis in remission has a rise in ANCA titre but no symptoms or signs, and urinalysis is normal. What is the best management?

options.A: Levamisole-adulterated cocaine
options.B: Antigen-specific immunoassays for PR3-ANCA and MPO-ANCA as the primary test
options.C: PR3-ANCA (c-ANCA) in GPA; GPA more often has granulomatous ENT or lung disease with PR3-ANCA whereas MPA usually has MPO-ANCA without granulomas
options.D: ANCA alone neither diagnoses vasculitis nor justifies escalation; assess the clinical phenotype and alternative causes, and in remission monitor more closely with clinical, urine and renal assessment
options.E: Rituximab maintenance for 24-48 months after remission induction

explanation: ANCA can be positive in infection (including endocarditis), drug exposure and other inflammatory disease; testing is most useful when a compatible syndrome exists. A rise or reappearance of ANCA modestly increases relapse risk (especially in PR3 and renal disease) but is an imperfect predictor. ANCA positivity without AAV: infective endocarditis (often PR3, with low complement), TB, HIV, hepatitis C, IBD and PSC (atypical p-ANCA), autoimmune hepatitis, drugs (hydralazine, PTU, minocycline, levamisole, allopurinol), anti-GBM disease, SLE, RA, cystic fibrosis. In remission with rising ANCA: review every 1–3 months with urinalysis, creatinine and symptoms. Consider early retreatment only when the clinical relapse risk is high (PR3, prior relapses), as a shared decision.

question: What is induction therapy for organ- or life-threatening GPA or MPA (for example PR3-GPA with RPGN, creatinine 240, haemoptysis and sinus disease), and which trial supports rituximab? Also tested as: Which trial result supports rituximab for remission induction in severe ANCA-associated vasculitis?

options.A: Glucocorticoids (IV pulses then the reduced-dose PEXIVAS taper) with rituximab or cyclophosphamide rituximab was non-inferior to cyclophosphamide and superior in relapsing disease (RAVE)
options.B: Rituximab with glucocorticoids, with methotrexate or mycophenolate as alternatives
options.C: Avacopan
options.D: Rituximab maintenance for 24-48 months after remission induction
options.E: PR3-ANCA (c-ANCA) in GPA; GPA more often has granulomatous ENT or lung disease with PR3-ANCA whereas MPA usually has MPO-ANCA without granulomas

explanation: Organ- or life-threatening GPA or MPA needs urgent induction with rituximab or IV cyclophosphamide. The 2025 BSR recommendations prefer rituximab for relapsing disease, and it is a first-line option particularly in PR3-ANCA disease and when fertility preservation matters. Oral prednisolone follows the reduced-dose (PEXIVAS) taper to 5 mg/day by 4–5 months, which is as effective as standard dosing with fewer infections. Avacopan can be considered to spare glucocorticoids. Pulmonary–renal syndrome: AAV, anti-GBM disease (or double-positive), SLE, cryoglobulinaemia, IgA vasculitis, TTP, catastrophic APS, infection (Legionella, leptospirosis, hantavirus, endocarditis), pulmonary oedema with AKI, PE with renal infarct. Rituximab: 375 mg/m² weekly × 4, or 1 g × 2 two weeks apart (RAVE, RITUXVAS). Cyclophosphamide: IV 15 mg/kg (adjusted for age and renal function) at weeks 0, 2 and 4, then every 3 weeks for 3–6 months (CYCLOPS). Some centres combine rituximab with low-dose IV cyclophosphamide for severe GN. Adjuncts: - PJP prophylaxis: co-trimoxazole for ≥6 months after the last rituximab or cyclophosphamide dose. - Screening: HBV, HCV, HIV, TB, Strongyloides; baseline IgG. - Vaccines: before rituximab. - Protection: bone, PPI, VTE prophylaxis (high risk when active), ACE inhibitor or ARB for proteinuria. - Fertility: preservation before cyclophosphamide. - Bladder cancer: surveillance for haematuria once disease is inactive.

question: A 49-year-old woman has new GPA limited to sinus disease and nasal crusting, with no renal or other organthreatening involvement. Which induction regimen is most appropriate?

options.A: Rituximab with glucocorticoids, with methotrexate or mycophenolate as alternatives
options.B: Urgent airway assessment with ENT and respiratory input, alongside disease-directed treatment
options.C: PR3-ANCA (c-ANCA) in GPA; GPA more often has granulomatous ENT or lung disease with PR3-ANCA whereas MPA usually has MPO-ANCA without granulomas
options.D: Glucocorticoids (IV pulses then the reduced-dose PEXIVAS taper) with rituximab or cyclophosphamide rituximab was non-inferior to cyclophosphamide and superior in relapsing disease (RAVE)
options.E: Colchicine with topical treatments first; for refractory ulcers, apremilast (randomised trial evidence) or a

explanation: Cyclophosphamide is reserved for organ-or life-threatening disease. For non-organ-threatening disease, EULAR recommends glucocorticoids with rituximab, and the 2025 BSR recommendations allow methotrexate or mycophenolate, with a lower glucocorticoid regimen (LoVAS-style) considered. Non-organ-threatening disease: GC plus rituximab is preferred. Methotrexate (if eGFR >50) or MMF are alternatives with higher relapse rates. Co-trimoxazole can be an adjunct in limited ENT disease (it reduces relapse and S. aureus carriage). Nasal douching and ENT care.

question: A 70-year-old woman with MPA has a creatinine rising to 420 micromol/L due to active crescentic glomerulonephritis. Which adjunct may be considered?

options.A: Urgent surgical and medical assessment for mesenteric ischaemia, alongside vasculitis treatment
options.B: Rituximab with glucocorticoids, with methotrexate or mycophenolate as alternatives
options.C: PR3-ANCA (c-ANCA) in GPA; GPA more often has granulomatous ENT or lung disease with PR3-ANCA whereas MPA usually has MPO-ANCA without granulomas
options.D: Plasma exchange
options.E: Avacopan

explanation: Plasma exchange may be considered when creatinine exceeds 300 micromol/L due to active glomerulonephritis. It did not reduce death or end-stage kidney disease overall in a large trial and is not used routinely, including for alveolar haemorrhage alone. PEXIVAS showed no overall benefit of PLEX for death or ESKD. A later meta-analysis suggested a reduced 12-month ESKD risk with high creatinine. PLEX remains mandatory for anti-GBM double positivity. For DAH with hypoxaemia it is an individual decision.

question: A patient with newly diagnosed severe MPA also has poorly controlled diabetes and osteoporosis. Which agent may be used with rituximab or cyclophosphamide to substantially reduce glucocorticoid exposure?

options.A: Colchicine with topical treatments first; for refractory ulcers, apremilast (randomised trial evidence) or a
options.B: Rituximab maintenance for 24-48 months after remission induction
options.C: PR3-ANCA (c-ANCA) in GPA; GPA more often has granulomatous ENT or lung disease with PR3-ANCA whereas MPA usually has MPO-ANCA without granulomas
options.D: Avacopan
options.E: Plasma exchange

explanation: Avacopan, an oral C5a receptor antagonist, was non-inferior for remission at 26 weeks and superior for sustained remission at 52 weeks compared with a prednisolone taper. LFTs need monitoring. ADVOCATE: avacopan (30 mg twice daily for 52 weeks) was non-inferior for remission at 26 weeks and superior for sustained remission at 52 weeks, with better eGFR recovery (especially at low eGFR) and lower GC toxicity. Monitor LFTs (hepatotoxicity, rare vanishing bile duct syndrome). It is a CYP3A4 substrate, so watch for interactions.

question: After rituximab-based induction, a patient with GPA is in remission. Which maintenance strategy is most appropriate?

options.A: Rituximab maintenance for 24-48 months after remission induction
options.B: PR3-ANCA (c-ANCA) in GPA; GPA more often has granulomatous ENT or lung disease with PR3-ANCA whereas MPA usually has MPO-ANCA without granulomas
options.C: Continue mycophenolate-based therapy (with belimumab, a calcineurin inhibitor or obinutuzumab where used) for at least 3 years, with hydroxychloroquine and glucocorticoid withdrawal
options.D: Glucocorticoids (IV pulses then the reduced-dose PEXIVAS taper) with rituximab or cyclophosphamide rituximab was non-inferior to cyclophosphamide and superior in relapsing disease (RAVE)
options.E: Urgent airway assessment with ENT and respiratory input, alongside disease-directed treatment

explanation: The 2025 BSR recommendations prefer rituximab (500-1000 mg every 4-6 months) for maintenance for 24-48 months, with azathioprine or methotrexate as alternatives and mycophenolate if these are unsuitable. Glucocorticoids may be withdrawn within 6-12 months. MAINRITSAN: rituximab was superior to azathioprine. MAINRITSAN-3 showed fewer relapses with extended rituximab. Relapse risk is higher with PR3, ENT or lung disease, prior relapse, persistent ANCA and S. aureus carriage. Rituximab 500 mg every 6 months (or 1 g every 4–6 months) for 24–48 months, longer in high-risk patients. Check IgG before each dose (IVIG if low with infections). Major relapse: treat as new disease, preferring rituximab. Minor relapse: increase GC and optimise maintenance.

question: A patient with GPA develops increasing stridor due to subglottic stenosis. What is the best immediate approach?

options.A: Rituximab with glucocorticoids, with methotrexate or mycophenolate as alternatives
options.B: Antigen-specific immunoassays for PR3-ANCA and MPO-ANCA as the primary test
options.C: PR3-ANCA (c-ANCA) in GPA; GPA more often has granulomatous ENT or lung disease with PR3-ANCA whereas MPA usually has MPO-ANCA without granulomas
options.D: Urgent airway assessment with ENT and respiratory input, alongside disease-directed treatment
options.E: Rituximab maintenance for 24-48 months after remission induction

explanation: Subglottic stenosis can threaten the airway and may not track systemic markers; it often needs local procedures as well as immunosuppression. Stridor or hoarseness in a rheumatology patient: GPA subglottic stenosis; relapsing polychondritis (laryngotracheal chondritis or tracheomalacia); RA cricoarytenoid arthritis; amyloid; post-intubation stenosis; angioedema (ACE inhibitors, HUV, C1-inhibitor deficiency); vocal cord palsy (aortic aneurysm, mediastinal mass); SLE; Behçet's. Flow–volume loop, CT of the airway, laryngoscopy. Intralesional steroid injection with dilatation (laser or balloon); tracheostomy for critical stenosis. Stenosis can progress despite systemic remission.

question: What proportion of EGPA patients are ANCA-positive, what is a leading cause of death, and what treats relapsing non-organ-threatening EGPA that relapses below 10 mg prednisolone? Also tested as: A 44-year-old man with EGPA (asthma, eosinophilia, sinusitis) has no organ-threatening features but relapses whenever prednisolone falls below 10 mg daily. Which treatment is most appropriate?

options.A: Levamisole-adulterated cocaine
options.B: Pulmonary complications: interstitial lung disease and pulmonary arterial hypertension
options.C: Direct-acting antiviral therapy for hepatitis C
options.D: Colchicine with topical treatments first; for refractory ulcers, apremilast (randomised trial evidence) or a
options.E: About 30–40% are ANCA-positive (usually MPO); cardiac involvement is a leading cause of death mepolizumab (or benralizumab) treats relapsing, steroid-dependent disease

explanation: ANCA positivity is associated with glomerulonephritis, neuropathy and purpura; ANCA-negative disease more often features cardiac and lung involvement. ECG, troponin, echocardiography and cardiac MRI are performed at diagnosis. Anti-IL-5/IL-5R therapy reduces relapses and glucocorticoid exposure and is recommended by the 2025 BSR recommendations for non-life- or organ-threatening EGPA and for maintenance. Severe EGPA is treated with glucocorticoids plus cyclophosphamide, or rituximab if cyclophosphamide is unsuitable. Hypereosinophilia: EGPA vs hypereosinophilic syndrome (FIP1L1-PDGFRA, tryptase, B12, T-cell clonality), parasites (Strongyloides serology before steroids), ABPA, drug reaction (DRESS), chronic eosinophilic pneumonia, eosinophilic fasciitis, lymphoma (Hodgkin, T-cell), adrenal insufficiency, mastocytosis, IgG4-RD. Mepolizumab 300 mg SC every 4 weeks (MIRRA). Benralizumab 30 mg SC every 4 weeks was non-inferior to mepolizumab in MANDARA, with more patients stopping GC. REOVAS: rituximab was not superior to conventional therapy in EGPA but is commonly used. Maintenance after severe disease: azathioprine, methotrexate, MMF or rituximab, with or without anti-IL-5. Asthma and sinus care: inhaled therapy and ENT management of polyps. Cardiac EGPA needs aggressive immunosuppression plus heart failure therapy.

question: A 32-year-old woman has retiform purpura with necrosis of both earlobes, arthralgia, neutropenia and very high titre MPO-ANCA, with PR3-ANCA also positive. What is the most likely cause?

options.A: ANCA alone neither diagnoses vasculitis nor justifies escalation; assess the clinical phenotype and alternative causes, and in remission monitor more closely with clinical, urine and renal assessment
options.B: Levamisole-adulterated cocaine
options.C: Serial urinalysis for blood and protein, blood pressure and renal function
options.D: Direct-acting antiviral therapy for hepatitis C
options.E: Antigen-specific immunoassays for PR3-ANCA and MPO-ANCA as the primary test

explanation: Levamisole-contaminated cocaine causes cutaneous vasculopathy, neutropenia and dual ANCA positivity, often with anti-elastase and antiphospholipid antibodies. Management centres on stopping cocaine. Retiform purpura or necrosis: levamisole, cryoglobulinaemia (type I), APS or CAPS, calciphylaxis, cholesterol emboli, warfarin or heparin necrosis, purpura fulminans (protein C deficiency, meningococcaemia), ecthyma gangrenosum, vasculitis (PAN, AAV). Levamisole-cocaine causes retiform purpura (ears, cheeks), neutropenia or agranulocytosis, very high MPO with PR3 (dual positivity), anti-elastase, aPL, low complement, and occasionally GN. Cocaine cessation (with addiction services) and wound care. GC or immunosuppression only for organ-threatening disease. Recurrence follows re-exposure.

question: A man has testicular pain, mononeuritis multiplex, livedo, hypertension and renal and mesenteric microaneurysms on angiography, ANCA-negative and HBsAg-positive. What distinguishes PAN from AAV, and how is HBV-PAN treated? Also tested as: Which feature helps distinguish polyarteritis nodosa from ANCA-associated vasculitis?

options.A: PR3-ANCA (c-ANCA) in GPA; GPA more often has granulomatous ENT or lung disease with PR3-ANCA whereas MPA usually has MPO-ANCA without granulomas
options.B: Levamisole-adulterated cocaine
options.C: Urgent assessment and treatment of active vasculitic neuropathy, because prompt therapy may prevent permanent deficit
options.D: PAN affects medium-sized arteries, causing microaneurysms and organ infarction without glomerulonephritis; HBV-PAN is treated with antivirals plus short-course glucocorticoids and plasma exchange
options.E: Antigen-specific immunoassays for PR3-ANCA and MPO-ANCA as the primary test

explanation: HBV-associated PAN is immune-complex mediated. Prolonged immunosuppression promotes viral replication, so antivirals (entecavir or tenofovir) are combined with brief glucocorticoids and plasma exchange. PAN causes neuropathy, skin lesions, renal artery aneurysms and mesenteric ischaemia; glomerulonephritis and lung haemorrhage point to small-vessel vasculitis. Other microaneurysm causes: segmental arterial mediolysis, fibromuscular dysplasia, endocarditis (mycotic), vEDS, DADA2 (young, lacunar strokes, livedo), cocaine or amphetamines, atrial myxoma emboli, hairy cell leukaemia-associated PAN. Feature PAN MPA small (± Vessels medium arteries medium) MPO in 70– ANCA negative 90% absent (infarcts, GN RPGN renovascular hypertension) DAH, ILD Lung spared Microaneurysms yes rare HBV link yes no uncommon (20–30%) Relapse common Idiopathic PAN: non-severe disease, GC ± methotrexate or azathioprine; severe disease (FFS ≥1: neurological, renal, GI, cardiac), GC plus cyclophosphamide then maintenance. Cutaneous PAN (often post-streptococcal): NSAIDs, colchicine, dapsone, short GC. DADA2: TNF inhibitors. Screen all PAN patients for HBV.

question: A patient with suspected medium-vessel vasculitis has abdominal pain out of proportion to examination and a rising lactate. What is the immediate priority?

options.A: Antigen-specific immunoassays for PR3-ANCA and MPO-ANCA as the primary test
options.B: Plasma exchange
options.C: Urgent surgical and medical assessment for mesenteric ischaemia, alongside vasculitis treatment
options.D: Serial urinalysis for blood and protein, blood pressure and renal function
options.E: Take blood and joint cultures rapidly if feasible, but do not delay antibiotics and resuscitation

explanation: Bowel ischaemia is life-threatening and requires urgent imaging and surgical input. Urgent CT angiography, surgical review and pulse GC. Bowel ischaemia, perforation, gallbladder or appendix infarction and pancreatitis can all occur in PAN. GI involvement scores in the FFS. Consider cyclophosphamide.

question: A 57-year-old woman has palpable purpura, arthralgia, peripheral neuropathy and low C4. Type II cryoglobulins are present and hepatitis C RNA is positive. Disease is mild without organ threat. What is the first-line treatment?

options.A: Direct-acting antiviral therapy for hepatitis C
options.B: Development of MALT lymphoma
options.C: Levamisole-adulterated cocaine
options.D: Serial urinalysis for blood and protein, blood pressure and renal function
options.E: B-cell targeted therapy with rituximab plus glucocorticoids, adding plasma exchange for lifethreatening disease

explanation: Mild to moderate HCV-associated cryoglobulinaemic vasculitis often responds to viral eradication. Severe disease may need rituximab, with glucocorticoids and/or plasma exchange, alongside antivirals. HCV accounts for 70–90% of mixed cryoglobulinaemic vasculitis. Cryoglobulins are found in 40–60% of chronic HCV, but only 5–15% become symptomatic. Meltzer triad (purpura, arthralgia, weakness) is present in only 25–30% at diagnosis. Organ involvement: skin 70–90% (orthostatic purpura, ochre pigmentation, malleolar ulcers); joints 40– 80%; painful axonal sensory neuropathy 20–60%; MPGN 20–35% (a major adverse prognostic factor); lymphoma 5– 10%. Mechanism: the HCV E2 protein binds CD81 on B cells, with t(14;18) and BAFF promoting clonal RFproducing B cells. Severity Treatment DAAs (sofosbuvir/velpatasvir for 12 Mild to moderate weeks, or glecaprevir/pibrentasvir for 8 weeks; SVR >95%) Severe (GN, rituximab ± moderate GC, then or with ulcers, motor DAAs neuropathy) Life-threatening PLEX + IV methylprednisolone + rituximab; DAAs as soon as feasible Vasculitis persists or relapses after SVR in 10–20% (autonomous clone, lymphoma), so give rituximab. Screen for HBV before DAAs (reactivation risk). Rituximab can complex with cryoglobulins (serum sickness), so with a high cryocrit use PLEX first or a lower dose. Interferon regimens are obsolete. Low-grade splenic marginal zone lymphoma may regress after HCV eradication.

question: A 52-year-old man has palpable purpura over the legs, abdominal pain and arthralgia after an upper respiratory infection. Skin biopsy shows leukocytoclastic vasculitis with IgA deposits. What is the most important follow-up investigation?

options.A: Infective endocarditis
options.B: Direct-acting antiviral therapy for hepatitis C
options.C: Urgent surgical and medical assessment for mesenteric ischaemia, alongside vasculitis treatment
options.D: Levamisole-adulterated cocaine
options.E: Serial urinalysis for blood and protein, blood pressure and renal function

explanation: Adults with IgA vasculitis more often develop significant nephritis than children. Renal biopsy is needed for significant proteinuria or impaired function. Palpable purpura: IgA vasculitis, cryoglobulinaemic vasculitis, AAV, drug hypersensitivity vasculitis (antibiotics, NSAIDs, allopurinol), infection (meningococcaemia, gonococcaemia, endocarditis, hepatitis B or C), SLE or RA vasculitis, HUV, paraneoplastic vasculitis (haematological malignancy), Schamberg's disease (non-palpable), scurvy (perifollicular). Take a deep punch biopsy within 24–48 hours for H&E and direct IF (IgA). IgA vasculitis features purpura on the legs and buttocks, arthritis, abdominal pain (intussusception in children) and IgA nephritis. Adults have a worse renal prognosis and more often an underlying cause (malignancy, infection, IBD). Supportive care for mild disease. GC for GI or severe disease. Nephritis is managed like IgA nephropathy (RAAS blockade, GC; MMF or cyclophosphamide for crescentic disease). Monitor urine for at least 6 months (children) and longer in adults.

question: A 45-year-old woman has urticarial lesions lasting more than 24 hours that leave bruising, with arthralgia, low C3, C4 and C1q, and anti-C1q antibodies. Which diagnosis best fits, and what associations should be sought?

options.A: Serial urinalysis for blood and protein, blood pressure and renal function
options.B: Direct-acting antiviral therapy for hepatitis C
options.C: Levamisole-adulterated cocaine
options.D: Hypocomplementaemic urticarial vasculitis; associations include SLE and obstructive lung disease
options.E: Disseminated gonococcal infection; IV ceftriaxone, with testing for other STIs and partner notification

explanation: Individual urticarial vasculitis lesions persist beyond 24 hours, may burn or hurt and leave pigmentation. The hypocomplementaemic form overlaps with SLE and can cause COPD-like lung disease, angioedema, glomerulonephritis and uveitis. Urticaria with systemic features: urticarial vasculitis (normocomplementaemic or hypocomplementaemic), Schnitzler syndrome (monoclonal IgM, fever, bone pain), CAPS (neutrophilic urticaria from childhood), adult-onset Still's (evanescent rash), SLE, serum sickness, chronic spontaneous urticaria (lesions <24 hours, no bruising, antihistamine-responsive). Skin biopsy (leucocytoclastic vasculitis). Mild disease: antihistamines, dapsone, colchicine, HCQ. Systemic disease: GC plus MMF or azathioprine; rituximab, omalizumab, anakinra or canakinumab for refractory disease. Screen for SLE, HCV, malignancy and COPD (HUV causes early emphysema; avoid smoking).

question: A patient with systemic vasculitis develops acute foot drop from mononeuritis multiplex. What is the most appropriate approach?

options.A: Urgent assessment and treatment of active vasculitic neuropathy, because prompt therapy may prevent permanent deficit
options.B: PAN affects medium-sized arteries, causing microaneurysms and organ infarction without glomerulonephritis; HBV-PAN is treated with antivirals plus short-course glucocorticoids and plasma exchange
options.C: Pulmonary embolism, alongside other acute cardiopulmonary causes
options.D: Infective endocarditis
options.E: Serial urinalysis for blood and protein, blood pressure and renal function

explanation: New motor neuropathy indicates organ-threatening disease. Nerve conduction studies and, where needed, nerve biopsy support the diagnosis. Mononeuritis multiplex is a stepwise, asymmetric painful neuropathy in multiple named nerves (foot drop, wrist drop). Causes: PAN (60–70%), EGPA (45–75%), MPA, GPA, cryoglobulinaemia, RA vasculitis, SLE, Sjögren's, sarcoid, diabetes, HIV, HNPP, leprosy, lymphoma (neurolymphomatosis), amyloid. NCS show an axonal multifocal pattern. Combined sural nerve and muscle biopsy (sural plus peroneus brevis) increases yield. Induction as for severe vasculitis. Neuropathic pain treatment, AFO or splints and physiotherapy. Recovery is slow (months).

question: A previously well man has a hot swollen knee and fever. Which organism most commonly causes native joint septic arthritis in adults, and what is the initial management if he has no prosthesis, MRSA risk or penicillin allergy? Also tested as: Which organism most commonly causes native joint septic arthritis in adults?

options.A: Staphylococcus aureus; aspirate the joint and take blood cultures, then start IV flucloxacillin
options.B: Worsening beyond 48 hours with fever and systemic upset
options.C: Take blood and joint cultures rapidly if feasible, but do not delay antibiotics and resuscitation
options.D: Septic arthritis is a major concern; send cultures and treat urgently if clinical suspicion is high
options.E: Washout may be needed for large joints, purulent fluid or failure to improve (guided by orthopaedic assessment); about 2 weeks of targeted therapy is non-inferior to 4 weeks after drainage

explanation: Empirical flucloxacillin is used for adults without risk factors; clindamycin if penicillin-allergic, vancomycin if MRSA risk, and a third-generation cephalosporin for older or frail patients or suspected gonococcal or Gram-negative infection. Gonococcus is considered in young sexually active adults, and Gram-negative organisms in the elderly, immunosuppressed and people who inject drugs. Kingella is a cause in young children. Acute hot joint: septic arthritis; crystal arthritis (gout, CPP; can coexist); reactive arthritis; haemarthrosis (trauma, anticoagulants, haemophilia, PVNS/TGCT); inflammatory arthritis flare; Lyme disease; viral arthritis; acute rheumatic fever; cellulitis or bursitis mimicking a joint; osteomyelitis near the joint; Charcot joint; SONK or insufficiency fracture. Fever is present in about 60%. Blood cultures are positive in about 50%. CRP, ESR and WCC support but cannot rule out infection. Procalcitonin and synovial lactate may help. Inoculate synovial fluid into blood culture bottles. Screen for the source (skin, urine, endocarditis); do gonococcal NAAT if relevant. Use ultrasound for hip effusion and guided aspiration, and MRI for osteomyelitis or abscess. Hold biologics and JAKi. Early physiotherapy once controlled.

question: A hot swollen native knee has a synovial fluid white cell count of 80,000/mm³ with 90% neutrophils. Which interpretation is safest?

options.A: Washout may be needed for large joints, purulent fluid or failure to improve (guided by orthopaedic assessment); about 2 weeks of targeted therapy is non-inferior to 4 weeks after drainage
options.B: Treat urgently while obtaining investigations in parallel
options.C: Staphylococcus aureus; aspirate the joint and take blood cultures, then start IV flucloxacillin
options.D: Duodenal biopsy for PAS staining and T. whipplei PCR
options.E: Septic arthritis is a major concern; send cultures and treat urgently if clinical suspicion is high

explanation: High cell counts with neutrophil predominance raise concern for infection, but no cut-off is perfectly diagnostic and crystal arthritis can overlap. WCC guide: non-inflammatory 200–2,000; inflammatory 2,000–50,000; septic usually >50,000 with >90% neutrophils (but lower in early, partially treated, gonococcal, TB or immunosuppressed cases). Crystal arthritis can exceed 50,000. Crystals do not exclude infection. Synovial glucose is low and lactate high in sepsis.

question: A patient with suspected septic arthritis is hypotensive and tachycardic. What is correct regarding aspiration and antibiotics?

options.A: Urgent surgical and medical assessment for mesenteric ischaemia, alongside vasculitis treatment
options.B: Take blood and joint cultures rapidly if feasible, but do not delay antibiotics and resuscitation
options.C: Washout may be needed for large joints, purulent fluid or failure to improve (guided by orthopaedic assessment); about 2 weeks of targeted therapy is non-inferior to 4 weeks after drainage
options.D: Pulmonary embolism, alongside other acute cardiopulmonary causes
options.E: Staphylococcus aureus; aspirate the joint and take blood cultures, then start IV flucloxacillin

explanation: In sepsis, resuscitation and antibiotics take priority. In stable patients, aspiration before antibiotics improves culture yield. Sepsis-6 within the hour: cultures, IV antibiotics, fluids, lactate, oxygen, urine output. Image-guided aspiration as soon as feasible, without delaying antibiotics. Urgent orthopaedic washout. Consider an MRSA-active agent in healthcare-associated cases.

question: What is the role of joint washout in septic arthritis, and how long should antibiotics continue in uncomplicated S. aureus native-knee infection that improves rapidly after washout? Also tested as: A man with Staphylococcus aureus native-knee septic arthritis improves rapidly after washout and IV antibiotics, with no bacteraemia, osteomyelitis or prosthesis. How long should antibiotics continue?

options.A: Septic arthritis is a major concern; send cultures and treat urgently if clinical suspicion is high
options.B: Staphylococcus aureus; aspirate the joint and take blood cultures, then start IV flucloxacillin
options.C: Duodenal biopsy for PAS staining and T. whipplei PCR
options.D: Washout may be needed for large joints, purulent fluid or failure to improve (guided by orthopaedic assessment); about 2 weeks of targeted therapy is non-inferior to 4 weeks after drainage
options.E: Take blood and joint cultures rapidly if feasible, but do not delay antibiotics and resuscitation

explanation: Daily needle aspiration, arthroscopic washout or open debridement are used depending on joint, response and organism; the hip usually needs surgery. Older guidance advised about 2 weeks IV followed by 4 weeks oral, without trial evidence. Randomised data now support shorter targeted courses after surgical drainage in uncomplicated native-joint infection, with early switch to oral therapy (OVIVA showed oral is non-inferior to IV in bone and joint infection). Bacteraemia, osteomyelitis, prostheses and resistant organisms need longer treatment. Intra-articular antibiotics cause chemical synovitis and are not used. Monitor clinical response, CRP and repeat aspiration. Physiotherapy to restore range. Recheck the diagnosis if there is no improvement (TB, fungi, crystals).

question: A patient develops a painful, warm, swollen knee after total knee replacement, either 9 months later (clinically stable) or 2 weeks after surgery with wound erythema and fever but a well-fixed implant. What is the first action, and which strategy suits early infection? Also tested as: Two weeks after a total knee replacement, a 68-year-old man develops a hot, swollen, painful knee with wound erythema and fever. Radiographs show a well-fixed implant. Which management strategy is most appropriate after joint aspiration for culture?

options.A: Rituximab maintenance for 24-48 months after remission induction
options.B: Urgent orthopaedic referral for aspiration, ideally before any antibiotics; early postoperative (or acute haematogenous) infection with a stable implant and short symptom duration suits DAIR (debridement, antibiotics and implant retention)
options.C: Septic arthritis is a major concern; send cultures and treat urgently if clinical suspicion is high
options.D: Avoid steroid injection within about 3 months of arthroplasty
options.E: Staphylococcus aureus; aspirate the joint and take blood cultures, then start IV flucloxacillin

explanation: Antibiotics before aspiration reduce culture yield and can compromise decisions on debridement, implant retention or revision, so they should, where possible, be withheld until aspirate and intraoperative samples have been taken. Chronic or late infections usually need one- or two-stage revision in a specialist MDT. Painful prosthesis: PJI vs aseptic loosening (X-ray cannot separate them), instability, periprosthetic fracture, metallosis or ALVAL (metal-on-metal), crystal arthritis in the replaced joint, referred hip or spine pain, CRPS, haemarthrosis. DAIR (with exchange of mobile parts) suits infection with symptoms <3–4 weeks, a stable implant and a susceptible organism. One-stage revision suits a known susceptible organism with good soft tissues. Two-stage revision is for difficult or unknown organisms or poor soft tissue. Suppressive antibiotics when surgery is impossible. Prevention: optimise diabetes, skin, weight and smoking; decolonise S. aureus; perioperative prophylaxis; DMARD timing; avoid IA steroid within 3 months before surgery.

question: A 23-year-old sexually active woman has migratory polyarthralgia, tenosynovitis of the wrist and a few painless pustules on her hands. What is the most likely diagnosis and treatment?

options.A: Disseminated gonococcal infection; IV ceftriaxone, with testing for other STIs and partner notification
options.B: Chikungunya virus
options.C: Brucellosis; combination antibiotics for at least 6 weeks
options.D: Duodenal biopsy for PAS staining and T. whipplei PCR
options.E: Diffuse infiltrative lymphocytosis syndrome (DILS)

explanation: The arthritis-dermatitis-tenosynovitis triad is characteristic. Blood, synovial fluid and mucosal site cultures with NAAT should be taken.
