question: A 64-year-old man has a chronic non-itchy urticarial rash, recurrent fever, bone pain and a monoclonal IgM paraprotein, unresponsive to antihistamines. What is the diagnosis and treatment?

options.A: Schnitzler syndrome; IL-1 blockade (such as anakinra)
options.B: Urinary mevalonic acid during an attack, with MVK genetics
options.C: Somatic UBA1 mutation testing
options.D: TNF receptor-associated periodic syndrome (TRAPS)
options.E: IL-1 blockade (canakinumab or anakinra)

explanation: Schnitzler syndrome is an acquired autoinflammatory disorder of later life: urticarial rash, monoclonal IgM (or IgG), fever, bone pain and raised inflammatory markers. IL-1 inhibition gives dramatic responses. Patients need monitoring because of the risk of progression to lymphoproliferative disease. Strasbourg criteria: 2 major (urticarial rash plus monoclonal IgM or IgG) plus ≥2 minor (recurrent fever, abnormal bone remodelling or pain, neutrophilic dermal infiltrate, leucocytosis or raised CRP). 15–20% progress to Waldenström's or lymphoma. Bone scintigraphy or MRI shows increased uptake at the distal femur and proximal tibia. Anakinra gives a dramatic, near-universal response; canakinumab and tocilizumab also work. Long-term haematology follow-up of the paraprotein. Risk of AA amyloid if untreated.

question: A 9-year-old has livedo racemosa, recurrent fevers, two lacunar strokes and mesenteric aneurysms suggesting polyarteritis nodosa, along with mild hypogammaglobulinaemia. Which test and treatment are most appropriate?

options.A: Urinary mevalonic acid during an attack, with MVK genetics
options.B: Fever resolving promptly after one dose of prednisolone
options.C: Somatic UBA1 mutation testing
options.D: ADA2 enzyme activity and genetics; treat with a TNF inhibitor
options.E: Schnitzler syndrome; IL-1 blockade (such as anakinra)

explanation: Deficiency of adenosine deaminase 2 (DADA2) causes early-onset PAN-like vasculitis, lacunar strokes, livedo and immunodeficiency. TNF inhibitors are highly effective at preventing strokes, whereas glucocorticoids and conventional immunosuppressants are less effective. Haematopoietic stem cell transplantation is used for severe haematological disease. DADA2 (AR): early-onset PAN-like vasculitis, lacunar strokes (often before age 5), livedo racemosa, hepatosplenomegaly, hypogammaglobulinaemia, cytopenias including pure red cell aplasia, bone marrow failure. TNF inhibitors (etanercept, adalimumab) prevent strokes. Avoid anticoagulants and antiplatelets after strokes (haemorrhage risk). HSCT for the haematological phenotype. Screen siblings. Consider DADA2 in young or familial PAN, and in Sneddon-like presentations.

question: A 3-year-old has boggy, painless swelling of the wrists and ankles (tenosynovitis), granulomatous panuveitis and a tan-coloured scaly ichthyosiform rash. A parent had uveitis in childhood. The chest radiograph is normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.A: Diffuse tenosynovial giant cell tumour (PVNS)
options.B: IL-1 blockade (canakinumab or anakinra)
options.C: Blau syndrome (NOD2-associated granulomatous disease)
options.D: Osseous sarcoidosis
options.E: Löfgren's syndrome; usually self-limiting, treated with NSAIDs

explanation: Blau syndrome (and early-onset sarcoidosis) is caused by gain-of-function NOD2 variants. It presents before age 5 with the triad of granulomatous arthritis or tenosynovitis, uveitis and rash, and the lungs are usually spared. Ocular disease is the main threat, and TNF inhibitors are often needed. Childhood granulomatous disease: Blau, CGD, CVIDassociated granulomas, TB, cat-scratch disease, Crohn's, JIA (non-granulomatous), sarcoid (adult-type is rare in young children). Blau syndrome (familial) and early-onset sarcoidosis (sporadic) are both NOD2 gain-of-function (AD) and present before 5 with a granulomatous triad: boggy synovitis and tenosynovitis with large cystic swelling, panuveitis (sight-threatening), and ichthyosiform or papular rash. Also camptodactyly, fever, vasculitis, hepatic granulomas. The lungs are spared. GC, methotrexate, TNFi (adalimumab or infliximab) for the eyes; ophthalmology surveillance; IL-1 blockade or JAKi for refractory disease.

question: A 46-year-old Afro-Caribbean woman with lupus pernio has painful swelling of several fingers. Hand radiographs show 'lace-like' lytic lesions and cysts in the middle and distal phalanges with intact joint spaces. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.A: Blau syndrome (NOD2-associated granulomatous disease)
options.B: Löfgren's syndrome; usually self-limiting, treated with NSAIDs
options.C: Serum IGF-1
options.D: Diffuse tenosynovial giant cell tumour (PVNS)
options.E: Osseous sarcoidosis

explanation: Bone sarcoid usually affects the phalanges, with a lacy lytic pattern, and strongly correlates with chronic cutaneous disease such as lupus pernio. Asymptomatic lesions need no treatment. Painful or destructive disease is treated with glucocorticoids and steroid-sparing agents such as methotrexate, with TNF inhibitors for refractory cases. Lytic phalangeal lesions: sarcoid, enchondroma, gout (punched-out with overhanging edges), hyperparathyroidism (subperiosteal resorption, acroosteolysis), TB dactylitis, metastasis (lung), osteomyelitis, glomus tumour, PsA acro-osteolysis. Bone sarcoid occurs in up to 15% (phalanges with "lacelike" lytic lesions; vertebral or pelvic lytic or sclerotic lesions that mimic metastases on PET or MRI). Muscle granulomas are found in 50–80% at biopsy, usually silently. Joints: acute (Löfgren's) or chronic, oligo- or polyarticular, sometimes destructive; dactylitis. First line: GC (pulmonary 20–40 mg, taper over 3–6 months; course 6–12 months; relapse in a third). Second line: methotrexate (10–20 mg/week), azathioprine, MMF, leflunomide. HCQ for skin, joints and hypercalcaemia. Third line: infliximab or adalimumab for refractory lung, cutaneous (lupus pernio), cardiac or neurological disease. Not effective: ciclosporin. Efzofitimod missed its phase 3 primary endpoint. JAKi are promising for skin. Biomarkers: ACE is not diagnostic; sIL-2R and chitotriosidase are better activity markers. Prognosis: spontaneous remission in 60–70%; mortality <5%.

question: A 44-year-old man with known pulmonary sarcoidosis reports palpitations and an episode of presyncope. ECG shows new first-degree heart block with right bundle branch block. What is the most appropriate investigation?

options.A: Diffuse tenosynovial giant cell tumour (PVNS)
options.B: Urgent assessment for neurosarcoidosis and other causes, as organ-threatening disease may need systemic treatment
options.C: Cardiac MRI and/or FDG-PET with Holter monitoring
options.D: Serum protein electrophoresis, immunofixation and free light chains
options.E: Immediate factor VIII replacement with rest, ice and analgesia

explanation: Cardiac sarcoidosis causes conduction block, ventricular arrhythmias and sudden death, and is under-recognised. New conduction abnormalities need cardiac MRI (late gadolinium enhancement) and/or FDG-PET. Treatment includes immunosuppression and, often, device therapy. ACE levels do not guide management. Cardiac sarcoid is clinically evident in about 5% (up to 25% on imaging or at autopsy): conduction block, VT, sudden death, heart failure. Screen everyone with ECG and symptoms, plus Holter and echo if abnormal. CMR (patchy mid-wall or subepicardial LGE, especially basal septum) and cardiac FDG-PET (after a high-fat, lowcarbohydrate preparation). GC plus an early steroidsparing agent (methotrexate); infliximab for refractory disease. ICD or pacing for high-degree block or VT (an ICD is often indicated even if the block recovers). Transplant for end-stage disease.

question: A man has knee pain, diabetes insipidus, symmetrical long-bone osteosclerosis and 'hairy kidney' perirenal infiltration; biopsy shows CD68-positive, CD1a-negative foamy histiocytes. Which molecular test guides treatment?

options.A: Systemic glucocorticoids, while investigating the marrow
options.B: Somatic UBA1 mutation testing
options.C: Serum IGF-1
options.D: Diabetic cheiroarthropathy (limited joint mobility)
options.E: BRAF V600E mutation analysis

explanation: Erdheim-Chester disease is a histiocytic neoplasm with symmetrical long-bone osteosclerosis, retroperitoneal and perirenal infiltration and diabetes insipidus. About half of patients carry BRAF V600E and respond to BRAF inhibitors such as vemurafenib. Others often have MAPK pathway variants treatable with MEK inhibitors. Histiocytoses: LCH (CD1a+, langerin+, Birbeck granules, lytic lesions), Rosai–Dorfman (emperipolesis), multicentric reticulohistiocytosis, IgG4-RD (retroperitoneal fibrosis), retroperitoneal lymphoma. Erdheim–Chester disease: a non-Langerhans histiocytosis (CD68+, CD1a-, S100 variable) with symmetrical diaphyseal and metaphyseal osteosclerosis of the legs, "hairy kidney" perirenal infiltration, "coated aorta", retroorbital masses, DI, xanthelasma, right atrial pseudotumour and CNS involvement. BRAF V600E is present in about half. BRAF inhibitors (vemurafenib, dabrafenib) or MEK inhibitors (cobimetinib) for MAPK-pathway variants. Interferon-α historically. Bone scan or PET for staging.

question: A woman has a destructive DIP-predominant arthritis and red-brown 'coral bead' papules around the nail folds and on the face. What is the diagnosis, and what must be screened for?

options.A: Osseous sarcoidosis
options.B: Multicentric reticulohistiocytosis; underlying malignancy
options.C: Systemic glucocorticoids, while investigating the marrow
options.D: Acute Charcot foot: immediate offloading in a total contact cast and urgent MDT referral
options.E: Deep full-thickness biopsy including fascia

explanation: Multicentric reticulohistiocytosis combines papulonodular skin lesions (histiocytes and multinucleated giant cells) with an aggressive DIP-predominant arthritis that can progress to arthritis mutilans. Around a quarter of cases are associated with malignancy. Treatment includes methotrexate, bisphosphonates and TNF inhibitors. Screen for malignancy (CT chest, abdomen and pelvis; age-appropriate tests; skin biopsy). Treatment: methotrexate, cyclophosphamide, bisphosphonates, TNFi or tocilizumab, GC; treat the tumour. Early aggressive therapy aims to prevent arthritis mutilans.

question: After intensive weight training, a man develops woody induration of the forearms and calves with a 'groove sign', sparing hands and face, with no Raynaud's and marked eosinophilia. Which investigation best confirms the diagnosis?

options.A: Diabetic cheiroarthropathy (limited joint mobility)
options.B: Serum protein electrophoresis, immunofixation and free light chains
options.C: Look for an underlying malignancy
options.D: Pulmonary arterial hypertension and interstitial lung disease
options.E: Deep full-thickness biopsy including fascia

explanation: Eosinophilic fasciitis causes fascial inflammation and thickening with prominent eosinophilia. A deep en-bloc biopsy including fascia, or MRI showing fascial enhancement, confirms it. Most patients respond to glucocorticoids, often with methotrexate. Haematological malignancy is an occasional association. Eosinophilic fasciitis (Shulman syndrome) is often triggered by strenuous exercise and sometimes by statins or checkpoint inhibitors. Rapid woody induration of the limbs ("peau d'orange", groove sign) spares the hands, feet and face. There is no Raynaud's, capillaroscopy is normal, eosinophilia and hypergammaglobulinaemia are present, and morphoea coexists in about a third. Associations: aplastic anaemia, lymphoma, MDS. MRI (fascial thickening and enhancement) and fullthickness en-bloc biopsy. GC (often 0.5–1 mg/kg) plus methotrexate early; MMF, IVIG, tocilizumab, JAKi or sirolimus for refractory disease. Physiotherapy for contractures. FBC surveillance for haematological disease.

question: A 30-year-old man has a 2-year history of recurrent atraumatic swelling of the right knee, with blood-stained aspirates. MRI shows nodular synovial proliferation with low signal and 'blooming' on gradient-echo sequences. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.A: Immediate factor VIII replacement with rest, ice and analgesia
options.B: Cardiac MRI and/or FDG-PET with Holter monitoring
options.C: Somatic UBA1 mutation testing
options.D: Diffuse tenosynovial giant cell tumour (PVNS)
options.E: Blau syndrome (NOD2-associated granulomatous disease)

explanation: Tenosynovial giant cell tumour (the current name for PVNS) is a CSF1-driven synovial neoplasm. Haemosiderin deposition gives a characteristic 'blooming' artefact on gradient-echo MRI. Treatment is surgical synovectomy. CSF1 receptor inhibitors are now an option for diffuse disease that is not amenable to surgery. Recurrent atraumatic haemarthrosis: TGCT/PVNS, haemophilia or von Willebrand disease, anticoagulation, synovial haemangioma, CPPD, Charcot joint, synovial sarcoma, scurvy. Gradient-echo "blooming" (haemosiderin) also occurs in haemophilic arthropathy. Localised (nodular) vs diffuse TGCT; the knee is the commonest site in diffuse disease. CSF1 translocation causes CSF1 overexpression. X-ray may show erosions or cysts with preserved joint space. Surgical synovectomy (open or arthroscopic), with high recurrence in diffuse disease. CSF1R inhibitors (pexidartinib, with hepatotoxicity; vimseltinib) for disease not amenable to surgery. Radiosynovectomy is an adjunct. Arthroplasty for end-stage disease.

question: A man being investigated for myelodysplasia develops fever, neutrophilia and tender red plaques; skin biopsy shows a dense neutrophilic infiltrate without vasculitis. What is the most appropriate treatment?

options.A: Diabetic cheiroarthropathy (limited joint mobility)
options.B: Systemic glucocorticoids, while investigating the marrow
options.C: BRAF V600E mutation analysis
options.D: Urinary mevalonic acid during an attack, with MVK genetics
options.E: IL-1 blockade (canakinumab or anakinra)

explanation: Sweet syndrome (acute febrile neutrophilic dermatosis) responds quickly to glucocorticoids, with colchicine, dapsone or potassium iodide as alternatives. It may be idiopathic, drug-induced (for example, by G-CSF) or associated with malignancy, especially AML and MDS. VEXAS syndrome should also be considered in older men with Sweet-like lesions and macrocytosis. Neutrophilic dermatoses: Sweet's, pyoderma gangrenosum, Behçet's, bowel-associated dermatosis– arthritis syndrome, neutrophilic urticarial dermatosis (Still's, CAPS, Schnitzler, SLE), erythema elevatum diutinum, infection (cellulitis, mycobacteria), leukaemia cutis. Sweet's syndrome criteria: abrupt tender red plaques or nodules with a dense neutrophilic infiltrate without vasculitis (major), plus fever, an association (malignancy, infection, IBD, pregnancy, drugs), neutrophilia and raised ESR, and a rapid GC response. Associations: AML, MDS, G- CSF, azacitidine, ATRA, vaccination, IBD, Behçet's, VEXAS. Prednisolone 0.5–1 mg/kg (rapid response). Alternatives: colchicine, dapsone, potassium iodide, ciclosporin, IL-1 blockade. Treat the underlying cause, and do FBC, film and marrow examination in older patients. Check for macrocytosis and UBA1 in older men.

question: A woman with ulcerative colitis has a rapidly enlarging, very painful leg ulcer with a violaceous undermined border that began after minor trauma. What is the key management principle?

options.A: Acute Charcot foot: immediate offloading in a total contact cast and urgent MDT referral
options.B: This pattern usually parallels bowel activity and is self-limiting
options.C: Pelvic imaging and CA-125 (ovarian cancer)
options.D: Avoid debridement (pathergy); give systemic immunosuppression
options.E: Immediate factor VIII replacement with rest, ice and analgesia

explanation: Pyoderma gangrenosum is a neutrophilic dermatosis associated with IBD, inflammatory arthritis and haematological disease. Surgical trauma can worsen it through pathergy. First-line treatment for extensive disease is systemic glucocorticoids or ciclosporin, with TNF inhibitors as effective options, particularly with IBD. Leg ulcers in rheumatology patients: pyoderma gangrenosum (IBD, RA, PsA, myeloma or IgA paraprotein, AML, PAPA), vasculitic ulcers (RA vasculitis, PAN, cryoglobulinaemia, AAV), Felty's leg ulcers, APS or livedoid vasculopathy, calciphylaxis, venous or arterial ulcers, infection (atypical mycobacteria, fungi, ecthyma gangrenosum), malignancy (SCC), hydroxyurea ulcers, Martorell ulcer (hypertensive). PG is a diagnosis of exclusion (Delphi or PARACELSUS criteria). Biopsy the edge to exclude infection and malignancy, and expect pathergy. Local: potent topical steroid or tacrolimus, moist dressings, no sharp debridement. Systemic: prednisolone or ciclosporin (STOP GAP trial showed equivalence). TNFi (infliximab, adalimumab), especially with IBD; IL-1, IL-23 or IL-17 blockade, JAKi or IVIG for refractory disease. Treat the associated disease. Plan any surgery with immunosuppression cover. malignancy

question: A man with long-standing type 1 diabetes cannot press his palms flat together and has thick, waxy finger skin, without Raynaud's and with normal capillaroscopy. What is the diagnosis?

options.A: Pelvic imaging and CA-125 (ovarian cancer)
options.B: Systemic glucocorticoids, while investigating the marrow
options.C: BRAF V600E mutation analysis
options.D: Diabetic cheiroarthropathy (limited joint mobility)
options.E: Deep full-thickness biopsy including fascia

explanation: Limited joint mobility in diabetes produces the 'prayer sign' and waxy skin thickening from glycation of connective tissue. It is associated with microvascular complications. Absent Raynaud's, normal capillaroscopy and no autoantibodies distinguish it from systemic sclerosis. Limited hand mobility with thick skin: diabetic cheiroarthropathy vs SSc (Raynaud's, capillaroscopy, antibodies), scleredema diabeticorum (upper back), Dupuytren's, palmar fasciitis and polyarthritis (paraneoplastic, rapid onset), eosinophilic fasciitis (spares hands), hypothyroid myxoedema, amyloid, stiff skin syndrome, chronic GVHD. Optimise glycaemic control, stretching and hand therapy. Screen for microvascular complications (retinopathy, nephropathy), which are associated.

question: A woman with diabetic neuropathy has a warm, swollen, red midfoot, 3°C warmer than the other foot, with no ulcer and normal radiographs. What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.A: Immediate factor VIII replacement with rest, ice and analgesia
options.B: Avoid debridement (pathergy); give systemic immunosuppression
options.C: Multicentric reticulohistiocytosis; underlying malignancy
options.D: Acute Charcot foot: immediate offloading in a total contact cast and urgent MDT referral
options.E: Systemic glucocorticoids, while investigating the marrow

explanation: Acute Charcot foot can present with normal radiographs. A temperature difference over 2°C in a neuropathic foot should be treated as Charcot until proven otherwise. Immediate offloading prevents collapse and rocker-bottom deformity. MRI shows early bone marrow oedema, and infection is unlikely without an ulcer. Warm swollen neuropathic foot: acute Charcot vs cellulitis, osteomyelitis (usually with an ulcer; forefoot), gout, DVT, fracture, septic arthritis. Other neuropathic arthropathies: tabes dorsalis (knee), syringomyelia (shoulder, elbow), leprosy, alcohol, congenital insensitivity to pain, amyloid neuropathy. Charcot occurs in 0.1–1% of people with diabetes, mostly at the midfoot (Lisfranc), then the ankle. The temperature difference is >2 °C. X-ray progresses through the "6 Ds": distension, density, debris, disorganisation, dislocation, destruction. Rocker-bottom deformity follows. Total contact cast or removable walker until the temperature difference is <2 °C (often 3–6+ months), then custom footwear. Diabetic foot MDT. Surgery for unstable deformity. Bisphosphonates have limited evidence.

question: A 49-year-old man has bilateral carpal tunnel syndrome, knee pain, increasing shoe and ring size and coarse facial features. Hand radiographs show widened MCP joint spaces and the heel pad is thickened. Which test is most appropriate first?

options.A: Serum IGF-1
options.B: Osseous sarcoidosis
options.C: BRAF V600E mutation analysis
options.D: Paternal low-dose methotrexate exposure is considered compatible with conception
options.E: Immediate factor VIII replacement with rest, ice and analgesia

explanation: Acromegalic arthropathy causes cartilage hypertrophy with widened joint spaces, then secondary OA. Carpal tunnel syndrome is common. Serum IGF-1 is the screening test (older texts suggested a skull radiograph), confirmed by failure of GH suppression on an oral glucose tolerance test and by pituitary MRI. Acromegaly arthropathy affects about 70%: early joint space widening (cartilage hypertrophy), then premature OA with large osteophytes. Also CTS, Raynaud's, proximal myopathy, back pain with DISH-like changes and posterior vertebral scalloping, spade-like hands, heel pad >22–23 mm, prognathism, sleep apnoea, cardiomyopathy, colonic polyps. IGF-1 (screen), then OGTT GH suppression (confirm), then pituitary MRI. Transsphenoidal surgery, somatostatin analogues, pegvisomant. Joint changes are only partly reversible.

question: A 61-year-old woman has 4 months of proximal muscle aching, cramps and weakness, with slow-relaxing ankle reflexes. CK is 1,400 U/L. She is not taking a statin. What is the most important next investigation?

options.A: CT of the chest
options.B: Serum protein electrophoresis, immunofixation and free light chains
options.C: Stop leflunomide and perform cholestyramine washout, confirming low plasma levels, while switching to a pregnancy-compatible DMARD
options.D: Pelvic imaging and CA-125 (ovarian cancer)
options.E: Thyroid function tests

explanation: Hypothyroid myopathy can mimic inflammatory myositis, with raised CK and proximal weakness, and is reversible with thyroxine. It should be excluded before invasive investigation for myositis. Muscle hypertrophy with stiffness (Hoffmann's syndrome) is a rare variant. Raised CK with weakness: myositis, hypothyroidism, statin or other drug myopathy (colchicine, HCQ, zidovudine, alcohol), muscular dystrophy, metabolic myopathy (McArdle, Pompe), hypokalaemia, hypophosphataemia, rhabdomyolysis, exercise, IM injection, macro-CK, African ancestry (higher baseline CK), cardiac troponin confusion. Hypothyroid myopathy occurs in 30–80% of untreated patients: proximal weakness, cramps, myalgia, slowrelaxing reflexes, CK 2–10× (sometimes higher). EMG is near-normal, MRI shows little oedema, and biopsy shows type II atrophy without inflammation. Hypothyroidism also raises statin myopathy risk. ANA and RF are often positive in autoimmune thyroid disease without CTD. Levothyroxine (myopathy resolves over weeks to months). Recheck CK and strength. Investigate for myositis only if weakness persists when euthyroid.

question: A 45-year-old man has early large-joint osteoarthritis, disc calcification, blue-black ear cartilage and urine that darkens on standing. Which treatment targets the metabolic defect?

options.A: Paternal low-dose methotrexate exposure is considered compatible with conception
options.B: Diabetic cheiroarthropathy (limited joint mobility)
options.C: Nitisinone
options.D: Immediate factor VIII replacement with rest, ice and analgesia
options.E: Serum IGF-1

explanation: Alkaptonuria (homogentisate dioxygenase deficiency) causes ochronosis: homogentisic acid deposits in cartilage, causing pigmentation and premature arthropathy. Nitisinone inhibits an upstream enzyme and markedly lowers homogentisic acid, slowing progression. Alkaptonuria (AR, HGD deficiency): dark urine on standing or alkalinisation, blue-black pigmentation of the ear and scleral cartilage, disc calcification with fusion (mimics AS), early spinal and large-joint arthropathy, tendon rupture, aortic stenosis, renal and prostatic stones. Diagnose with urinary homogentisic acid. Nitisinone (SONIA 2 trial; it raises tyrosine, so use a lowprotein diet and eye monitoring for keratopathy). Joint replacement, physiotherapy, cardiac surveillance.

question: A 19-year-old man with severe haemophilia A has an acutely painful, warm, swollen right knee after minor trauma. What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.A: Diffuse tenosynovial giant cell tumour (PVNS)
options.B: Immediate factor VIII replacement with rest, ice and analgesia
options.C: Avoid debridement (pathergy); give systemic immunosuppression
options.D: Acute Charcot foot: immediate offloading in a total contact cast and urgent MDT referral
options.E: Cardiac MRI and/or FDG-PET with Holter monitoring

explanation: Prompt factor replacement is the key treatment for haemarthrosis in haemophilia. Aspiration is not routine and is done only with factor cover if infection or a tense effusion is suspected. Recurrent bleeds lead to synovitis and haemophilic arthropathy, so prophylaxis is important. Recurrent haemarthroses cause synovitis and haemophilic arthropathy (knees, elbows, ankles), with "target joints" and pseudotumours. X-ray shows epiphyseal overgrowth, squared patella and widened intercondylar notch. Factor replacement or emicizumab prophylaxis, physiotherapy, radiosynovectomy for chronic synovitis, arthroplasty with factor cover. Avoid NSAIDs (use COX-2 cautiously); avoid IM injections. HCV and HIV screening in older patients (historical transfusion).

question: A teenager with sickle cell disease has fever and a painful swollen tibia. Apart from Staphylococcus aureus, which organism characteristically causes osteomyelitis in sickle cell disease?

options.A: Avoid debridement (pathergy); give systemic immunosuppression
options.B: Acute Charcot foot: immediate offloading in a total contact cast and urgent MDT referral
options.C: Salmonella species
options.D: Immediate factor VIII replacement with rest, ice and analgesia
options.E: Systemic glucocorticoids, while investigating the marrow

explanation: Functional hyposplenism and bowel infarction predispose people with sickle cell disease to Salmonella osteomyelitis, although S. aureus remains common. Bone infarction is far more frequent than osteomyelitis, so blood cultures and, where possible, bone or subperiosteal aspirate help guide therapy. Bone pain in sickle cell disease: vaso-occlusive bone infarction (far commoner) vs osteomyelitis (Salmonella, S. aureus), septic arthritis, AVN of the femoral or humeral head, dactylitis (hand–foot syndrome in infants), gout (increased turnover). Blood cultures and MRI (osteomyelitis vs infarct is difficult to separate), with aspirate or biopsy where feasible. Empirical cover for Salmonella and S. aureus (for example a third-generation cephalosporin plus an antistaphylococcal agent). Treat 6 weeks or more.

question: A 67-year-old man has back pain, weight loss, anaemia, hypercalcaemia, raised creatinine, normal ALP and a vertebral compression fracture. What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.A: CT of the chest
options.B: Cardiac MRI and/or FDG-PET with Holter monitoring
options.C: Serum protein electrophoresis, immunofixation and free light chains
options.D: Deep full-thickness biopsy including fascia
options.E: Paternal low-dose methotrexate exposure is considered compatible with conception

explanation: Anaemia, hypercalcaemia, renal impairment and bone lesions suggest myeloma. ALP is usually normal and bone scans are often falsely negative, because myeloma lesions are purely lytic. Serum protein electrophoresis, immunofixation and free light chains are the key tests, followed by whole-body low-dose CT or MRI. Back pain with hypercalcaemia and anaemia: myeloma, metastases (breast, prostate, lung, kidney), lymphoma or ATLL, hyperparathyroidism with osteoporotic fracture, sarcoid with vertebral fracture, TB spondylitis. CRAB: calcium >2.75 mmol/L (or >0.25 above ULN), renal (creatinine >177 µmol/L or CrCl <40), anaemia (Hb <100 g/L), bone (≥1 lytic lesion ≥5 mm). SLiM: ≥60% marrow plasma cells, FLC ratio ≥100, >1 MRI focal lesion. SPEP + immunofixation + FLC detects >97%. Renal disease is mainly cast nephropathy, plus AL or LCDD and Fanconi syndrome. Whole-body low-dose CT (has replaced the skeletal survey), PET-CT or whole-body MRI, bone marrow with FISH, R2-ISS staging. Urgent haematology referral. Hydrate and avoid NSAIDs and contrast. Bisphosphonate or denosumab for all treated patients. Vertebral augmentation for painful fractures. Daratumumab-based quadruplets; CAR-T and bispecifics for relapse.

question: A 63-year-old smoker has painful swelling of the ankles and wrists, finger clubbing, and tenderness over the distal tibiae. Radiographs show smooth periosteal new bone along the tibial and fibular diaphyses. What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.A: Immediate factor VIII replacement with rest, ice and analgesia
options.B: Diabetic cheiroarthropathy (limited joint mobility)
options.C: Serum protein electrophoresis, immunofixation and free light chains
options.D: Look for an underlying malignancy
options.E: CT of the chest

explanation: Hypertrophic pulmonary osteoarthropathy (clubbing, periostitis and arthropathy) is strongly associated with intrathoracic malignancy, particularly non-small cell lung cancer, and also with chronic lung suppuration and cyanotic heart disease. Bone scintigraphy shows parallel 'tram-line' cortical uptake. Symptoms may improve after tumour resection. Secondary HOA causes: NSCLC (commonest), mesothelioma, metastases; bronchiectasis, CF, lung abscess, ILD; cyanotic heart disease, infective endocarditis; IBD, cirrhosis, coeliac disease; thyroid acropachy (Graves'); localised forms (infected vascular grafts, aneurysms). Clubbing without periostitis: the same list. Primary HOA (pachydermoperiostosis; HPGD or SLCO2A1; adolescent boys) features pachydermia, cutis verticis gyrata and hyperhidrosis. Secondary HOA (about 90% of adult cases) is caused by megakaryocyte or platelet clumps bypassing the lung, releasing VEGF and PDGF, plus raised PGE2. Bone pain is worse on dependency and eased by elevation. Synovial fluid is non-inflammatory. Treat the cause (tumour resection can produce dramatic improvement). NSAIDs or COX-2 inhibitors. IV bisphosphonates (pamidronate, zoledronate) for pain. Octreotide or anti-VEGF in refractory cases.

question: A 79-year-old man develops sudden, symmetrical synovitis of both wrists and hands with marked pitting oedema of the dorsum of both hands. RF and anti-CCP are negative. He improves rapidly on low-dose prednisolone. Which additional step is most appropriate?

options.A: Glucocorticoids at the lowest effective dose (moderate-dose prednisolone), usually continuing immunotherapy in discussion with oncology, with an early csDMARD or a biologic (TNF or IL-6 inhibition) if steroid- dependent
options.B: Look for an underlying malignancy
options.C: Paternal low-dose methotrexate exposure is considered compatible with conception
options.D: Pelvic imaging and CA-125 (ovarian cancer)
options.E: Deep full-thickness biopsy including fascia

explanation: RS3PE (remitting seronegative symmetrical synovitis with pitting oedema) typically affects older men and responds well to low-dose glucocorticoids. It can be paraneoplastic, with solid tumours and haematological malignancies reported. A poor steroid response or systemic features should prompt a search for cancer. Elderly-onset symmetrical synovitis with oedema: RS3PE vs PMR with distal oedema (overlapping), elderly-onset RA (ACPA), CPPD, PsA, SpA, paraneoplastic arthritis, DPP-4 inhibitor-associated RS3PE, heart failure, nephrotic syndrome, hypothyroidism. Prednisolone 10–15 mg gives a rapid response (taper over months). Screen for malignancy (CT, SPEP, PSA, ageappropriate tests), especially with a poor steroid response, constitutional symptoms or very high ESR. HCQ for steroid sparing. Associated cancers are found in up to about 25%.

question: A patient on pembrolizumab (for example for melanoma, tumour responding) develops seronegative inflammatory polyarthritis that persists and limits function despite NSAIDs. What is the most appropriate management? Also tested as: A 61-year-old man on pembrolizumab for melanoma develops symmetrical polyarthritis 3 months into treatment. RF and anti-CCP are negative and symptoms persist despite NSAIDs. What is the most appropriate step?

options.A: Glucocorticoids at the lowest effective dose (moderate-dose prednisolone), usually continuing immunotherapy in discussion with oncology, with an early csDMARD or a biologic (TNF or IL-6 inhibition) if steroid- dependent
options.B: Look for an underlying malignancy
options.C: Paternal low-dose methotrexate exposure is considered compatible with conception
options.D: Pelvic imaging and CA-125 (ovarian cancer)
options.E: Thyroid function tests

explanation: Immune checkpoint inhibitor-induced arthritis is often persistent. Rheumatology input, glucocorticoids at the lowest effective dose and early steroid-sparing csDMARDs are recommended; TNF or IL-6 receptor inhibitors are options for refractory disease. Close collaboration with oncology aims to control arthritis while continuing cancer immunotherapy where possible, and immunotherapy can usually continue for arthritis that is not life-threatening, through shared decision with oncology. New arthritis during cancer therapy: ICI arthritis vs aromatase inhibitor arthralgia, paraneoplastic arthritis, bone metastases, G-CSF bone pain, crystal arthritis (tumour lysis), septic arthritis (neutropenia), BRAF or MEK inhibitor arthralgia. Rheumatic irAEs affect about 5–10% of ICI recipients: RAlike, PMR-like or SpA-like arthritis (usually seronegative, sometimes persisting after stopping the ICI), sicca, myositis (with myocarditis and myasthenia), GCA-like vasculitis, sarcoid-like reactions, lupus-like disease. Anti-CTLA-4 plus anti-PD-1 combinations carry the highest risk. Pre-existing autoimmune disease is not an absolute contraindication, but flares are common. Grade by CTCAE. Grade 1: NSAIDs, IA steroid. Grade 2: prednisolone 10–20 mg. Grade 3–4: 0.5–1 mg/kg, hold the ICI, then steroid-sparing methotrexate, SSZ or HCQ, then IL-6R or TNFi. Check troponin and CK if myalgia or weakness occurs (3M overlap). Screen for HBV, HCV and TB before biologics.

question: A 59-year-old woman develops rapidly progressive bilateral palmar thickening with flexion contractures of the fingers ('woody hands') and an inflammatory polyarthritis. Nailfold capillaroscopy is normal. Which investigation is most important?

options.A: Diabetic cheiroarthropathy (limited joint mobility)
options.B: Pelvic imaging and CA-125 (ovarian cancer)
options.C: Look for an underlying malignancy
options.D: Thyroid function tests
options.E: Serum protein electrophoresis, immunofixation and free light chains

explanation: Palmar fasciitis and polyarthritis syndrome is a paraneoplastic disorder strongly associated with ovarian carcinoma, and also with other adenocarcinomas. It can precede the diagnosis of cancer and responds poorly to immunosuppression. It can resemble Dupuytren's disease or scleroderma, but onset is rapid and inflammatory. PFPAS (palmar fasciitis and polyarthritis syndrome): rapid "woody" palmar thickening with flexion contractures, polyarthritis, swollen hands, nodules. It is strongly associated with ovarian cancer, and also pancreatic, breast, lung and gastric adenocarcinoma. It may precede the cancer and responds poorly to immunosuppression. Pelvic and transvaginal ultrasound, CA-125, CT chest, abdomen and pelvis or PET-CT. Treating the tumour may improve the hands. Hand therapy. Other paraneoplastic syndromes to remember: carcinomatous polyarthritis, panniculitis–arthritis–pancreatitis syndrome (lipase, pancreatic acinar carcinoma), Lambert–Eaton (VGCC; SCLC), erythromelalgia (MPN), paraneoplastic Raynaud's or digital ischaemia.

question: A woman with inflammatory arthritis plans pregnancy in the next year. What is the best overall plan?

options.A: Low-dose aspirin to reduce the risk of pre-eclampsia
options.B: Switch to azathioprine (with or without tacrolimus), stopping mycophenolate at least 6 weeks before conception, and confirm stable disease before conceiving
options.C: At least 1 month before conception, continuing folic acid
options.D: Hydroxychloroquine, sulfasalazine and azathioprine
options.E: Preconception counselling aiming for low disease activity on pregnancy-compatible medicines for several months before conception

explanation: Active disease itself increases risks such as pre-eclampsia, preterm birth and growth restriction, so planned transition to compatible therapy before conception is ideal. Why outcomes go wrong in inflammatory arthritis pregnancy: active disease (the main driver; DAS28-CRP >3.2), prednisolone >7.5 mg, NSAID-related subfertility, unplanned conception on a teratogen, undiagnosed aPL or anti-Ro, unrecognised cervical spine instability (anaesthesia), postpartum flare after stopping treatment. RA improves in about 50–65% (more in seronegative disease) but often with moderate residual activity; 40–60% flare within 3–6 months postpartum. axSpA usually does not improve (worse night pain in the second trimester; 50– 80% flare postpartum). Psoriasis often improves; PsA behaves more like RA. Time to pregnancy is longer with active disease, NSAIDs and prednisolone >7.5 mg/day; methotrexate does not prolong it once stopped. 1. Before conception: treat to remission; switch MTX or leflunomide to sulfasalazine and/or HCQ ± a TNF inhibitor (certolizumab if needed throughout); screen aPL and anti-Ro/La where relevant; folic acid; rubella and varicella immunity; review cervical spine in longstanding RA. 2. During pregnancy: assess activity each trimester with DAS28-CRP (ESR rises physiologically); avoid NSAIDs late; lowest-dose prednisolone or intra-articular steroid for flares. 3. Third trimester: anaesthetic review (cervical spine, hips, lumbar ankylosis). 4. Postpartum: review at 6–12 weeks and restart treatment promptly; breastfeeding does not worsen RA. Disease activity, not the diagnosis, drives risk of pre-eclampsia, preterm birth, SGA and caesarean section. A Danish registry linked miscarriage to younger women with recently diagnosed (active) RA. Continuing TNF inhibitors late in pregnancy, or restarting promptly, lowers postpartum flare risk.

question: Which DMARDs are generally considered compatible with pregnancy?

options.A: Low-dose aspirin to reduce the risk of pre-eclampsia
options.B: Give routine non-live vaccines as scheduled, but defer live vaccines until 6 months of age
options.C: Hydroxychloroquine, sulfasalazine and azathioprine
options.D: Certolizumab pegol
options.E: Preconception counselling aiming for low disease activity on pregnancy-compatible medicines for several months before conception

explanation: The 2024 EULAR recommendations also list colchicine, ciclosporin and tacrolimus as compatible, and TNF inhibitors can be used throughout pregnancy; prednisolone is tapered to 5 mg/day or less where possible. Sulfasalazine should be given with folic acid 5 mg daily. Not compatible: methotrexate, leflunomide (unless washed out), mycophenolate, cyclophosphamide (except lifethreatening disease after the first trimester), JAK inhibitors, thalidomide, warfarin (switch before week 6), ACE inhibitors and ARBs, endothelin receptor antagonists (bosentan, ambrisentan, macitentan). Limited data: rituximab, tocilizumab, abatacept, anakinra, IL-17 and IL-23 inhibitors, belimumab — use only if no compatible alternative controls disease. Compatible in pregnancy (2024 EULAR and the course agree): HCQ, sulfasalazine (with folic acid 5 mg), azathioprine (≤2 mg/kg), ciclosporin, tacrolimus, colchicine, IVIG, LMWH, low-dose aspirin, prednisolone and TNF inhibitors. Prednisolone target: the source explanation cites tapering to ≤5 mg/day where possible; the EULAR course table gives ≤7.5–10 mg/day. Long-term doses above 10–15 mg/day raise GDM, hypertension, preeclampsia, PROM, infection and preterm birth. Use prednisolone (not dexamethasone or betamethasone) for maternal disease, because placental 11β-HSD2 inactivates most of it. Give stress-dose hydrocortisone at delivery after prolonged use above 5 mg/day. IV methylprednisolone pulses are acceptable for severe flares. Among biologics with limited data, anakinra and rituximab (given before conception) have the most experience. Belimumab may be continued in SLE when needed for disease control; registry data are reassuring. Accidental first-trimester biologic exposure is not a reason to terminate.

question: A 30-year-old woman with RA on methotrexate 20 mg weekly plans to conceive. When should methotrexate be stopped? Also tested as: What is an absolute contraindication to methotrexate?

options.A: Optimise it: increase to 20–25 mg weekly, switch to subcutaneous administration (better bioavailability and tolerability), optimise folic acid and reassess within 1–3 months
options.B: Paternal low-dose methotrexate exposure is considered compatible with conception
options.C: At least 1 month before conception, continuing folic acid
options.D: Add an IL-17 or IL-23 inhibitor
options.E: Before conception, after the post-treatment contraception interval in the product information

explanation: Methotrexate is teratogenic and is stopped before conception; UK (BSR) guidance advises at least 1 month before, replaced by a compatible drug, and continuing folic acid. Inadvertent first-trimester exposure warrants stopping, high-dose folic acid and specialist fetal assessment. Timing advice varies: BSR — stop ≥1 month before conception; 2024 EULAR and the EULAR course — stop 1–3 months before. Many clinicians use 3 months as the cautious figure. Continue high-dose folic acid (5 mg daily) through the first trimester. Methotrexate is teratogenic and abortifacient (aminopterin or methotrexate embryopathy: craniofacial, limb and CNS anomalies; miscarriage). This is why pregnancy is its absolute contraindication. Relative contraindications or cautions include moderate renal impairment (dose reduction), heavy alcohol use, significant liver disease, active serious infection, and pre-existing significant lung disease; older age alone is not a contraindication. Severe renal impairment (eGFR <30) is usually treated as a contraindication. Plan the switch (sulfasalazine, HCQ, TNF inhibitor) and confirm control before stopping contraception. Inadvertent exposure: stop the drug immediately; folic acid 5 mg; early fetal assessment and detailed anomaly scan; report to a pregnancy registry; switch to a compatible drug to prevent flare. Absolute malformation risk with low-dose MTX exposure is about 6–10% vs a background of 3–4%, often lower than patients fear — exposure is not by itself an indication for termination.

question: A 34-year-old man with PsA on methotrexate 15 mg weekly asks whether he must stop it before trying for a baby. What is the correct advice? Also tested as: A 35-year-old man with RA controlled on sulfasalazine and his partner are planning pregnancy. What is the most appropriate advice?

options.A: Switch to a pregnancy-compatible antihypertensive such as labetalol or nifedipine before conception or
options.B: Avoid NSAIDs in the third trimester because of the risk of premature ductus arteriosus closure and oligohydramnios
options.C: Paternal low-dose methotrexate exposure is considered compatible with conception
options.D: At least 1 month before conception, continuing folic acid
options.E: TNF inhibitors are compatible with breastfeeding

explanation: The 2024 EULAR recommendations state that men trying to conceive may continue methotrexate at 25 mg/week or less; data show no increase in miscarriage or malformations. Cyclophosphamide is the main drug where paternal exposure is a concern (dose-related irreversible infertility). Male subfertility in rheumatic disease: sulfasalazine oligospermia, cyclophosphamide gonadotoxicity, active inflammation, erectile dysfunction (vascular disease, depression, drugs), hypogonadism from chronic glucocorticoids or opioids, varicocele, Behçet's epididymoorchitis, mumps orchitis, unrelated female-partner factors. Paternal exposure — EULAR course summary: Drug Advice for fathers Stop ≥3 months before Cyclophosphamide conception; offer sperm banking Can be continued (2024 Methotrexate EULAR: ≤25 mg/week); no increase in miscarriage or malformations Mycophenolate Can be continued Azathioprine, HCQ, TNF Can be continued inhibitors, most biologics Can be continued; reversible Sulfasalazine oligospermia (recovers ~3 months after stopping) Limited data, no harm signal JAK inhibitors (2024 EULAR suggests considering a switch) Thalidomide Condoms required Reassure for most drugs. If conception is delayed beyond 12 months on sulfasalazine, perform semen analysis, consider switching, and investigate both partners. Offer sperm banking before cyclophosphamide.

question: A 31-year-old woman on leflunomide wishes to conceive within 6 months. What is the most appropriate advice?

options.A: Paternal low-dose methotrexate exposure is considered compatible with conception
options.B: Take part in cervical screening, with consideration of more frequent screening and HPV vaccination because of increased risk
options.C: Switch to a pregnancy-compatible antihypertensive such as labetalol or nifedipine before conception or
options.D: Neonatal lupus, including congenital heart block
options.E: Stop leflunomide and perform cholestyramine washout, confirming low plasma levels, while switching to a pregnancy-compatible DMARD

explanation: The active metabolite persists for up to 2 years. Washout is cholestyramine 8 g three times daily for 11 days, with two plasma levels below 0.02 mg/L 14 days apart. Teriflunomide (active metabolite) has enterohepatic recirculation and can persist for up to 2 years. Washout: cholestyramine 8 g three times daily for 11 days (alternative: activated charcoal 50 g four times daily for 11 days), then confirm two plasma levels <0.02 mg/L at least 14 days apart. Switch to a compatible DMARD during or before washout. Use effective contraception until levels are confirmed. Cholestyramine reduces absorption of other drugs (including oral contraceptives), so use additional contraception during washout. The EULAR course notes that leflunomide can be continued until conception if washout is started promptly once pregnancy is confirmed; exposed pregnancies with prompt washout show no excess malformations, so the old 2-year wait without washout is no longer needed. This is a more permissive approach than many UK practices, which still prefer pre-conception washout.

question: A woman with lupus nephritis on mycophenolate plans pregnancy. What is the most appropriate approach?

options.A: Blood pressure control with ACE inhibitor or ARB for proteinuria, lipid management, and an SGLT2 inhibitor where appropriate
options.B: Switch to azathioprine (with or without tacrolimus), stopping mycophenolate at least 6 weeks before conception, and confirm stable disease before conceiving
options.C: Low-dose aspirin to reduce the risk of pre-eclampsia
options.D: Take part in cervical screening, with consideration of more frequent screening and HPV vaccination because of increased risk
options.E: Preconception counselling aiming for low disease activity on pregnancy-compatible medicines for several months before conception

explanation: Mycophenolate causes orofacial clefts, ear and limb anomalies. Disease should be quiescent for at least 6 months on the new regimen, and hydroxychloroquine continued. Predictors of poor outcome in SLE pregnancy (PROMISSE and others): active disease or LN in the 6 months before conception, lupus anticoagulant, hypertension, thrombocytopenia, prior LN, prednisolone >10 mg, non- White ethnicity. Advise against pregnancy with severe PAH, severe restrictive lung disease, advanced CKD, heart failure, or severe flare or stroke within 6 months. Mycophenolate embryopathy: microtia or ear canal atresia, cleft lip and palate, micrognathia, hypertelorism, limb and heart defects, and first-trimester miscarriage (up to ~45%). Pregnancy prevention programme with two forms of contraception. Switch MMF to azathioprine ± tacrolimus, stop MMF ≥6 weeks before conception, and confirm stability on the new regimen (EULAR course: ~3 months; LN inactive ≥6 months overall). Continue HCQ; start low-dose aspirin; stop ACEi or ARB at conception and use labetalol or nifedipine; baseline creatinine, uPCR, complement, anti-dsDNA, aPL and anti- Ro/La. Renal risk is highest with creatinine >1.5 mg/dL (~130 µmol/L), proteinuria >1 g/day or hypertension. About 80% of women with stable mild-to-moderate SLE in PROMISSE had no adverse outcome.

question: A woman with RA on tofacitinib wants to conceive. When should tofacitinib be stopped?

options.A: Avoid NSAIDs in the third trimester because of the risk of premature ductus arteriosus closure and oligohydramnios
options.B: At least 1 month before conception, continuing folic acid
options.C: TNF inhibitors are compatible with breastfeeding
options.D: Stop leflunomide and perform cholestyramine washout, confirming low plasma levels, while switching to a pregnancy-compatible DMARD
options.E: Before conception, after the post-treatment contraception interval in the product information

explanation: JAK inhibitors have animal teratogenicity and insufficient human data, so the 2024 EULAR recommendations advise avoiding them in pregnancy and breastfeeding. They should be stopped before conception, observing the contraception interval in the product information. For men, data are limited and EULAR suggests considering a switch when trying to conceive. JAK inhibitors are small molecules that cross the placenta and are teratogenic in animals; human data remain insufficient. They are also avoided during breastfeeding. Stop 1–3 months before conception (follow the product's contraception interval; it varies by agent). Bridge to a compatible strategy before stopping: TNF inhibitor (certolizumab if continued throughout) ± sulfasalazine or HCQ. Inadvertent exposure: stop, specialist fetal assessment, registry report.

question: A 28-year-old woman with active axial SpA needs a TNF inhibitor and wants to continue it throughout pregnancy and breastfeeding with minimal placental transfer. Which drug is most suitable?

options.A: Before conception, after the post-treatment contraception interval in the product information
options.B: TNF inhibitors are compatible with breastfeeding
options.C: Consider gradual tapering of the TNF inhibitor rather than stopping it
options.D: Certolizumab pegol
options.E: Low-dose aspirin to reduce the risk of pre-eclampsia

explanation: Certolizumab lacks an Fc region, so active placental transfer is minimal. Other TNF inhibitors are also compatible, often with consideration of stopping later in pregnancy if disease is quiescent to reduce infant exposure. Certolizumab pegol is a PEGylated Fab' fragment with no Fc region, so it is not actively transported by the neonatal Fc receptor (FcRn). The CRIB study found no or minimal cord blood levels, and CRADLE showed negligible transfer into milk. Infliximab, adalimumab and golimumab (IgG1) cross actively in the third trimester; etanercept (fusion protein with Fc) crosses less than infliximab or adalimumab. In stable disease, other TNF inhibitors are often stopped at about 20–32 weeks to limit infant exposure, but can be continued if needed (risk of postpartum flare if stopped). Certolizumab is preferred when active treatment is needed in late pregnancy. In axSpA: NSAIDs only before 20 weeks; sulfasalazine for peripheral disease; switch IL-17 or IL-23 inhibitors to a TNF inhibitor when planning, unless refractory. axSpA flares in the second trimester and 50–80% flare at 4–12 weeks postpartum; uveitis can flare. Lumbar ankylosis may make neuraxial anaesthesia difficult and hip disease may limit vaginal delivery, so arrange anaesthetic review in the third trimester.

question: A woman with spondyloarthritis received adalimumab throughout pregnancy, with the last dose at 36 weeks. Her baby is now 6 weeks old. What vaccination advice is correct?

options.A: Paternal low-dose methotrexate exposure is considered compatible with conception
options.B: Avoid NSAIDs in the third trimester because of the risk of premature ductus arteriosus closure and oligohydramnios
options.C: Continue hydroxychloroquine throughout pregnancy and breastfeeding
options.D: Low-dose aspirin to reduce the risk of pre-eclampsia
options.E: Give routine non-live vaccines as scheduled, but defer live vaccines until 6 months of age

explanation: Infants exposed to TNF inhibitors (other than certolizumab) in later pregnancy may have detectable drug for months. National advice on specific live vaccines, such as rotavirus, should be checked. Fc-containing monoclonal antibodies given in the third trimester can be detectable in the infant for 6–12 months (longest with infliximab). Inactivated vaccines should be given on schedule. Certolizumab exposure does not require a delay. Defer live vaccines for the first 6 months after thirdtrimester exposure; in practice in the UK this mainly affects BCG (deferred) and oral rotavirus vaccine (withheld or given only on specialist advice) — check the current national schedule (Green Book). After late-pregnancy rituximab exposure, check the infant's B-cell count before live vaccines. Tell the paediatrician and health visitor about the exposure. Neonatal infection rates in exposed infants are similar to unexposed infants.

question: A 27-year-old woman with SLE on hydroxychloroquine 200 mg twice daily is 6 weeks pregnant. Her disease is quiescent. What is the correct advice?

options.A: Avoid NSAIDs in the third trimester because of the risk of premature ductus arteriosus closure and oligohydramnios
options.B: Switch to a pregnancy-compatible antihypertensive such as labetalol or nifedipine before conception or
options.C: Continue hydroxychloroquine throughout pregnancy and breastfeeding
options.D: Neonatal lupus, including congenital heart block
options.E: Low-dose aspirin to reduce the risk of pre-eclampsia

explanation: Stopping hydroxychloroquine increases flare risk. It also reduces the risk of congenital heart block in anti-Ro-positive women. SLE pregnancy complications to anticipate: flare (second and third trimesters, postpartum), pre-eclampsia (10–30%) and HELLP, fetal growth restriction, preterm birth (~20– 30%), miscarriage and stillbirth, maternal thrombosis, neonatal lupus. HCQ in SLE pregnancy reduces flares, pre-eclampsia, preterm birth and congenital heart block (anti-Ro-positive women). Withdrawal increases flare risk. It is compatible with breastfeeding. Continue screening for retinopathy as usual (doses ≤5 mg/kg/day actual body weight). Continue HCQ; low-dose aspirin from before 16 weeks (ideally ~12 weeks); azathioprine, ciclosporin or tacrolimus as steroid-sparing agents; IVIG for severe thrombocytopenia or refractory disease; calcium and vitamin D (especially on steroids or heparin); monitor BP, urinalysis, platelets, complement and anti-dsDNA each trimester; uterine artery Doppler at 20–24 weeks; serial growth scans.

question: A pregnant woman with RA at 33 weeks' gestation has a flare and asks to take naproxen. What is the correct advice?

options.A: Paternal low-dose methotrexate exposure is considered compatible with conception
options.B: Continue hydroxychloroquine throughout pregnancy and breastfeeding
options.C: Rising anti-dsDNA with falling complement and an active urinary sediment
options.D: TNF inhibitors are compatible with breastfeeding
options.E: Avoid NSAIDs in the third trimester because of the risk of premature ductus arteriosus closure and oligohydramnios

explanation: The 2024 EULAR recommendations advise using NSAIDs only intermittently in pregnancy, preferring short-acting non-selective agents such as ibuprofen, and stopping them after 28 weeks because of premature ductus closure and oligohydramnios. Prednisolone or intra-articular steroid are safer late in pregnancy. Non-selective NSAIDs are compatible with breastfeeding. Cut-offs differ: 2024 EULAR — stop after 28 weeks; EULAR course — avoid from 20 weeks and stop by 28–32 weeks. Selective COX-2 inhibitors have insufficient pregnancy data. NSAIDs inhibit prostaglandin synthesis: premature closure of the ductus arteriosus (third trimester), fetal renal dysfunction and oligohydramnios (from about 20 weeks; FDA 2020 warning), and possibly miscarriage if used around conception. They also impair ovulation (luteinised unruptured follicle). Late-pregnancy flare: oral prednisolone at the lowest effective dose, intra-articular steroid for monoarticular flares, paracetamol, physiotherapy, or a TNF inhibitor if sustained. Ibuprofen is compatible with breastfeeding.

question: A 34-year-old woman with SLE and hypertension takes ramipril and wishes to conceive. What is the most appropriate advice?

options.A: Switch to a pregnancy-compatible antihypertensive such as labetalol or nifedipine before conception or
options.B: Stop leflunomide and perform cholestyramine washout, confirming low plasma levels, while switching to a pregnancy-compatible DMARD
options.C: Continue hydroxychloroquine throughout pregnancy and breastfeeding
options.D: Take part in cervical screening, with consideration of more frequent screening and HPV vaccination because of increased risk
options.E: Paternal low-dose methotrexate exposure is considered compatible with conception

explanation: as soon as pregnancy is confirmed ACE inhibitors and ARBs are fetotoxic in the second and third trimesters. Enalapril and captopril are compatible with breastfeeding. ACE inhibitors and ARBs are fetotoxic in the second and third trimesters (fetal renal failure, oligohydramnios, skull hypoplasia, growth restriction, neonatal hypotension). Firsttrimester exposure carries lower risk; stop on confirmation of pregnancy. Pregnancy-compatible antihypertensives: labetalol (first line), nifedipine (modified release), methyldopa (avoid postpartum because of depression). Postpartum: enalapril or captopril are compatible with breastfeeding and useful for proteinuria. Target BP ≤135/85 mmHg in pregnancy (NICE). Exception: scleroderma renal crisis — ACE inhibitors are still used in pregnancy because they save the mother's life. Risk is highest in early diffuse disease (<4 years), anti-RNA polymerase III positivity and steroids >15 mg/day, and renal crisis can mimic pre-eclampsia.

question: A woman with RA controlled on etanercept has just given birth and wants to breastfeed. What is the correct advice? Also tested as: A patient asks whether she can continue methotrexate while breastfeeding. What is the safest advice?

options.A: Paternal low-dose methotrexate exposure is considered compatible with conception
options.B: Before conception, after the post-treatment contraception interval in the product information
options.C: At least 1 month before conception, continuing folic acid
options.D: Avoid NSAIDs in the third trimester because of the risk of premature ductus arteriosus closure and oligohydramnios
options.E: TNF inhibitors are compatible with breastfeeding

explanation: TNF inhibitors pass into milk in very small amounts and are poorly absorbed by the infant. Methotrexate in breastfeeding — guidance differs: BSR advises against it; the EULAR course table lists it as not compatible; the 2024 EULAR recommendations allow lowdose MTX (≤25 mg/week) to be considered only when no compatible alternative exists (some advise withholding feeds for 24 hours after a dose). Breastfeeding-compatible: HCQ, sulfasalazine (healthy term infants), azathioprine, ciclosporin, tacrolimus, colchicine, prednisolone (if >20 mg, delay feeding by 4 hours), TNF inhibitors (large proteins with minimal oral absorption), most other biologics likely compatible, ibuprofen, warfarin, LMWH, enalapril and captopril. Avoid: methotrexate (see below), leflunomide, mycophenolate, cyclophosphamide, JAK inhibitors, thalidomide. Do not make women choose between breastfeeding and treatment: restart compatible therapy early postpartum. Check for neonatal jaundice or prematurity before sulfasalazine. Review postnatal depression, thyroiditis and bone health.

question: A 29-year-old woman with SLE and previous lupus nephritis is planning pregnancy. Her disease has been quiescent for 9 months on hydroxychloroquine and azathioprine. Which additional medication should be started from 12 weeks of pregnancy?

options.A: Continue hydroxychloroquine throughout pregnancy and breastfeeding
options.B: Low-dose aspirin to reduce the risk of pre-eclampsia
options.C: Paternal low-dose methotrexate exposure is considered compatible with conception
options.D: Neonatal lupus, including congenital heart block
options.E: Switch to azathioprine (with or without tacrolimus), stopping mycophenolate at least 6 weeks before conception, and confirm stable disease before conceiving

explanation: SLE, particularly with renal disease or aPL, increases pre-eclampsia risk. Low-dose aspirin (75–150 mg nightly; NICE uses 75–150 mg) from 12 weeks (before 16 weeks) until delivery or about 36 weeks reduces pre-eclampsia. Indications include SLE, APS or aPL, CKD, chronic hypertension, diabetes, previous hypertensive disease of pregnancy, and moderate risk factors combined (first pregnancy, age ≥40, BMI ≥35, multiple pregnancy, family history). Add LMWH if APS (prophylactic for obstetric APS; therapeutic for thrombotic APS) or other thrombotic risk. Monitor BP, urine protein, platelets and renal function; uterine artery Doppler at 20–24 weeks; sFlt-1/PlGF ratio when pre-eclampsia is suspected. Continue HCQ and azathioprine. APS in pregnancy: aPL-positive without events → aspirin (± 6 weeks' postpartum LMWH if high-risk profile); obstetric APS → aspirin + prophylactic LMWH from a positive test, LMWH for 6 weeks postpartum; thrombotic APS → therapeutic LMWH (switch warfarin before week 6) + aspirin, restart warfarin postpartum; refractory obstetric APS → add HCQ, low-dose prednisolone in the first trimester, IVIG or higher-dose LMWH. Live-birth rates with standard therapy are about 70–80%.

question: A pregnant woman with SLE and anti-Ro/SSA antibodies asks about risks to her baby. Which fetal risk should be discussed? Also tested as: A 31-year-old woman with SLE and anti-Ro antibodies is 8 weeks pregnant. Her previous baby had congenital heart block. What is the most appropriate management?

options.A: Continue hydroxychloroquine throughout pregnancy and breastfeeding
options.B: Switch to a pregnancy-compatible antihypertensive such as labetalol or nifedipine before conception or
options.C: Rising anti-dsDNA with falling complement and an active urinary sediment
options.D: Avoid NSAIDs in the third trimester because of the risk of premature ductus arteriosus closure and oligohydramnios
options.E: Neonatal lupus, including congenital heart block

explanation: Anti-Ro and anti-La cross the placenta. Heart block typically develops between 16 and 26 weeks and is often irreversible; neonatal lupus rash is transient. Fetal bradycardia: CHB (anti-Ro), structural heart disease (left atrial isomerism, congenitally corrected transposition), long QT, fetal distress, maternal β-blockers, sinus node dysfunction. Anti-Ro (Ro52 and Ro60) and anti-La IgG cross the placenta from about 16 weeks. The mother may have SLE, Sjögren's, UCTD, or no disease. Cutaneous neonatal lupus affects 15–25% of exposed infants (annular periorbital "raccoon eye" rash, cytopenias, transaminitis), clearing by 6–8 months. Congenital heart block: ~1–2% in a first pregnancy, ~15–18% after one affected child, ~50% after two; higher anti-Ro60 titres carry more risk. Mortality is ~15–20% and 60–70% need pacing; endocardial fibroelastosis and cardiomyopathy can also occur. 1. HCQ for every anti-Ro-positive pregnancy, started before 10 weeks (PATCH: CHB recurrence fell from ~18% to ~7.5%). 2. Fetal echocardiography (mechanical PR interval) weekly or every 2 weeks from 16 to 26 weeks; twice-daily home handheld Doppler allows detection within hours. 3. Complete block is irreversible: fluorinated steroids do not reverse it and cause fetal harm, so they are not routine. First- or second-degree block or myocarditis may be treated with dexamethasone ± IVIG in a fetal medicine centre (limited evidence). 4. Deliver where neonatal cardiology and pacing are available; check the baby's ECG, skin, FBC and LFTs.

question: A pregnant woman with SLE develops new hypertension and proteinuria at 30 weeks. Which feature favours a lupus flare over pre-eclampsia?

options.A: Neonatal lupus, including congenital heart block
options.B: Rising anti-dsDNA with falling complement and an active urinary sediment
options.C: Switch to a pregnancy-compatible antihypertensive such as labetalol or nifedipine before conception or
options.D: Continue hydroxychloroquine throughout pregnancy and breastfeeding
options.E: Avoid NSAIDs in the third trimester because of the risk of premature ductus arteriosus closure and oligohydramnios

explanation: The two can be hard to distinguish and may coexist. Active serology and red cell casts favour a flare, whereas new hypertension, abnormal LFTs, low platelets and stable complement favour pre-eclampsia. New hypertension and proteinuria in SLE pregnancy: LN flare, pre-eclampsia (can coexist), HELLP, APS nephropathy or catastrophic APS, TTP or atypical HUS, scleroderma renal crisis (overlap), acute fatty liver of pregnancy, pre-existing CKD revealed by pregnancy. Distinguishing features: Feature LN flare Pre-eclampsia Any time, After 20 weeks Timing including before 20 weeks Active (red cells, Urinary Bland red cell casts) sediment Falling C3/C4 Complement Normal or rising (physiological rise) Anti-dsDNA Rising Stable Uric acid Normal Raised LFTs, Raised transaminases, Usually normal (unless SLE low platelets (HELLP) platelets cytopenia) sFlt-1/PlGF Normal High ratio Rash, arthritis, Absent; headache, Other SLE visual disturbance, features serositis epigastric pain After delivery Persists Improves Joint rheumatology–obstetric–renal care. Renal biopsy is possible before about 28 weeks if the result would change management. LN flare: steroids (including IV pulses), azathioprine, tacrolimus. Pre-eclampsia: BP control (labetalol, nifedipine), magnesium sulfate for severe disease, and delivery timing.

question: A patient with SLE on mycophenolate and prednisolone asks about cervical screening. What is the most appropriate advice?

options.A: Stop leflunomide and perform cholestyramine washout, confirming low plasma levels, while switching to a pregnancy-compatible DMARD
options.B: Take part in cervical screening, with consideration of more frequent screening and HPV vaccination because of increased risk
options.C: Switch to a pregnancy-compatible antihypertensive such as labetalol or nifedipine before conception or
options.D: Urgent assessment and treatment for neutropenic sepsis, with review of drug toxicity
options.E: Paternal low-dose methotrexate exposure is considered compatible with conception

explanation: Women with SLE, especially on immunosuppression, have more HPV infection and cervical dysplasia. Other malignancy risks in SLE: non-Hodgkin lymphoma, vulvovaginal, anal and lung cancers, and bladder cancer after cyclophosphamide; lower risk of breast, endometrial and possibly prostate cancer. Women with SLE have more persistent high-risk HPV infection, cervical dysplasia and cervical cancer than the general population; risk is higher with immunosuppression (cyclophosphamide, mycophenolate, azathioprine, glucocorticoids). Similar concerns apply to other heavily immunosuppressed patients (e.g. after transplant, or on long-term biologics). Encourage participation in the national cervical screening programme; some guidance advises more frequent screening for heavily immunosuppressed women (local policy varies — UK NHS screening for most immunosuppressed women follows the standard schedule, with annual screening for women with HIV). Offer HPV vaccination (non-live, safe on immunosuppression; EULAR 2019 vaccination recommendations support it in SLE), ideally before or early in immunosuppression. Treat CIN promptly and refer suspicious lesions.
